The `payload.summaries ?? []` note at useLibrary.tsx:114 is right too (a string summaries field iterates by character into upsert). Blast-radius numbers corrected below.
findings.reachability: Ordinary user action, no hand-editing of storage required: Profile -> Data Management -> Restore, then pick any JSON file whose top level has a `books` array. Third-party or hand-edited backups, or backups from a future/older schema, all qualify.
findings.blastRadius: The write boundary is 2 lines, but everything downstream consumes what it lets through: 14 non-test `books.*` and 8 non-test `summaries.*` call sites (the finding's '22 / 6' miscounts). Local-first with no server, so a corrupted record is the user's only copy.

plain.title: The storage layer writes whatever it is handed, with no checks of its own
plain.what: All writes are funnelled through one storage module by design, but that module performs no validation. It trusts the shape declared by whoever calls it.
plain.whyItMatters: The backup restore path feeds it a user-picked file, so the one place that could stop bad data reaching permanent storage does not try. Extra fields ride along unnoticed, including the bulky embedded data the project explicitly bans.
plain.whatToDo: Validate and strip records at this single chokepoint, so every writer is covered by one check rather than each one being trusted individually.

findings.title: Three independent Book fields encode the single fact "is this book summarised", and they disagree on how to spell "no"
findings.description: src/types.ts:47-50 encodes one fact — is this book summarised — across three independently-mutable fields that disagree on how absence is spelled: `oneSentenceTakeaway?` and `summaryId?` use undefined, while `readingTimeMinutes` is required and uses a magic 0 (written by useLibrary.tsx:157 for every Goodreads row). Six of the eight combinations are impossible states the compiler cannot reject. Live consequences: BookCard.tsx:89 prints 'Not summarised yet' while BookCard.tsx:95 prints '0 min read' on the same card, and StatsView.tsx:17 folds those zeroes into Total Learning, understating it for Goodreads-imported Finished books. The type weakness is also what let migrate.ts:105-119 persist summaryId without oneSentenceTakeaway and still compile (F043). NOTE: the original finding cited useLibrary.tsx:82-83 as a partial-update write path; that branch is dead code (its only caller always passes a summary whose id already matches), so the live inconsistent producers are migrate.ts:105-119 and useLibrary.tsx:150-160.
findings.verifierNote: Held at high, but one cited write path is wrong and must be replaced. Verified at src/types.ts:41-50: `readingTimeMinutes: number` is required while `oneSentenceTakeaway?` and `summaryId?` are optional, so the three fields that jointly mean 'this book is summarised' disagree on how absence is spelled and 6 of the 8 combinations are representable. The magic-zero claim is right: useLibrary.tsx:150-160 writes `readingTimeMinutes: 0` for every Goodreads row, and GoodreadsRow.status is BookStatus (goodreads.ts:6), so such a book can be 'Finished'. The two-line contradiction is real and I read both: BookCard.tsx:89 narrows the optional and prints 'Not summarised yet' while BookCard.tsx:95 prints '0 min read' on the same card, because a required number has no absent state to narrow — and for a migrated book (F043) the same card prints 'Not summarised yet' next to '12 min read'. What is wrong: the finding's proof that 'no write path is forced to keep them consistent' cites useLibrary.tsx:82-83, which is dead code — saveSummary's only caller is BookDetailPage.tsx:44-47 via BookDetail.tsx:186, which always operates on an existing summary whose id already equals book.summaryId, so the `book.summaryId !== summary.id` branch never runs. The live producer of the inconsistent state is migrate.ts:105-119 (sets summaryId and readingTimeMinutes, omits oneSentenceTakeaway — F043) plus the Goodreads import above; I have swapped the citation. Also softened: StatsView.tsx:17 summing zeroes does not corrupt the total arithmetically, it understates Total Learning for Goodreads-imported Finished books. Severity stays high despite F043 carrying the concrete bug, because this is the type-level cause in the core domain type (33 files import from src/types.ts), it has a different fix from F043, and it covers a second live inconsistency (Goodreads) that F043 does not. The report should present F043 as the instance and F050 as the cause, not as two bugs.
findings.reachability: Two live paths, no hand-editing. (a) Import a Goodreads CSV, then look at the library grid: the card says 'Not summarised yet' and '0 min read' simultaneously (BookCard.tsx:89 and :95), and there is no in-app way to give that book a summary afterwards — books gain summaries only through addBook (AddBookModal, LibraryPage.tsx:91), never for an existing row. (b) Migrate legacy data: the same card says 'Not summarised yet' next to a real reading time (F043).
findings.blastRadius: src/types.ts is imported by 33 files; `Book` flows through 14 non-test `books.*` call sites and every list, card, stats, export and markdown renderer.

plain.title: Three separate book fields try to answer one question, and they disagree about how to say 'no'
plain.what: Whether a book has been summarised is expressed by three independent fields, two of which mark absence by being missing while the third uses a zero. Any combination of them is permitted.
plain.whyItMatters: This is the shared root cause behind the wrong library cards, the wrong statistics, and the controls offered on books that cannot use them. Nothing prevents a new writer from setting one field and forgetting the others.
plain.whatToDo: Fix the shipped data bug first, then collapse the three fields into one tagged shape so the group can only be written together.

findings.title: LibraryExport declares a fully-formed backup shape but is only ever produced by an unchecked cast of a user-supplied file
findings.description: `LibraryExport` is the declared shape of a backup file the user picks off disk. The only place it is constructed from external data is `src/components/ProfileView.tsx:117`, which does `JSON.parse(content) as LibraryExport` with no validation beyond a shallow `Array.isArray(data.books)` check on line 119. Every `Book` and `Summary` inside is then trusted as fully-formed and written straight into IndexedDB by `src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:111` (`bookRepo.create({ ...book, profileId: profile.id })`). The type claims `books: Book[]` and `summaries: Summary[]` are non-optional and that each element has every required `Book` field; the runtime guarantees neither. The author evidently knew this: `useLibrary.tsx:109` and `:114` write `payload.books ?? []` and `payload.summaries ?? []` — nullish-coalescing fallbacks on two fields the type declares non-optional, which TypeScript considers unreachable dead code. That defensive `??` is the tell that the declared type and the real runtime shape have already diverged. Concrete failure: a hand-edited or truncated backup whose books lack `readingTimeMinutes` is written to the `books` store, then `src/components/StatsView.tsx:17` computes `finished.reduce((acc, b) => acc + b.readingTimeMinutes, 0)` and the whole total-reading-time stat becomes `NaN`, while `src/components/BookCard.tsx:95` renders the literal text `undefined min read`. The corruption is persistent — it survives reload because it went into IndexedDB. Correct behaviour: parse the file into `unknown` and run a real validator (a hand-written guard or a schema library) before anything reaches `bookRepo.create`, so `LibraryExport` is only ever obtained by proof rather than by assertion.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present and unchanged. `LibraryExport` at src/types.ts:98-103 declares `books: Book[]` and `summaries: Summary[]` as required, fully-formed arrays. The only external producer is src/components/ProfileView.tsx:117 `const data = JSON.parse(content) as LibraryExport;`. The only guard is src/components/ProfileView.tsx:119 `if (!Array.isArray(data.books))` — a shallow array check on ONE of the two fields; `data.summaries` is never checked at all, and no element of either array is inspected. `data` then flows to `onImportLibrary(data)` (ProfileView.tsx:132) -> `importLibrary` (src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:102-122), which writes elements straight into IndexedDB: `await bookRepo.create({ ...book, profileId: profile.id })` (useLibrary.tsx:111) and `await summaryRepo.upsert(summary)` (useLibrary.tsx:115). I read src/lib/storage/repo.ts:51-61 — `books.create` spreads the input, fills only `id` and `addedAt`, and calls `db.put('books', book)`. There is ZERO field validation anywhere on this path. The discoverer's `??`-tell is real and verified: useLibrary.tsx:109 `for (const book of payload.books ?? [])` and useLibrary.tsx:114 `for (const summary of payload.summaries ?? [])` are nullish fallbacks on two fields the declared type marks non-optional — unreachable by the type, which is the author admitting the type is a fiction. Both downstream consequences reproduce verbatim in current source: src/components/StatsView.tsx:17 `const totalTime = finished.reduce((acc, b) => acc + b.readingTimeMinutes, 0);` yields NaN if any finished book lacks the field, and src/components/BookCard.tsx:95 `{book.readingTimeMinutes} min read` renders the literal text 'undefined min read'. Because the bad record went through `db.put`, the corruption is durable across reloads. Severity `high` is correct per the spec — this is the codebase's only untrusted-file -> IndexedDB ingress, and the spec calls boundary-without-validation 'the most dangerous category'.
findings.reachability: Fully reachable, no gating. Profile page -> Data Management section -> 'Import Data' button (src/components/ProfileView.tsx:334-353) opens a file input with `accept=".json"` (ProfileView.tsx:327-333) wired to `handleImport` (ProfileView.tsx:109). Any user-supplied JSON file — hand-edited, truncated, from an older app version, or crafted — reaches `bookRepo.create` after passing only `Array.isArray(data.books)`. No API key required (the app is explicitly key-free for import/export), so this path is exercised by every user restoring a backup.
findings.blastRadius: Type symbol `LibraryExport` has 6 references (src/types.ts:98, ProfileView.tsx:2/33/34/117, useLibrary.tsx:8/90/103). The real radius is the persisted data: every consumer of `Book` and `Summary` in the app inherits the unvalidated records — BookCard.tsx:89/95, StatsView.tsx:17/20/25, BookDetail.tsx:452/461/470, DailyWisdomModal.tsx:60, markdown.ts:22, prompts.ts:61/81. There is no test file for ProfileView (src/components/ has zero *.test.tsx), so nothing covers this ingress.

plain.title: The backup format is described precisely in the code but never actually verified against a file
plain.what: A detailed description of what a backup file contains exists, but the only place a real file is turned into that description is a bare assumption with no checking.
plain.whyItMatters: The precise description gives false confidence to every reader and every tool: it looks like the shape is guaranteed when in fact nothing has confirmed it.
plain.whatToDo: Prove the shape at the point the file is read, before anything reaches storage.

findings.title: QuizQuestion declares every field required but is populated by an unchecked cast of an LLM response
findings.description: `QuizQuestion` declares all four fields as required. Its only producer is `src/lib/ai/quiz.ts:16`: `const data = JSON.parse(response.text || '{}') as { questions?: QuizQuestion[] }` followed by `return data.questions ?? []` — raw Gemini output, asserted into the domain type with no per-element validation. A responseSchema is passed to the model (`src/lib/ai/schemas.ts:55-83`) but that is a generation hint, not an enforced contract, and it does not run on the client. The codebase already knows this rule and applied it correctly one file over: `src/lib/ai/schemas.ts:85-97` declares `RawBookResponse` with every field optional and the explicit comment 'Every field is optional because a model can always omit one, schema or not'. `QuizQuestion` is the same class of data and did not get the same treatment, so the two AI response types apply opposite discipline to identical risk. Concrete failure: the model omits `options` for one question, `data.questions` still passes the `?? []` guard, and `src/components/QuizModal.tsx:183` maps over `undefined` and throws a TypeError that takes down the quiz modal; if it instead omits `explanation`, the UI renders the string 'undefined' to the user. Correct behaviour: mirror `RawBookResponse` — declare a `RawQuizQuestion` with all fields optional, validate/normalise each element (drop malformed questions, backfill defaults) at the `quiz.ts` boundary, and only then hand out a `QuizQuestion` whose required fields are actually guaranteed.
findings.verifierNote: Confirmed, and the blast radius is materially worse than described — amending the description, not the severity. Pattern verified verbatim: src/types.ts:105-110 declares all four `QuizQuestion` fields required; its sole producer src/lib/ai/quiz.ts:16-17 is `const data = JSON.parse(response.text || '{}') as { questions?: QuizQuestion[] }; return data.questions ?? [];` — a bare assertion over raw Gemini JSON with no per-element check. The QUIZ_SCHEMA at src/lib/ai/schemas.ts:55-83 does mark all four `required`, but it is a generation hint sent to the model, not a client-side validator, exactly as claimed. The in-house counter-example is real and verbatim: src/lib/ai/schemas.ts:85-97 defines `RawBookResponse` with every field optional under the comment 'Every field is optional because a model can always omit one, schema or not', and src/lib/ai/summarize.ts:34 shows the matching normalisation (`data.oneSentenceTakeaway || 'No takeaway available.'`). Two AI response types, opposite discipline, identical risk — confirmed. The render crash is real, at src/components/QuizModal.tsx:182 `{questions[currentQuestionIndex].options.map((option, idx) => {` (the discoverer cited 183; 183 is the `isCorrect` line — one-line drift). WHAT THE DISCOVERER MISSED, and why I am amending: the malformed question is PERSISTED to IndexedDB before/alongside the crash. QuizModal.tsx:50-62 loops every returned question and calls `reviewCards.upsert(newCard({ ..., options: question.options, correctAnswerIndex: question.correctAnswerIndex, explanation: question.explanation }))`. `newCard` (src/lib/srs.ts:22-36) copies `input.options` straight through into a `ReviewCard`, whose `options: string[]` (src/types.ts:88) is also declared required. So a question missing `options` becomes a stored review card with `options: undefined`, and src/features/review/ReviewPage.tsx:93 `{current.options.map((option, index) => {` then throws on every visit to the Review page — permanently, surviving reload, on a page that has nothing to do with quizzes. Note src/features/review/reviewQueue.test.tsx:149 exercises `options: []` but never `undefined`. Severity stays `high`: the ingress is the Gemini boundary and the damage is durable, but I am not promoting to critical because the responseSchema makes omission unlikely in practice and no observed malformed response is on record.
findings.reachability: Fully reachable. Book detail page -> 'Knowledge check' opens QuizModal, whose effect at QuizModal.tsx:41-71 calls `generateBookQuiz(book, summary)` on mount. Requires a Gemini key (AI-gated, per CLAUDE.md), and requires the model to drop a field despite the responseSchema. Once it happens, the review-page corruption needs no further AI call to keep firing.
findings.blastRadius: `QuizQuestion` is referenced at src/types.ts:105, src/lib/ai/quiz.ts:6/16/8, src/components/QuizModal.tsx:4/33. But the persisted radius extends into the `reviewCards` store: QuizModal.tsx:52-61 -> src/lib/srs.ts:22-36 -> src/features/review/ReviewPage.tsx:93 and src/features/review/reviewQueue.ts. Neither QuizModal nor ReviewPage has a test that feeds a malformed question (src/components/ has zero test files).

plain.title: The quiz question format lists every field as required, but nothing enforces that
plain.what: The shared definition of a quiz question says all four of its parts are always present. Its only source is an unchecked assumption about the AI's reply.
plain.whyItMatters: Every consumer, including the permanent review queue, relies on a guarantee that was never established. This is the type-level cause of the review-queue defects reported elsewhere.
plain.whatToDo: Add a separate all-optional shape for what the AI actually returns, and convert to the strict shape only after checking.

findings.title: ReviewCard.correctAnswerIndex has no type-level relation to options, and out-of-range LLM values are persisted permanently
findings.description: ReviewCard.correctAnswerIndex (types.ts:89) has no type-level relation to ReviewCard.options (types.ts:88), and the value arrives unvalidated from Gemini — schemas.ts:69-72 expresses the 0-3 range only as prose, quiz.ts:16 casts JSON.parse output straight to QuizQuestion[], srs.ts:29 copies it verbatim, and QuizModal.tsx:52 persists the card to IndexedDB. An out-of-range index makes the card permanently unanswerable at ReviewPage.tsx:76/94, and because a wrong answer grades 1 the SM-2 scheduler (srs.ts:45-46) resets the interval to one day, so the corrupt card resurfaces every day until the book is deleted. Unvalidated AI ingress plus durable persistence puts this at high.
findings.verifierNote: Confirmed end to end and promoted. types.ts:88-89 places `options: string[]` and `correctAnswerIndex: number` side by side with no expressed relation. The value's origin is Gemini: schemas.ts:69-72 constrains it only with the natural-language description 'Index (0-3) of the correct answer in the options array' (and options only with 'Array of 4 possible answers.'), and quiz.ts:16 takes it off a raw `JSON.parse(response.text || '{}') as { questions?: QuizQuestion[] }` cast. QuizModal.tsx:50-61 then feeds each question straight into srs.ts:22-35 newCard, which copies correctAnswerIndex verbatim at srs.ts:29, and QuizModal.tsx:52 persists the card with reviewCards.upsert. There is no bounds check on any of those five hops. Consumers compare for equality: ReviewPage.tsx:76 `selected === current.correctAnswerIndex` and :94 `index === current.correctAnswerIndex`, plus QuizModal.tsx:78. This satisfies the spec's High bar on two counts — a known-runtime-data ingress with no validation, and durability: the bad index is written to IndexedDB, and because a wrong answer grades 1, scheduleCard (srs.ts:45-46) resets intervalDays to 1, so the unanswerable card returns every single day, permanently.
findings.reachability: Take a quiz on any book with a Gemini key. A model that returns 1-based indices (a classic structured-output failure the schema's prose description does not prevent) yields correctAnswerIndex 4 on a 4-element options array: every option renders un-highlighted, ReviewPage.tsx:76 is false for every choice, the card can never be answered correctly, and it resurfaces daily forever. Only deleting the book (books.remove -> reviewCards.removeByBook, repo.ts:72) clears it.
findings.blastRadius: One ingress (quiz.ts:16) feeding one writer (QuizModal.tsx:52-61 via srs.ts:29) and three consumer sites (ReviewPage.tsx:76, ReviewPage.tsx:94, QuizModal.tsx:78). Every review card in the database originates here.
findings.suggestedPatch: In quiz.ts, replace `return data.questions ?? []` (line 17) with a validating filter: `return (data.questions ?? []).filter((q) => Array.isArray(q.options) && q.options.length > 0 && Number.isInteger(q.correctAnswerIndex) && q.correctAnswerIndex >= 0 && q.correctAnswerIndex < q.options.length)`. Risk: a model returning 1-based indices now produces an empty quiz instead of a broken one, so QuizModal should surface a toast when the filtered list is empty rather than rendering a zero-question quiz.

plain.title: Nothing in the stored review card ties the answer position to the list of options
plain.what: A review card stores its answer choices and the index of the correct one as two unrelated values. There is no rule linking the index to the list it refers to.
plain.whyItMatters: Because the values come straight from the AI without checking, an out-of-range index is stored permanently and makes that card impossible to answer correctly and impossible to remove.
plain.whatToDo: Validate the pair together where the AI output becomes stored data, and consider keeping the correct answer's text rather than its position.

findings.title: no-non-null-assertion is not enabled — 12 unguarded `!` assertions, and nothing stops more being added
findings.description:
`@typescript-eslint/no-non-null-assertion` is not part of `tseslint.configs.recommended` (it lives in the stylistic set) and the `rules` block in `eslint.config.js` does not add it. Confirmed via `--print-config`: the rule resolves to `-- NOT SET --`. The codebase currently carries 12 non-null assertions on 11 lines across 5 files: `src/components/ui/useFocusTrap.ts:47,48` (production — `items[0]!` and `items[items.length - 1]!`), plus 10 in tests (`src/lib/storage/migrate.test.ts` x4, `src/components/ui/toastStore.test.ts` x3, `src/features/review/reviewQueue.test.tsx` x2, `src/features/profile/ProfileContext.test.tsx` x1).

Each `!` is a claim the compiler is forbidden from checking and that crashes at runtime if wrong. The two production ones in `useFocusTrap.ts` sit on a focus-trap path where an empty `items` list is plausible (a dialog rendered before its children mount), and the test ones assert that repository reads returned a row — when that assumption breaks the test fails with an opaque `Cannot read properties of undefined` instead of a clear assertion message.

Correct behaviour: enable the rule (at minimum as `warn`) so the count cannot grow silently, and replace the existing sites with explicit guards or `toBeDefined()` assertions in tests. Adoption cost is trivial — 11 lines. This should land in the same change as L01-F02, because enabling `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` without this rule invites 10 new `!` as the path of least resistance.
findings.evidence:
eslint.config.js — rules block, no non-null-assertion entry
 17      rules: {
 18        'react-hooks/rules-of-hooks': 'error',
 19        'react-hooks/exhaustive-deps': 'warn',
 20        '@typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars': ['error', { argsIgnorePattern: '^_' }],
 21        '@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports': 'error',
 22        'no-console': ['warn', { allow: ['warn', 'error'] }],

$ npx eslint --print-config ...  ->  @typescript-eslint/no-non-null-assertion  -- NOT SET --

12 occurrences / 5 files (ripgrep):
  src/components/ui/useFocusTrap.ts:47   const first = items[0]!;
  src/components/ui/useFocusTrap.ts:48   const last  = items[items.length - 1]!;
  src/lib/storage/migrate.test.ts:93,103,113,116   src/components/ui/toastStore.test.ts:25(x2),30
  src/features/review/reviewQueue.test.tsx:95,112  src/features/profile/ProfileContext.test.tsx:16
findings.verifierNote: The lint-config gap is real; the risk narrative around it is not. VERIFIED TRUE: `@typescript-eslint/no-non-null-assertion` is genuinely not configured — I ran `npx eslint --print-config src/components/ui/useFocusTrap.ts` and the rule resolves to `undefined` (the recommended set only contributes `no-extra-non-null-assertion` and `no-non-null-asserted-optional-chain`). eslint.config.js:17-28 has no entry for it. The count is also exactly right: 12 assertions on 11 lines in 5 files (src/components/ui/useFocusTrap.ts:47,48; src/lib/storage/migrate.test.ts:93,103,113,116; src/components/ui/toastStore.test.ts:25 x2, :30; src/features/review/reviewQueue.test.tsx:95,112; src/features/profile/ProfileContext.test.tsx:16). VERIFIED FALSE — two independent reasons the title's word 'unguarded' and the claim that 'an empty items list is plausible' do not survive a read of the file: (1) src/components/ui/useFocusTrap.ts:45 is `if (items.length === 0) return;`, immediately above the two assertions at lines 47-48. An empty list provably cannot reach them. (2) The assertions are redundant no-ops under this repo's tsconfig. I proved it with the repo's own tsc 6.0.3: with `--strict` alone (matching tsconfig.json, which has no `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`), `const first = items[0]; const t: string = first.tag;` compiles with exit 0; adding `--noUncheckedIndexedAccess` produces `TS18048: 'first' is possibly 'undefined'`. So `items[0]` is already typed `HTMLElement`, and the `!` asserts nothing. That leaves 10 of 12 sites in `*.test.ts(x)` files, where the worst outcome is an opaque 'Cannot read properties of undefined' instead of a clean assertion failure. Nothing here can cause a production incident, which is the spec's own dividing line: `low` is 'worth fixing for hygiene but won't cause incidents'. Amending medium -> low. The forward-looking argument (enable the rule before `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` lands, or 10 new `!` become the path of least resistance) stands and is why this is still worth doing.
findings.reachability: The two production sites are unreachable-when-wrong: useFocusTrap.ts:45 returns before them whenever `items` is empty, and the Tab handler at line 42 only runs on a Tab keypress inside an open dialog. The other 10 sites execute only under Vitest.
findings.blastRadius: 12 assertions / 11 lines / 5 files, of which 10 assertions in 4 files are test-only. Production exposure: 2 assertions in 1 file, both guarded and both no-ops. Enabling the rule as `warn` would surface exactly these 12 and nothing else.
findings.suggestedPatch:
Two-part, both trivial. (1) Add the rule to the `rules` block in eslint.config.js after line 21:

```js
'@typescript-eslint/no-non-null-assertion': 'warn',
```

(2) Because the production pair is redundant, just delete the two `!` — src/components/ui/useFocusTrap.ts:47-48 become:

```ts
const first = items[0];
const last = items[items.length - 1];
```

This typechecks unchanged today (proved above) and the `items.length === 0` guard at line 45 already establishes the invariant. For the 10 test sites, swap `x!.id` for an explicit `expect(x).toBeDefined()` before the read, or narrow with `if (!x) throw new Error(...)`, so a broken repository read fails with a readable message. RISK: if `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is later enabled (a separate finding), useFocusTrap.ts:47-48 will then need real narrowing rather than the deleted `!` — hoist to `const [first] = items; const last = items.at(-1); if (!first || !last) return;`.

plain.title: The rule that bans 'trust me' overrides is not switched on
plain.what: The linter rule that flags forced non-null overrides is not part of the enabled rule set, and nothing else prevents new ones from being added.
plain.whyItMatters: Twelve such overrides exist today, including the two behind the app-wide crash, and the codebase has no guard against the count growing.
plain.whatToDo: Enable the rule as a warning now and as an error once the existing sites are cleaned up.

findings.title: useRouteError() is unknown but is narrowed only by `instanceof Error`, so every 404 renders a generic message
findings.description:
`useRouteError()` is declared `(): unknown` (node_modules/react-router/dist/development/lib/hooks.d.ts:723). At runtime it yields one of two shapes: a thrown `Error`, or react-router's `ErrorResponse`. `ErrorResponseImpl` does NOT extend `Error` — it is a plain class (node_modules/react-router/dist/development/lib/router/utils.js:787 `var ErrorResponseImpl = class { status; statusText; data; ... }`). So `error instanceof Error` is definitively false for the whole `ErrorResponse` arm, and the component silently falls to the generic string.

CONCRETE FAILURE: navigate to any unmatched URL (mistyped path, stale bookmark, shared link with a typo). react-router builds `new ErrorResponseImpl(404, 'Not Found', new Error('No route matches URL "/typo"'), true)` (router.js:2742-2750). Because `routeTable` has exactly one top-level route, `getShortCircuitMatches` (router.js:2721 — `routes.length === 1 ? routes[0] : ...`) attaches that error to the root route, whose `errorElement` is this component (src/app/routes.tsx:16). The user therefore gets 'Something went wrong / An unexpected error occurred.' for a 404, and `status`, `statusText` and `data` are all discarded. Note the route table has no `path: '*'` catch-all, so this is the only 404 surface in the app.

react-router exports the discriminator for exactly this: `isRouteErrorResponse(error): error is ErrorResponse` (lib/router/utils.d.ts:958). It is not imported here. Adding it turns `unknown` into a real two-arm narrow and lets the boundary distinguish 'page not found' from 'the app crashed'.

VERIFIED NEGATIVE worth recording: there is NO `(error as Error).message` cast here. A thrown string, number, `null` or plain object falls to the fallback string rather than crashing the boundary. The `unknown` handling is safe, just incomplete.

BLAST RADIUS: every unmatched URL plus every `Response`/`ErrorResponse` thrown from anywhere in the route tree. `src/app/routing.test.tsx` covers `/`, `/book/:id`, `/stats` and back-navigation but never exercises the error path, so this is untested.
findings.verifierNote: Every link in the chain checks out against the actual react-router build in node_modules. src/app/ErrorBoundary.tsx:5-6 is verbatim as reported: `const error = useRouteError();` then `const message = error instanceof Error ? error.message : 'An unexpected error occurred.';`. `ErrorResponseImpl` really is a plain class with no `extends Error` — node_modules/react-router/dist/development/index-react-server.js:805 reads `var ErrorResponseImpl = class { status; statusText; data; error; internal; constructor(status, statusText, data, internal = false) {...} }`, so `instanceof Error` is definitively false for that entire arm. The 404 path is exactly as described: `handleNavigational404` (lib/router/router.js:1211-1214) calls `getInternalRouterError(404, { pathname })`, which returns `new ErrorResponseImpl(status || 500, 'Not Found', new Error('No route matches URL "<path>"'), true)` (router.js ~2735-2750), and then `getShortCircuitMatches(routesToUse)` (router.js:2720) which begins `let route = routes.length === 1 ? routes[0] : ...`. src/app/routes.tsx:12-26 has exactly one top-level route, so the 404 is attached to it, and that route carries `errorElement: <ErrorBoundary />` (routes.tsx:16). Confirmed there is no `path: '*'` catch-all anywhere in routes.tsx, so this component is the app's only 404 surface. Result: every mistyped URL renders 'Something went wrong / An unexpected error occurred.' while `status` (404), `statusText` ('Not Found') and `data` are discarded. The discriminator exists and is exported: `isRouteErrorResponse(error: any): error is ErrorResponse` (index-react-server.d.ts:999, re-exported from 'react-router' at index.d.ts:44) — and react-router's own default boundary uses it at lib/hooks.js:628 (`isRouteErrorResponse(error) ? `${error.status} ${error.statusText}` : error instanceof Error ? error.message : JSON.stringify(error)`), which is precisely the three-arm narrow this component is missing. The discoverer's VERIFIED NEGATIVE also holds: there is no `(error as Error).message` cast here, so a thrown primitive falls to the fallback string rather than crashing the boundary — the `unknown` handling is safe but incomplete, which is the right characterisation. Test coverage confirmed absent: src/app/routing.test.tsx has 6 `it(...)` blocks (library route, book navigation, back button, stats-by-URL, dark theme, unknown-book-id redirect) and none renders the error boundary. Severity `medium` is right — a reachable, user-visible degradation with no crash or data loss.
findings.reachability: Fully reachable with no gating: type any unmatched path into the address bar, follow a stale bookmark, or open a shared link with a typo. Also fires for any `Response`/`ErrorResponse` thrown from anywhere in the route tree.
findings.blastRadius: One component, but it is the single error surface for the entire route tree (6 routes plus the shell) and the only 404 handler in the app. `useRouteError` is imported exactly once, at src/app/ErrorBoundary.tsx:1.

plain.title: The error screen only recognises one of the two kinds of error the router can hand it
plain.what: The error screen narrows the failure by checking whether it is a standard error object. The router's not-found responses are not one, so they fall through to the generic branch.
plain.whyItMatters: Every unmatched address shows 'An unexpected error occurred' instead of a helpful not-found page.
plain.whatToDo: Use the router's own check for a response-shaped error and add the missing branch.

findings.title: routeTable is exported with no RouteObject[] annotation, which disables excess-property checking on the whole route tree
findings.description:
`export const routeTable = [...]` carries no type annotation. Because the array literal is bound to a variable before it reaches `createBrowserRouter` at line 31, its type loses object-literal freshness, and TypeScript's excess-property check never runs on it. A misspelled route key therefore compiles clean and silently produces a route that does nothing.

EMPIRICALLY VERIFIED with this repo's own compiler (node_modules/.bin/tsc, TypeScript 6.0.3) on an isolated probe reproducing react-router's `RouteObject = IndexRouteObject | NonIndexRouteObject` union (lib/router/utils.d.ts:535-562): the identical literal containing `errorELement` compiles with ZERO errors when the const is unannotated, and errors `TS2561: Object literal may only specify known properties, but 'errorELement' does not exist in type 'NonIndexR'. Did you mean to write 'errorElement'?` the moment the annotation is added. All `BaseRouteObject` members are optional, so nothing else catches the typo either.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY: react-router pairs mutually-exclusive spellings that are easy to confuse — `element`/`Component`, `errorElement`/`ErrorBoundary`, `hydrateFallbackElement`/`HydrateFallback`. Writing `ErrorElement` or `Element` compiles today. If `errorElement` (line 16) were typo'd, the app would ship with no error boundary at all and `src/app/routing.test.tsx` would still pass — it covers `/`, `/book/:id`, `/stats` and back-navigation, never the error path.

NOTE ON CATEGORY: `routeTable` is an exported const, not a function. `untyped-public-function` is the closest enum member; the spec's Scope section explicitly lists 'exported value types' under missing/weak annotations. Re-bucket if the aggregate has a better home.

BLAST RADIUS: the entire route tree — six routes, the shell, and the error boundary. Fix shape is a one-word annotation: `export const routeTable: RouteObject[] = [...]`.
findings.evidence:
12: export const routeTable = [
13:   {
14:     path: '/',
15:     element: <AppShell />,
16:     errorElement: <ErrorBoundary />,
17:     children: [
18:       { index: true, element: <LibraryPage /> },
...
31:   const router = useMemo(() => createBrowserRouter(routeTable), []);
findings.verifierNote: Reproduced independently with this repo's own compiler. src/app/routes.tsx:12 is verbatim `export const routeTable = [` with no annotation, and it is bound to a variable before reaching `createBrowserRouter(routeTable)` at routes.tsx:31 — so object-literal freshness is gone and excess-property checking never runs. I built a probe reproducing react-router's union shape and ran node_modules/.bin/tsc (TypeScript 6.0.3) with `--noEmit --ignoreConfig --strict`: the identical literal containing `errorELement` assigned to an UNANNOTATED const produced zero errors, and the same literal assigned to an annotated `R[]` produced `error TS2561: Object literal may only specify known properties, but 'errorELement' does not exist in type 'R'. Did you mean to write 'errorElement'?`. The discoverer's empirical claim is exactly right. The fix is also confirmed viable end-to-end: `createBrowserRouter(routes: RouteObject[], opts?: DOMRouterOpts): Router` (node_modules/react-router/dist/development/lib/dom/lib.d.ts:525) and `type RouteObject` is publicly exported from 'react-router' (index.d.ts:44). The confusable-key argument is verified in node_modules/react-router/dist/development/lib/router/utils.d.ts: `ErrorBoundary?: React.ComponentType | null` at line 515 is documented 'Mutually exclusive with `errorElement`' (line 513), and `errorElement?: React.ReactNode | null` sits at line 520; the same pattern repeats for `HydrateFallback` (525) / `hydrateFallbackElement` (530). Every `BaseRouteObject` member is optional, so nothing else catches a misspelling. Test coverage confirmed absent for the failure mode: src/app/routing.test.tsx has 6 tests and none exercises the error boundary, so a typo'd `errorElement` would ship green. Keeping `medium`: this is not cosmetic — it is a compiler check that is switched off across the whole route tree, which is precisely the spec's medium definition ('erodes confidence and refactor safety but isn't on a critical path'). CATEGORY CAVEAT stands as the discoverer noted: `routeTable` is an exported const, not a function, so `untyped-public-function` is a forced fit; the spec's Scope section does explicitly list 'exported value types' under missing/weak annotations, so I am leaving the category rather than inventing one.
findings.reachability: No present defect — there is no typo in routes.tsx today. The exposure is prospective: any future edit to the route table can introduce a silently-ignored key that compiles clean, and the most damaging variant (misspelled `errorElement`) would remove the app's only error boundary with no test failure.
findings.blastRadius: The whole route tree: 1 top-level route + 6 children + the shell + the error boundary, all in src/app/routes.tsx:12-26. `routeTable` is exported and consumed at routes.tsx:31 and by src/app/routing.test.tsx.
findings.suggestedPatch:
One-line annotation plus a type-only import (the repo enforces `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports` at eslint.config.js:21). In src/app/routes.tsx line 2 area add:

```tsx
import type { RouteObject } from 'react-router';
```

and change line 12 to:

```tsx
export const routeTable: RouteObject[] = [
```

This restores excess-property checking on all seven route objects, proved above to catch `errorELement` as TS2561. RISK: minimal — `createBrowserRouter` already declares this exact parameter type (lib/dom/lib.d.ts:525), so the annotation cannot narrow anything the call site did not already require; if the annotation surfaces a pre-existing incompatibility, that is a real defect being revealed, not introduced.

plain.title: The route table has no declared type, which switches off typo checking for the whole route tree
plain.what: The list of routes is exported without stating what it is, so the compiler stops checking that its property names are real.
plain.whyItMatters: A misspelled route property compiles cleanly and silently disables whatever it was meant to configure, including the error screen for a whole branch of the app. This was proven with the project's own compiler.
plain.whatToDo: Add the route-array type annotation; it is one line and immediately restores typo checking.

findings.title: Routing test drives an unsummarised book to its detail page and stops one click short of the summary! crash
findings.description: src/app/routing.test.tsx is the repo's only test that mounts the real BookDetail through the router, and its fixture (lines 12-22) creates a book with no summaryId, so BookDetail receives `summary === undefined` — precisely the state in which BookDetail.tsx:534/536's `summary!` assertions are lies. The test navigates there (line 51) but then asserts only `window.location.pathname` (line 53): it never asserts the detail page rendered and never clicks Chat or Quiz. The result is that the entire unsummarised-book detail surface — the default state of every book a user imports from Goodreads — is exercised by the suite without a single assertion, and the Critical crash in F002/F003 ships with a green build. Coverage gap only; the crash itself is F002/F003.
findings.verifierNote: Every factual claim checks out, but the severity is a double-count of F002. Verified: the fixture at src/app/routing.test.tsx:12-22 passes no summaryId, so useBookRoute.ts:21 -> summaries.getByBook() (repo.ts:112-114) resolves to undefined and BookDetailPage.tsx:42 hands `summary={undefined}` down; BookDetailPage.tsx:39-53 never passes `isPreview`, so BookDetail.tsx:337 `{!isPreview && (` is true and both buttons render; BookDetail.tsx:534/536 then pass `summary!`. The test at routing.test.tsx:47-54 asserts only `window.location.pathname` on line 53 and never clicks Chat or Quiz. I also confirmed the crash mechanism the description asserts (chat.ts:15 -> prompts.ts:61, and react-router's RenderErrorBoundary at node_modules/react-router/dist/development/lib/hooks.js:645-673 is a real React class error boundary with getDerivedStateFromError + componentDidCatch, so a throw out of ChatModal's useEffect does reach src/app/ErrorBoundary.tsx). What is wrong is the severity: this finding is a *test-coverage gap*, and a missing assertion cannot itself crash anything. The production defect it masks is already filed as F002 (BookDetail.tsx:534/536) and F003 (ChatModal.tsx:11). Rating this Critical triple-counts one bug across the severity table. Downgraded to Medium: it is the repo's only router-integration test and the gap is exactly where the bug lives, which is genuinely worth fixing, but the impact is 'the suite is green on a broken path', not 'users crash'.
findings.reachability: Not directly user-reachable — this is test code. The masked production path is F002's (Goodreads-import a book -> open it -> click Chat). The coverage gap is what let that path ship green.
findings.blastRadius: 1 test file, 6 tests. src/app/routing.test.tsx is the only test in src/ that mounts BookDetail through the real router (App.tsx:34 -> routes.tsx:19 -> BookDetailPage), so no other suite covers the unsummarised-book detail surface either.

plain.title: The routing test walks up to the crash on unsummarised books and stops one click short
plain.what: The only test that drives a real book page through the router uses a book with no summary, then checks the address bar instead of what the page offers.
plain.whyItMatters: The most damaging defect in this audit sits directly on that test's path and the suite still passes, so the crash could ship again after any refactor.
plain.whatToDo: Extend that test to assert that a book without a summary does not offer the summary-dependent controls.

findings.title: No test navigates to an unmatched URL, so useRouteError()'s unnarrowed unknown silently turns every 404 into a generic error
findings.description: The routing suite's only negative-path test (src/app/routing.test.tsx:94-98) covers `/book/does-not-exist`, a URL that DOES match `book/:id` (routes.tsx:19) and is redirected by useBookRoute.ts:17-19. No test ever visits a URL with no matching route, and routes.tsx:12-26 declares no catch-all `path: '*'`, so react-router raises its own 404 and — via getShortCircuitMatches (react-router/dist/development/lib/router/router.js:150-154) — assigns it to the root route's errorElement. src/app/ErrorBoundary.tsx:5-6 receives it from `useRouteError()`, whose declared return type is `unknown`, and narrows with a single `error instanceof Error`. react-router 8.3.0's ErrorResponseImpl (react-router/dist/development/lib/router/utils.js:787) does NOT extend Error, so that branch is never taken and every unmatched URL renders the generic 'An unexpected error occurred.' under 'Something went wrong' instead of a not-found page. This is the permanent-`unknown` pattern: an unknown crossing a boundary, narrowed once, with the residual arm silently swallowed while the library's own tag check, `isRouteErrorResponse`, goes unused. Severity is Medium rather than High: the outcome is a wrong error message on a typo'd or stale URL, not a crash or data loss, and the recovery links still work — but it will be user-visible once the Phase 4 public demo ships.
findings.verifierNote: Every mechanical claim verified — including the load-bearing one about react-router internals — but the impact is a wrong error message, not a failure, so High is a notch too high. CONFIRMED: src/app/routing.test.tsx:94-98 is the suite's only negative-path test and it covers `/book/does-not-exist`, which DOES match `book/:id` (routes.tsx:19) and is redirected by useBookRoute.ts:17-19 — so it exercises the redirect, not the 404. No test in the file visits an unmatched URL. routes.tsx:12-26 declares no catch-all `path: '*'` (read in full). src/app/ErrorBoundary.tsx:5-6 is verbatim as quoted: `useRouteError()` returns `unknown` and is narrowed by a lone `error instanceof Error`, with `isRouteErrorResponse` — the library's own tag check — unused. The key claim checks out in node_modules: react-router 8.3.0's `ErrorResponseImpl` is declared `var ErrorResponseImpl = class {` at node_modules/react-router/dist/development/lib/router/utils.js:787-802, with NO `extends Error` (it merely stores the Error in a `.error` field at line 799 when constructed from one). And the 404 does route to this boundary: router.js:150-154 calls `getShortCircuitMatches(dataRoutes.activeRoutes)` and sets `initialErrors = { [route.id]: error }`, which for a single-root route table resolves to the root route — the one carrying `errorElement: <ErrorBoundary />` at routes.tsx:16. So `error instanceof Error` is provably false and every unmatched URL renders 'Something went wrong / An unexpected error occurred.' WHY MEDIUM: the user-visible outcome is a generic error page instead of a not-found page. No crash, no data loss, no broken flow — the 'Back to library' link at ErrorBoundary.tsx:18-23 still works. Per the spec's scale that is 'erodes confidence... but isn't on a critical path'. It also, like F001, files a test-coverage gap under the severity of the production defect (which lives at ErrorBoundary.tsx:6, not in the test).
findings.reachability: Fully reachable, low consequence: type or follow any URL with no matching route (e.g. /libary, /settings, a stale deep link) -> react-router raises its internal 404 ErrorResponse -> router.js:150-154 assigns it to the root route -> ErrorBoundary.tsx:6's instanceof check fails -> the generic 'An unexpected error occurred.' renders under 'Something went wrong'. Matters more once the Phase 4 GitHub Pages demo is public and stale links exist.
findings.blastRadius: 1 narrowing site (ErrorBoundary.tsx:6) plus the missing test. That single `instanceof Error` check is the app's only error-message surface, so it swallows the detail of every non-Error thrown value, not just 404s.

plain.title: No test visits an unknown address, so all page-not-found errors show a generic message
plain.what: The error screen only recognises one of the two kinds of failure the router can deliver. Every test that touches it uses an address the router does match.
plain.whyItMatters: Typing or following any unrecognised link produces 'An unexpected error occurred' rather than a proper not-found message, and nothing in the suite notices.
plain.whatToDo: Use the router's own check to recognise a not-found response, add the missing branch, and add the test that visits an unmatched address.

findings.title: handleAiError is typed total over `unknown` but throws on a null or undefined throwable
findings.description:
`handleAiError: (error: unknown) => string` is the contract three feature modules consume through `useShell()` (BookDetailPage.tsx:15, LibraryPage.tsx:19, ReaderPage.tsx:11) plus `AddBookModal` via its `onAiError` prop. The signature promises totality: hand it ANY value, get a string back. The implementation does not deliver that.

The `unknown` is accepted at the boundary and never narrowed anywhere along the chain. AppShell.tsx:48 forwards it verbatim to `toAiError`, which reads a property off it through `statusOf` (src/lib/ai/errors.ts:39-42): `const status = (error as { status?: unknown }).status;`. That assertion has no null guard, so `toAiError(null)` and `toAiError(undefined)` throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'status')` rather than returning an `AiError`.

CONCRETE FAILURE: every call site is inside a `catch` block — LibraryPage.tsx:80, LibraryPage.tsx:98, AddBookModal.tsx:83. A throw from the error handler escapes the catch, propagates out of the render/event path, and unmounts the route into the root ErrorBoundary — which then (per L08-F02) renders 'An unexpected error occurred.' The failure handler becomes the crash.

REACHABILITY CAVEAT — stated honestly: nothing in `src/` throws a non-object (verified by grep for `throw null|undefined|'|"|{|<digit>` and bare `reject()` across src/ — zero hits), and `src/lib/ai/*` already wraps its throws in `toAiError`, so the common paths arrive as `AiError` and short-circuit at errors.ts:46. The trigger is a non-object rejection surfacing from `@google/genai` or `fetch`. Possible, not proven — hence medium, not high.

CORRECT SHAPE: narrow at the boundary. Either `statusOf` guards `typeof error === 'object' && error !== null` before the property read, or `handleAiError` narrows before forwarding. The permanent un-narrowed `unknown` is what lets the lie through.

BLAST RADIUS: four call sites, all in catch blocks, all on AI-feature paths.
findings.verifierNote: The crash is real and I proved it, but the finding is anchored to the wrong file, line and category, and undercounts the blast radius by 4x. Amending all three. WHAT IS TRUE: src/lib/ai/errors.ts:39-42 is `function statusOf(error: unknown): number | undefined { const status = (error as { status?: unknown }).status; return typeof status === 'number' ? status : undefined; }` — an unguarded property read through a bare assertion. I ran the exact logic under node: `statusOf(null)` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'status')` and `statusOf(undefined)` throws the undefined equivalent; string and number inputs return undefined harmlessly. `toAiError` reaches it: for `error = null`, errors.ts:46 (`instanceof AiError`) is false, errors.ts:48 gives `message = String(null) = 'null'`, none of the `quota`/`safety`/`SyntaxError`/`TypeError` branches at errors.ts:53-56 match, so control falls to errors.ts:58 `const status = statusOf(error);` and throws. So the function documented at errors.ts:44 as 'Normalises anything thrown by the Gemini SDK or fetch into an AiError' throws on two of the values in its own declared `unknown` domain — a genuine lying type. src/lib/ai/errors.test.ts covers AiError passthrough, status codes, quota, safety, TypeError-fetch and SyntaxError; it never passes null or undefined. WHAT IS WRONG: the finding is filed against src/app/ShellContext.ts:9 under `unknown-misuse`, but `handleAiError: (error: unknown) => string` is the CORRECT type for a catch-clause value — `unknown` is exactly what the spec says it should be there, and AppShell.tsx:47-56 forwards it faithfully. The defect lives entirely in the assertion at errors.ts:40, so the category is `type-assertion-as-T` and the anchor is src/lib/ai/errors.ts:40. BLAST RADIUS IS 4x LARGER than the claimed 'four call sites': `toAiError` is called from 16 places — 9 inside `src/lib/ai` catch blocks (client.ts:26, chat.ts:18, chat.ts:37, recommend.ts:41, quiz.ts:19, summarize.ts:56, summarize.ts:77, summarize.ts:101, tts.ts:32) and 7 in UI code (AppShell.tsx:48, BookDetail.tsx:169, BookDetail.tsx:189, QuizModal.tsx:65, ChatModal.tsx:72, EReader.tsx:213, ApiKeyDialog.tsx:33). Severity stays `medium`: the discoverer's reachability caveat was honest and correct — I re-checked and nothing in src/ throws a non-object, and every `src/lib/ai/*` path pre-wraps into `AiError` which short-circuits at errors.ts:46, so triggering this needs a non-object rejection escaping @google/genai or fetch. Larger radius but same unproven trigger nets out at medium.
findings.reachability: Not demonstrably reachable from src/ alone. All 9 `src/lib/ai` sites wrap their own throws, so values arriving at `toAiError` are already `AiError` and return at errors.ts:46. The trigger requires @google/genai or the platform to reject with `null`/`undefined`; `fetch` never does, and @google/genai throws Error subclasses. If it did occur, the consequence is severe out of proportion to the cause: every UI call site is inside a `catch` (e.g. AddBookModal.tsx:81-83, LibraryPage.tsx:79-80 and :97-98, QuizModal.tsx:63-65), so the error handler's own throw escapes the catch, unwinds the render/event path and drops the route into the root ErrorBoundary — which then renders the generic message per F054. The failure handler becomes the failure.
findings.blastRadius: 16 `toAiError` call sites across 12 files (9 in src/lib/ai, 7 in UI), plus the 4 `handleAiError`/`onAiError` consumers the discoverer counted (ShellContext.ts:9, AppShell.tsx:47/196, LibraryPage.tsx:19/80/98, AddBookModal.tsx:23/83). Every AI feature in the app funnels through this one function.

plain.title: The shared error handler promises to work on anything but throws on an empty failure
plain.what: The app-wide error handler accepts any thrown value by contract, but the classification underneath it assumes an object.
plain.whyItMatters: Three feature areas and sixteen call sites rely on this handler always returning a message. An empty failure replaces the intended message with a second error instead.
plain.whatToDo: Add the guard once at the source rather than at every call site.

findings.title: AddBookModal gates `priority` on status but not `rating`, so every Want-to-Read book is persisted with a phantom rating of 4 that the export and the status toggle both treat as real
findings.description: CONSTRUCTIBLE IMPOSSIBLE STATE: a Book with `status: 'Want to Read'` and `rating: 4` that the user never rated. `Book.status` decides which of `rating` and `priority` is meaningful — the modal knows this, because it shows the rating input only when `status === 'Finished'` (line 149) and the priority select only otherwise (line 167), and it correctly writes `priority: status === 'Want to Read' ? priority : undefined` (line 75). It then writes `rating` unconditionally on the very next line up (line 74), taking the value straight from `useState(4)` (line 32) — a field the user was never shown. `Book.rating: number` (types.ts:36) records no relationship to `status`, so the compiler cannot see the asymmetry. CONSUMERS THAT MISHANDLE IT: (1) markdown.ts:14 emits `**Rating:** ${book.rating}/5` unconditionally, so both the per-book export (BookDetail.tsx:417) and the whole-library Markdown backup (ProfileView.tsx:89) state 'Rating: 4/5' for books the user has not read. (2) BookDetail.tsx:215 `rating: newStatus === 'Finished' ? book.rating || 5 : book.rating` — marking that book finished keeps the phantom 4 rather than prompting, at which point StatsView.tsx:18-20 folds it into the average rating over finished books, permanently skewing the headline stat with a number the user never entered. BookCard.tsx:97 and BookDetail.tsx:268 both gate the display on `status === 'Finished'`, which is why this is invisible in the UI and only surfaces in the export and after a status flip. DISTINCT FROM PRIOR FINDINGS: F061 is about `rating: 0` conflating 'unrated' with 'rated zero' at StatsView:20, and RT-F008 is about the Goodreads parser's `0` sentinel; this is the opposite failure — a non-zero rating fabricated by the add-book UI for a status where the field has no meaning.
