findings.title: LegacyProfile declares current-app union types for unvalidated JSON, and those values are persisted as a typed Profile
findings.description: migrate.ts:38-44 borrows current-app union types (`favoriteVoice?: VoiceName`) for data that arrives as an unvalidated `JSON.parse(...) as T` assertion (migrate.ts:54-62), and `??` at repo.ts:20-24 substitutes only on nullish, never on a wrong type. The values are then persisted as a typed Profile and consumed by tts.ts:23 (voice name), ProfileView.tsx:281 (editor selection) and ProfileView.tsx:53 (goal division). Same root cause as F044 (same function, same fix); the severe joinedAt->createdAt consequence is filed at F046. The legacy producer declared the identical union, so an off-union value requires hand-edited localStorage.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern confirmed exactly as described: migrate.ts:38-44 declares `favoriteVoice?: VoiceName` (the current five-member app union, imported at line 3) on an interface whose only instantiation is `readJson<LegacyProfile>` at line 89, and readJson is `JSON.parse(raw) as T` (migrate.ts:54-62) — a bare assertion over localStorage JSON with zero validation. The values flow to profiles.create (migrate.ts:90-96) where repo.ts:20-24 uses `??`, which substitutes only on null/undefined. Consumers verified: profile.favoriteVoice -> BookDetailPage.tsx:43 and ReaderPage.tsx:26 -> tts.ts:15 -> tts.ts:23 `prebuiltVoiceConfig: { voiceName: voice }`; ProfileView.tsx:281 compares against the local VOICES list (ProfileView.tsx:10) so an off-list value renders every button unselected; ProfileView.tsx:53 divides finishedCount by profile.monthlyGoal (a non-numeric string yields NaN -> `width: NaN%`). Two reasons to downgrade. (1) Shared root cause: this is the profile arm of the identical `readJson<T>`-assertion + `??`-as-validation defect that F044 files for the book arm, in the same function, fixed by the same patch — F044 carries the high rating for that boundary. (2) Reachability of the mismatch is weak for the fields unique to this finding: the legacy producer was itself a TypeScript app declaring `UserProfile.favoriteVoice: 'Kore' | 'Puck' | 'Zephyr' | 'Charon' | 'Fenrir'` (git show 670b5fe:types.ts) and only ever assigned from the same five-item VOICES array (670b5fe components/ProfileView.tsx:200), and `monthlyGoal` came from `parseInt` whose NaN JSON-stringifies to null, which `??` does catch. So the off-union voice requires hand-edited localStorage, and its consequence is a rejected TTS request plus a cosmetic editor glitch — degraded, not a crash. The finding's one severe consequence (joinedAt -> createdAt) belongs to F046, which I have also corrected.
findings.reachability: Requires hand-edited `booksum_profile_<id>` localStorage (or data from a fork of the legacy app), then any Listen action to hit the TTS rejection. Not reachable from data the legacy app itself wrote.
findings.blastRadius: 9 non-test `profiles.*` call sites (the finding's '26' counts test files and the repo definitions). Profile is a singleton read on the boot path at ProfileContext.tsx:32.

plain.title: Old profile data borrows the current app's strict field types without checking the values
plain.what: The upgrade describes leftover profile data using the current app's restricted value lists, but that data was never validated against them.
plain.whyItMatters: An unrecognised voice or theme value is written into the stored profile, where it silently fails to match anything and leaves the setting apparently blank.
plain.whatToDo: Move the permitted value lists somewhere shared, then check the old values against them before storing.

findings.title: keyInsights/actionableSteps defaulted with ?? [] are declared string[] but a non-array legacy value survives
findings.description: `legacy.keyInsights ?? []` only replaces null/undefined. A legacy record holding a string, an object, or a comma-joined value is written straight into `Summary.keyInsights: string[]`. Consumers call array methods on it with no guard: src/lib/markdown.ts:24-25 does `.length > 0` then `.map(...)` (a string passes the length check and then throws `TypeError: ... .map is not a function`, breaking the export-to-markdown feature), and src/lib/ai/prompts.ts:36, 49, 67 and 82 call `.join(...)` on both fields when building the summarise/deep-dive/TTS prompts, which throws before the AI request is made. `detailedSummary: legacy.detailedSummary` at line 129 is passed with no check at all. Blast radius: every migrated summary; 6 summaries.* call sites plus the markdown export and four prompt builders. Correct behaviour: `Array.isArray(x) ? x.filter(i => typeof i === 'string') : []` at the migration boundary, so the declared string[] is true by construction.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present verbatim at src/lib/storage/migrate.ts:127-129: `keyInsights: legacy.keyInsights ?? []`, `actionableSteps: legacy.actionableSteps ?? []`, `detailedSummary: legacy.detailedSummary` with no check at all. `LegacyBook.keyInsights?: string[]` (migrate.ts:24) is a declaration over `JSON.parse(raw) as T` output (migrate.ts:54-61), so the type is a claim, not a guarantee, and `??` guards nullish only. Consumers verified in current source: src/lib/markdown.ts:24-25 does `summary.keyInsights.length > 0` then `.map(...)` - a string passes the length check and then throws `TypeError: ....map is not a function`, breaking the markdown export - and src/lib/ai/prompts.ts calls `.join(...)` at lines 36, 49, 67, 70 and 82 (one more site than the finding listed), which throws before the AI request is made. Reachability nuance worth recording, measured from the baseline commit: the original app produced these fields under a server-enforced Gemini response schema (`670b5fe:services/geminiService.ts:6-29`, `keyInsights: { type: Type.ARRAY, items: { type: Type.STRING } }`, listed in `required`) and wrote them as `data.keyInsights || []` at :215 and :255, so ordinary legacy records DO hold arrays. The trigger is therefore hand-edited or partially corrupted localStorage rather than the default path - which is precisely why medium, not high, is the right rating. Confirmed as filed; note the overlap with F044 (high, migrate.ts:110), which is the same `??`-guards-nullish-only defect applied to the `books.create` block seven lines earlier.
findings.reachability: Boot path. `migrateLegacyData()` is awaited at src/features/profile/ProfileContext.tsx:31 on first load for any user with `booksum_library_*` keys. A non-array `keyInsights` in that localStorage blob is written straight into `Summary.keyInsights: string[]` and then throws at the first markdown export or the first AI summarise/deep-dive/TTS call for that book.
findings.blastRadius: 1 write site (migrate.ts:122-132) affecting every migrated summary; 6 consumer sites that call array methods without a guard (markdown.ts:24, :25 and prompts.ts:36, 49, 67, 70, 82). `summaries.*` has 6 non-test call sites overall (recounted; the aggregate's blast-radius figures elsewhere were inflated by test files).
findings.suggestedPatch:
Make the declared type true by construction at src/lib/storage/migrate.ts:127:
  const strings = (v: unknown): string[] => (Array.isArray(v) ? v.filter((i): i is string => typeof i === 'string') : []);
  ...
  keyInsights: strings(legacy.keyInsights),
  actionableSteps: strings(legacy.actionableSteps),
  detailedSummary: typeof legacy.detailedSummary === 'string' ? legacy.detailedSummary : undefined,
Risk: none - a well-formed legacy record is unchanged; a malformed one migrates to an empty list instead of poisoning two downstream features.

plain.title: Old insight lists are defaulted in a way that lets non-list values through
plain.what: The upgrade replaces missing insight and step lists with empty ones, but that only handles values that are entirely absent, not values of the wrong kind.
plain.whyItMatters: A stored non-list value then breaks every screen that iterates it, including the book page and the markdown export.
plain.whatToDo: Build the lists by filtering for text rather than by substituting for absence.

findings.title: base64ToBytes is handed a value only declared to be a string, on the unguarded boot path
findings.description: `legacy.pdfData` and `legacy.audioData` are declared `string?` by the LegacyBook interface but originate from the unvalidated JSON.parse of L03-F01. The truthiness guards at lines 135 and 141 filter nullish/empty but not type or content. src/lib/base64.ts:6 then calls `atob(base64)`, which throws `InvalidCharacterError` for any string that is not valid base64 - including a legacy value that was truncated by a localStorage quota failure, which is precisely how large base64 PDFs failed in the original app (CLAUDE.md: 'No binary data in records... This is what broke the original app'). Because migrateLegacyData() is awaited unguarded at ProfileContext.tsx:31 and the MIGRATION_MARKER is only written at line 149, one bad pdfData string permanently blocks app boot - the same brick as L03-F01. Blast radius: one throw aborts the entire migration for every profile, and the partial writes already made are not rolled back. Correct behaviour: check `typeof x === 'string'` plus a base64 shape test (or wrap the decode per-record) so a single unreadable attachment is skipped rather than fatal.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present verbatim: src/lib/storage/migrate.ts:135-145 guards `if (legacy.pdfData)` / `if (legacy.audioData)` - truthiness only, no type or shape check - then calls `base64ToBytes(...)`, and src/lib/base64.ts:5-6 is `export function base64ToBytes(base64: string): Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer> { const binary = atob(base64); ... }`, which throws `InvalidCharacterError` on any non-base64 input. The brick is real and I verified the mechanism end to end: src/features/profile/ProfileContext.tsx:30-42 runs `void (async () => { await migrateLegacyData(); ...; setIsLoading(false); })()` with NO try/catch, so a throw leaves `isLoading` true forever and surfaces as an unhandled rejection; and because `localStorage.setItem(MIGRATION_MARKER, ...)` is only reached at migrate.ts:149, the whole migration retries and fails identically on every subsequent boot, with the partial writes from earlier profiles not rolled back. Reachability nuance, measured from the baseline commit rather than assumed: the original app stored bare base64 (`670b5fe:services/geminiService.ts:262` `pdfData: base64Data`, decoded with `atob(book.pdfData)` at `670b5fe:components/BookDetail.tsx:137`), so ordinary legacy values DO decode. The trigger is a corrupted or hand-edited value rather than the default path. That is what holds this at medium instead of high - and the specific boot-brick consequence is already carried at critical by F007 (migrate.ts:58, the `JSON.parse(raw) as T` ingress). Confirmed as filed; the per-record decode guard is a distinct, cheap fix from F007's.
findings.reachability: First boot of any user carrying `booksum_library_*` localStorage keys, if one attachment string is not valid base64. Outcome: the app never leaves its loading state, and re-launching reproduces it exactly, because the migration marker is never written. Unrecoverable without devtools.
findings.blastRadius: 2 decode sites (migrate.ts:136, :142) on the boot path; one throw aborts the migration for every profile in the loop (migrate.ts:88-147). 4 non-test `blobs.*` call sites overall (BookDetail.tsx:197, useLibrary.tsx:51, migrate.ts:137, :143) - recounted, the baseline's figure of 5 includes repo-internal use.

plain.title: Attachment data from the old app is passed to the decoder on the strength of a declaration alone
plain.what: The attachment fields are declared as text but originate from unchecked leftover storage. The truthiness checks before decoding catch blanks, not wrong types.
plain.whyItMatters: A non-text value reaches the decoder on the startup path, where a failure hangs the app rather than skipping one attachment.
plain.whatToDo: Check the value is text before decoding, and skip the attachment rather than aborting the upgrade.

findings.title: `readJson<T>` is a generic assertion factory: one `as T` that manufactures a fully-trusted type for every caller and hides from any `as`-grep
findings.description: Filed for the assertion-laundering angle only; the boundary/validation aspect of localStorage ingress is owned by another class and is not re-reported here. `readJson<T>(key): T | null` has an entirely unconstrained type parameter whose only binding is `JSON.parse(raw) as T` on line 58. `JSON.parse` returns `any` (confirmed by a compiler-API pass over the repo: it is one of only six expressions in all of src/** whose inferred type is `any`), and the function's sole job is to convert that `any` into whatever the caller names, with no runtime check of any kind. The effect on this audit's own census is the point: the cast count for this file is 1, but the number of unvalidated type claims is the number of call sites — migrate.ts:89 asserts a `LegacyProfile` and migrate.ts:99 asserts a `LegacyBook[]`, and neither line contains the word `as`, so neither appears in any assertion inventory. A helper like this makes the codebase look cleaner than it is and grows the risk silently as callers are added. The values it produces are consumed immediately and structurally: line 99's result is iterated with `for (const legacy of legacyBooks)`, which throws TypeError if the stored JSON was an object rather than an array; line 91 reads `legacyProfile?.name?.trim()`, which throws if `name` was stored as a number. The declared `LegacyBook`/`LegacyProfile` interfaces make every field optional, which reads as careful design but is undermined by the fact that nothing establishes the top-level shape at all.
findings.suggestedPatch: Make the helper honest about what it actually knows and push the assertion to the two sites that can reason about it. Minimal, no new dependency: change the signature to `function readJson(key: string): unknown` (drop the type parameter and the `as T`), then narrow at each caller with a two-line guard — line 99 becomes `const raw = readJson(key); const legacyBooks: LegacyBook[] = Array.isArray(raw) ? raw : [];` and line 89 becomes `const raw = readJson(key); const legacyProfile = (raw && typeof raw === 'object' && !Array.isArray(raw)) ? (raw as LegacyProfile) : null;`. That turns two invisible lies into two visible, greppable assertions each guarded by a real runtime check, converts the current TypeError-on-corrupt-storage into a clean skip, and costs about six lines. Do NOT keep `readJson<T>` and merely rename it — an unconstrained `<T>` over `JSON.parse` is the pattern itself.

plain.title: One generic helper manufactures a trusted type for every leftover-data read at once
plain.what: A single small helper reads leftover browser storage and hands the result back as whatever type the caller asked for, with no checking. It is the only such site in the upgrade code.
plain.whyItMatters: Because the assumption is made inside a generic helper rather than at each call, it does not appear in any search for unsafe conversions, and every caller inherits full confidence in unchecked data.
plain.whatToDo: Have the helper return an unknown value and make each caller prove the shape it needs.

findings.title: The only books.create fixture cannot produce a fat record, so the 'no binary data in records' invariant is unguarded
findings.description: `bookInput()` (repo.test.ts:13) types its overrides as `Partial<Parameters<typeof books.create>[0]>`, so no test in the storage suite exercises a record carrying keys outside `Book`. repo.ts:54-58 spreads and persists caller input verbatim, and TypeScript's excess-property check does not fire on spread-introduced properties (verified with tsc 6.0.3), so the fat-record failure mode the repo exists to prevent is untested. This is the test-coverage view of F048, which files the actual unvalidated producer at ProfileView.tsx:117 / useLibrary.tsx:111.
findings.verifierNote: The mechanics all check out; the severity and framing do not. Verified at src/lib/storage/repo.test.ts:13 that `overrides` is `Partial<Parameters<typeof books.create>[0]>` and is spread at line 24, and it is indeed the sole `books.create` fixture in the file (call sites at lines 49, 50, 59, 68, 90, 103, 116). I independently proved the excess-property-check claim with the repo's own compiler (typescript 6.0.3, `tsc --noEmit --strict --ignoreConfig` on a scratch file): passing a fat object as a *variable* compiles, `{ ...fat }` compiles, `{ ...fat, id: 'b' }` compiles, and only the fresh literal `{ id, title, pdfData }` errors TS2353 — so the spread at useLibrary.tsx:111 genuinely suppresses EPC, and repo.ts:54-58 persists whatever came in. But two things pull this down from high. (1) It is the test-side view of F048: the defect is that the import path (ProfileView.tsx:117 `JSON.parse(content) as LibraryExport`, guarded only by `Array.isArray(data.books)` at line 119) feeds unvalidated objects into repo writes; F048 files that with the actual producer, and a missing test cannot itself corrupt anything. (2) The claim that the fixture type 'forbids' the test is overstated — nothing stops a test from building its own object or casting; the test simply does not exist. That makes this a test-coverage gap, which the severity scale puts below 'the type weakness covers a public API boundary'. Downgraded to medium. I did confirm the coverage claim is true: `npx vitest run src/lib/storage/repo.test.ts` is green and migrate.test.ts:101 (`expect('pdfData' in (atomic as object)).toBe(false)`) is the only runtime guard for the no-binary-data invariant in the whole suite, and it covers the migration path only.
findings.reachability: Not user-reachable — test code. The uncovered production path is F048's: Profile -> Data Management -> Restore, picking a hand-edited or third-party JSON backup.
findings.blastRadius: 1 test file, 8 tests. The uncovered invariant ('no binary data in records', CLAUDE.md) governs the 14 non-test `books.*` call sites.

plain.title: No storage test can produce an oversized record, so the 'no binary data' rule is unguarded
plain.what: The test helper for creating books is typed so that it cannot express a record carrying extra fields. The real risk shape is therefore untestable.
plain.whyItMatters: The project's headline invariant — that large embedded data never lands on a book record — has no test that could fail if it were broken, and the restore path can break it.
plain.whatToDo: Add a test that feeds the real ingress shape rather than widening the helper's type.

findings.title: profiles.list() types getAll output from the DBSchema declaration and immediately calls a string method on it
findings.description: repo.ts:7-10 types `getAll('profiles')` purely from the db.ts:8 DBSchema declaration — idb performs no validation — and immediately calls `a.createdAt.localeCompare(...)` on the result. A non-string createdAt throws TypeError inside ProfileContext.tsx's boot IIFE, which is an unhandled rejection outside any error boundary, so `setIsLoading(false)` never runs and App.tsx:12-18 spins forever. Two limits on reachability the original finding missed: sort never calls the comparator for a single profile (measured), and no in-app producer writes a non-string createdAt — the legacy app declared `joinedAt: string` and only ever wrote `new Date().toISOString()` (670b5fe App.tsx:20), so a corrupt value needs a hand-edited store. Refactor-safety finding, not a live bug.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern confirmed, consequence confirmed, but the 'that is not hypothetical' claim is wrong and the severity has to come down with it. Verified at repo.ts:7-10: `getAll('profiles')` is typed `Profile[]` solely from the db.ts:8 DBSchema declaration, and line 9 calls `a.createdAt.localeCompare(b.createdAt)` with no guard. The consequence chain is real and I checked all of it: ProfileContext.tsx:30-42 runs `void (async () => { ... })()`, so a throw is an unhandled rejection — not caught by src/app/ErrorBoundary.tsx (that is a router errorElement, routes.tsx:16, and the throw is outside render) — and `setIsLoading(false)` at line 41 never runs, so App.tsx:12-18 renders the spinner forever with no in-app recovery. Two corrections, both measured. (1) `Array.prototype.sort` does not invoke the comparator for arrays of length < 2 — I ran it: 0 calls on a 1-element array, 1 call on a 2-element array. So the single-profile boot, which is the overwhelmingly common case, cannot throw here even with a corrupt record; you need >=2 profiles. (2) No in-app producer can write a non-string createdAt. The only writers are repo.ts:24 (`input.createdAt ?? new Date().toISOString()`) fed by migrate.ts:95, and repo.ts:31 fed by ProfileView's editor, which touches only name/bio/monthlyGoal/favoriteVoice/theme. And the legacy producer that migrate.ts:95 reads declared `joinedAt: string` and only ever wrote `new Date().toISOString()` (git show 670b5fe:App.tsx:20 and 670b5fe:components/ProfileView.tsx, which has no joinedAt setter). So the crash requires a hand-edited localStorage profile blob or a hand-edited IndexedDB record, plus a second profile. Downgraded to medium: the unvalidated read boundary and the string method on an unchecked field are genuinely worth fixing (a future writer or an older-schema record makes it live, and the failure mode is a bricked app), but it is refactor-safety, not a live bug.
findings.reachability: Needs two conditions together: >=2 profiles in the store (two legacy user ids at migration time, or the user creating a second profile via ProfilePicker), AND a createdAt that is not a string, which today only a hand-edited `booksum_profile_<id>` localStorage blob or hand-edited IndexedDB record can supply. Given both, the app hangs on App.tsx's spinner with no UI recovery.
findings.blastRadius: 9 non-test `profiles.*` call sites (the finding's '26' counts test files and the repo definitions). profiles.list() is the first storage read the app performs (ProfileContext.tsx:32) and is re-run after create/update/delete (lines 58, 66, 72).

plain.title: Profiles read from the database are sorted using a text operation on an unchecked field
plain.what: The profile list is sorted by calling a text method on a stored timestamp that nothing has verified is text.
plain.whyItMatters: A single malformed stored profile makes the sort throw during startup, and there is no in-app recovery. Reaching this requires a hand-edited store, so the risk is defence-in-depth rather than a live failure.
plain.whatToDo: Check the field is text at the read boundary and fall back to a safe ordering when it is not.

findings.title: books read path returns DBSchema-declared Book[] with no runtime guard; numeric fields are consumed in arithmetic downstream
findings.description: repo.ts:43-49 returns `Book[]` typed purely from the db.ts:9 DBSchema declaration with no runtime guard, and downstream consumers do arithmetic on the numeric fields (StatsView.tsx:17, :20) and date parsing on addedAt (LibraryPage.tsx:61), so a drifted row degrades silently rather than failing. Substantially the read-side view of F048's missing write-boundary validation — same pipe, same architectural fix. Its read-side-only contribution is exposure to rows written by earlier schema versions.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern confirmed at repo.ts:43-49: both `getAllFromIndex('books', 'by-profile', profileId)` and `get('books', id)` are typed from the db.ts:9 DBSchema declaration with no runtime check. Consumers verified: StatsView.tsx:17 `acc + b.readingTimeMinutes`, StatsView.tsx:20 the rating average, LibraryPage.tsx:61 `new Date(b.addedAt).getTime()`. I also found a producer the finding did not cite that strengthens its premise — summarize.ts:52 does `JSON.parse(response.text || '{}') as RawBookResponse` on the Gemini reply and summarize.ts:28-29 applies `data.rating ?? 0` / `data.readingTimeMinutes ?? 5`, so a stringified number in a model response reaches Book.readingTimeMinutes without any hand-editing. So the failure mode is real. The reason this is amended rather than confirmed is duplication: a value can only be READ from this boundary if it was WRITTEN through repo.ts's write side, and every unvalidated writer is already filed — F048 (the import path, with the untrusted user-picked file), F044 (the migration) and the AI ingress above. F047 proposes the same architectural fix as F048 from the other end of the same pipe. Its one genuinely read-side-only contribution is cross-version schema drift: rows written by an older release of the app that the current `Book` interface no longer describes. Downgraded to medium and cross-referenced to F048, which carries the high rating for this boundary.
findings.reachability: Reachable, but only via a producer filed elsewhere: import a hand-edited backup (F048) or migrate a legacy library whose Gemini-sourced readingTimeMinutes was a string (F044), then open /stats — StatsView.tsx:17 renders string concatenation (I measured `0 + '12' + 5 === '0125'`) with no error thrown.
findings.blastRadius: 14 non-test `books.*` call sites (the finding's '22' includes test files). listByProfile is the source for every list view, stats, export and search.

plain.title: Books read from the database are assumed valid, then used directly in arithmetic
plain.what: The book list comes back described exactly as the app's book type, but the database performs no checking of its own. Numeric fields are then added up and dates parsed without inspection.
plain.whyItMatters: A record written by the restore path with wrong-typed fields quietly produces nonsense totals on the statistics screen rather than an error.
plain.whatToDo: Fix this once on the write side, and add a cheap read-side check in the same change.

findings.title: blobs.get trusts record.bytes and record.type verbatim; a non-ArrayBuffer silently produces a corrupt Blob instead of an error
findings.description: repo.ts:142-145 constructs a Blob from `record.bytes` and `record.type` with no runtime check, and `new Blob([nonBlobPart])` stringifies rather than throwing — a `{}` yields a 15-byte '[object Object]' blob carrying a valid application/pdf MIME, which BookDetail.tsx:195-201 opens as a blank tab with no error. Reachability is the correction: the only writer to the blobs store is repo.ts:129-140, which always calls `blob.arrayBuffer()`, so no in-app path can produce a non-ArrayBuffer today; the fake-indexeddb hazard CLAUDE.md documents is already mitigated by storing ArrayBuffer. Defense-in-depth on a flagged conversion boundary, not a live bug.
findings.verifierNote: The pattern and the mechanism are exactly as described; the reachability is not, so it comes down to medium. Verified at repo.ts:142-145: `record.bytes` is ArrayBuffer only because types.ts:78 says so, `record.type` is an unconstrained string, and `new Blob([record.bytes], { type: record.type })` runs with no check. I measured the stringification claim in node: `new Blob([{}], { type: 'application/pdf' })` yields a 15-byte blob whose text is exactly '[object Object]' carrying a legitimate application/pdf MIME — no throw. The consumer is as cited: BookDetail.tsx:195-201 `handleOpenPdf` does createObjectURL + window.open with no validation, so the user would get a broken tab and no error. And the grep holds — there is no instanceof/typeof/Array.isArray check anywhere in src/lib/storage production code. What refutes the severity is the producer side: I grepped every writer to the blobs store and there is exactly one, `blobs.put` at repo.ts:129-140, which unconditionally does `await blob.arrayBuffer()`. The only callers are useLibrary.tsx:51 and migrate.ts:137/143, all passing real Blobs; the library-import path (F048) never touches blobs. So no code path in the app can put a non-ArrayBuffer into `bytes`. The `{}` scenario CLAUDE.md documents is fake-indexeddb collapsing a stored *Blob* — which is precisely why the repo stores ArrayBuffer instead, i.e. the hazard is already mitigated by design. Downgraded to medium: a real unvalidated boundary on a CLAUDE.md-flagged conversion point, worth a cheap assertion because the compiler cannot stop a future writer from breaking it, but not a live bug.
findings.reachability: No in-app producer. Requires a hand-edited IndexedDB record via devtools, or a future code change that writes the blobs store without going through repo.ts:129-140. Given that, the path is Book detail -> Open PDF (BookDetail.tsx:195-201) and the user sees a blank tab with no error.
findings.blastRadius: 5 non-test `blobs.*` call sites (the finding's '17' counts test files). blobs.get is the only read path for both PDF and generated audio.

plain.title: A stored attachment is rebuilt into a file without checking it is really file data
plain.what: Reading an attachment reconstructs it from the stored bytes and type with no verification. The browser's file constructor does not reject bad input; it silently converts it to text.
plain.whyItMatters: Instead of an error, the user gets a small, corrupt file that claims to be a PDF. Only one code path writes attachments today, so this is protective rather than a live failure.
plain.whatToDo: Make the failure loud rather than producing a plausible-looking corrupt file.

findings.title: summaries.getByBook returns an unverified index hit typed Summary, whose array fields are consumed without guards
findings.description: `getFromIndex('summaries', 'by-book', bookId)` is typed `Summary | undefined` from db.ts:10. The undefined half is honest (callers do check it - repo.ts:69-70 and BookDetail both guard), but the Summary half is a declaration, not a check. Whatever is on disk is handed to consumers that immediately call array and string methods on its fields: src/lib/markdown.ts:22-28 and src/lib/ai/prompts.ts:36-82. Records written by summaries.upsert (repo.ts:116, itself unvalidated - see L03-F04) or by the migration (L03-F10) can violate the declared shape, and the mismatch surfaces as a TypeError inside markdown export or prompt construction rather than at the read. Blast radius: 6 summaries.* call sites, feeding the book detail view, the markdown export, the quiz generator and all AI prompt builders. Correct behaviour: validate at this boundary so the failure is attributable to the bad record, not to the consumer three modules away.
findings.verifierNote: Verified. repo.ts:112-114 `getFromIndex('summaries', 'by-book', bookId)` is typed `Summary | undefined` purely by the db.ts:10 store declaration. The undefined half is honestly handled (repo.ts:69-70 `if (summary) await summaries.remove(summary.id)`; BookDetail receives `summary: Summary | undefined` at BookDetail.tsx:119 and guards at line 158). The Summary half is a declaration and nothing checks it, while consumers immediately call array methods on its fields: markdown.ts:24 `summary.keyInsights.length`, :25 `.map`, :27-28 the same for actionableSteps, and prompts.ts uses `summary.keyInsights.join('\n')` in both the detailed-summary and quiz prompts. The ingress that makes this live is the backup import: ProfileView.tsx:119 checks only `Array.isArray(data.books)` and never validates data.summaries, and useLibrary.tsx:114-115 upserts every element verbatim, so a file whose summary rows have `keyInsights` as a string or missing lands in IndexedDB and surfaces later as a TypeError inside the markdown export or a prompt builder — attributed to the exporter, not the bad record. migrate.ts:122-132 is a second, weaker ingress (its `?? []` defaults rescue null/undefined but pass a non-array through).
findings.reachability: Import a backup whose summaries array has a malformed row (or a legacy localStorage record whose keyInsights is not an array) -> summaryRepo.upsert -> later Export as Markdown (ProfileView.tsx:86-94) or a Deep Dive / quiz prompt throws TypeError.
findings.blastRadius: Recounted excluding tests: 6 summaries.* call sites — useLibrary.tsx 48/76/80/92/115 and migrate.ts:122; getByBook specifically has 3 readers (repo.ts:69, useLibrary.tsx:76, useLibrary.tsx:92). Discovery's count of 6 is accurate.
findings.suggestedPatch: Add a local guard beside the store and use it in getByBook: `const isSummary = (v: unknown): v is Summary => typeof v === 'object' && v !== null && typeof (v as Summary).summary === 'string' && Array.isArray((v as Summary).keyInsights) && Array.isArray((v as Summary).actionableSteps);` then `const row = await (await getDb()).getFromIndex(...); return isSummary(row) ? row : undefined;`. Risk: a malformed row now reads as 'no summary' rather than throwing later — log it so the loss is visible.

plain.title: A summary fetched by index is trusted completely, including its list fields
plain.what: Looking up a summary by book returns something described as a complete summary. The database performs no checking, and the list fields are used directly.
plain.whyItMatters: A record written by the restore path with wrong-typed list fields crashes the book page when it is opened.
plain.whatToDo: Add a check next to the store and use it at the read boundary.

findings.title: The stored MIME type is an unconstrained string, uncoupled from BlobKind, and is replayed into a same-origin blob: URL
findings.description: blobs.put writes `type: blob.type` verbatim at line 138 and blobs.get replays it into the reconstructed Blob at line 144. The repo already knows the BlobKind ('pdf' | 'audio-short' | 'audio-long'), so the MIME type is derivable and checkable, yet StoredBlob.type is declared as an open `string` with no relationship to kind - a 'pdf' record can legitimately carry any MIME string as far as the types are concerned. The write source is a user-picked File (src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:51, from the AddBookModal.tsx:232 input whose `accept=".pdf"` is a dialog hint, not enforcement), so blob.type is whatever the browser derived from the chosen file. On read, src/components/BookDetail.tsx:199-200 does `URL.createObjectURL(pdf)` then `window.open(url, '_blank')`; a blob: URL inherits the creating document's origin, so a stored `text/html` type means script executing in the app's origin with access to the Gemini API key that CLAUDE.md keeps in localStorage. Blast radius: 17 blobs.* call sites; the type string is written in exactly one place and read in exactly one place, so the fix is contained. Correct behaviour: derive or allow-list the MIME per BlobKind at the repo boundary instead of round-tripping an unconstrained string.
findings.verifierNote: Verified. repo.ts:129-139 blobs.put writes `type: blob.type` verbatim at line 138 and blobs.get replays it into `new Blob([record.bytes], { type: record.type })` at line 144, while types.ts:71/79 declare `kind: BlobKind` and `type: string` with no relationship — a 'pdf' record may legitimately carry any MIME string. The write source is confirmed as a user-picked File: AddBookModal.tsx:35 holds `File | null`, the accept='.pdf' attribute is a dialog hint only, and useLibrary.tsx:51 forwards it. The consumer chain is as described: BookDetail.tsx:197-200 gets the blob, `URL.createObjectURL(pdf)` (199) and `window.open(url, '_blank')` (200). The security reasoning is technically correct — a blob: URL inherits the creating document's origin, so a stored text/html type means script executing in the app's origin, where the Gemini key lives in localStorage. One reachability gate Discovery omits, which is why I am not promoting this to high: AddBookModal.tsx:59-67 only assigns `pdf = file` (line 66) after `summarizePdf(base64)` (line 65) resolves, so a non-PDF must first be accepted by Gemini as inlineData mimeType application/pdf; and a file merely renamed to .pdf is typed application/pdf by the browser and renders as a PDF, not as HTML.
findings.reachability: User selects an .html (or otherwise HTML-typed) file in the Add Book upload flow, the Gemini call succeeds anyway, the blob is stored with type text/html, and clicking 'Open Original PDF' (BookDetail.tsx:196-200) navigates to a blob: URL in the app's origin. Non-trivial to reach but not blocked by anything in the code.
findings.blastRadius: Recounted excluding tests: 4 blobs.* call sites — BookDetail.tsx:197, useLibrary.tsx:51, migrate.ts:137, migrate.ts:143 (the two migrate writes hardcode correct MIME types).
findings.suggestedPatch: In repo.ts add `const MIME_BY_KIND: Record<BlobKind, string> = { pdf: 'application/pdf', 'audio-short': 'audio/wav', 'audio-long': 'audio/wav' };`, write `type: MIME_BY_KIND[kind]` at line 138 and read `{ type: MIME_BY_KIND[record.kind] }` at line 144, and narrow StoredBlob.type at types.ts:79. Risk: deriving on read as well as write also repairs blobs already stored with a wrong type; nothing else consumes StoredBlob.type.

plain.title: The stored file type is free-form text and is replayed straight back into the browser
plain.what: When an attachment is saved, whatever type the browser reported is stored verbatim, and reading it back reuses that text to reconstruct the file.
plain.whyItMatters: The app already knows what kind of attachment it is, so the stored text adds nothing but does let a wrong value ride back into a same-origin file link.
plain.whatToDo: Derive the type from the attachment kind instead of storing whatever arrived.

findings.title: crypto.randomUUID() is typed as always available but is secure-context-only; every id in the app depends on it
findings.description: This is a platform-API boundary, not one of the `as`-cast cluster the prior findings enumerate. lib.dom declares `Crypto.randomUUID(): \`${string}-${string}-...\`` unconditionally, so the compiler guarantees availability. The runtime does not: `randomUUID` is a secure-context-only API, so on `http://` origins that are not localhost it is `undefined` and the call throws TypeError. That is not a theoretical origin for this app — the README's whole pitch is moving your library between devices, and `vite --host` on a LAN IP over plain http is the standard way to open a local-first app on a phone. In that context the failure is total, because the 5 call sites cover every write in the product: `repo.ts:4` (`newId`, used by profiles.create and books.create), `srs.ts:24` (every review card), `migrate.ts:102` (every migrated summary), `useLibrary.tsx:44` (every summary id) and `toastStore.ts:19` (every toast — so even the error message about the failure cannot render). Creating a profile is the very first action a new user takes, so the app is unusable rather than degraded.

plain.title: Every identifier in the app depends on a browser feature that is not always available
plain.what: New records get their identifiers from a browser function that the compiler treats as always present. It is only available on secure origins.
plain.whyItMatters: Served over plain HTTP from anything other than a local machine — a shared demo, a phone on the same network — creating a profile fails immediately and nothing in the app works.
plain.whatToDo: Route all identifier creation through one small helper with a fallback for when the browser feature is unavailable.

findings.title: ISO-8601 timestamps are bare strings whose format is load-bearing for sorting, and one is piped in unvalidated from localStorage
findings.description: ISO-8601 timestamps across Profile/Book/Summary/ReviewCard are bare strings whose lexicographic ordering is load-bearing (repo.ts:9, repo.ts:88-89), and one of them is fed unvalidated from localStorage: migrate.ts:95 pipes legacyProfile?.joinedAt (obtained through the `JSON.parse as T` assertion at migrate.ts:54-62) into profiles.create, which stores it verbatim at repo.ts:24. A non-string value there makes repo.ts:9 throw on every subsequent profile-list load. The actionable defect is the missing validation at the single migration ingress; branding all five fields is the larger structural fix.
findings.verifierNote: Every cited site verified. types.ts:24 `createdAt: string`, :39 `addedAt`, :40 `finishedAt?`, :62 `generatedAt`, :93 `dueAt` — all bare strings. The lexicographic dependence is real and load-bearing: repo.ts:9 `all.sort((a,b) => a.createdAt.localeCompare(b.createdAt))` and repo.ts:87-89 `.filter(card => card.dueAt <= cutoff).sort((a,b) => a.dueAt.localeCompare(b.dueAt))`, with the assumption written out in the comment at repo.ts:83. The live ingress is confirmed: migrate.ts:95 passes `legacyProfile?.joinedAt` — an arbitrary JSON value obtained through the `JSON.parse(raw) as T` assertion at migrate.ts:54-62 — into profiles.create, and repo.ts:24 stores it verbatim (`input.createdAt ?? new Date().toISOString()`; note `??` rescues null/undefined but not a number or an object). A stored number then makes repo.ts:9 throw 'a.createdAt.localeCompare is not a function' on every profile-list load, durably, and ProfileView.tsx:54 `new Date(profile.createdAt)` renders 'Invalid Date'. Amending the category: the defect that can actually bite is the unvalidated localStorage ingress at one line, not the absence of branding across five fields — branding is the fix shape, not the finding.
findings.reachability: Legacy user with `booksum_profile_<id>` in localStorage whose joinedAt is not a string (hand-edited, or written by an older build as a Date/number). migrateLegacyData runs once on boot (migrate.ts:80-96) -> profiles.create -> IndexedDB. Thereafter profiles.list() throws on every load and the profile picker cannot render.
findings.blastRadius: createdAt is read at repo.ts:9 and ProfileView.tsx:54; the same ISO-sorts-chronologically assumption also carries repo.ts:88-89 for dueAt (which has no external ingress — see F112). One unvalidated producer: migrate.ts:95.
findings.suggestedPatch: At migrate.ts:95: `createdAt: typeof legacyProfile?.joinedAt === 'string' && !Number.isNaN(Date.parse(legacyProfile.joinedAt)) ? legacyProfile.joinedAt : undefined` — repo.ts:24's `?? new Date().toISOString()` then supplies the fallback. Risk: none; a non-ISO legacy joinedAt is replaced by migration time rather than being persisted. Repo-wide `type IsoDate = string & { readonly __iso: unique symbol }` branding is a separate, larger change.

plain.title: Timestamps are plain text whose exact format silently drives sorting
plain.what: Dates across the app are stored as plain text, and two parts of the storage layer depend on that text having a specific format in order to sort correctly. One of those timestamps comes from unchecked leftover storage.
plain.whyItMatters: A differently-formatted timestamp sorts into the wrong position rather than failing, so books and review cards appear in an order that looks arbitrary.
plain.whatToDo: Validate the timestamp at the one place it enters from outside, and make the two sort routines agree on one comparison method.

findings.title: Book.hasPdf is a denormalised copy of blob-store existence that the caller must state twice, unchecked
findings.description: Book.hasPdf (types.ts:51) denormalises 'is there a blobs row keyed ${id}:pdf', and addBook (useLibrary.tsx:41-52) takes the flag and the bytes as two independent arguments it never reconciles. The reachable divergence is the backup round-trip: LibraryExport carries no blobs, yet importLibrary (useLibrary.tsx:109-112) restores rows with hasPdf:true, so BookDetail.tsx:196 renders the 'Open Original PDF' button and handleOpenPdf returns silently at line 198 — a dead control after every restore. Fix by deriving hasPdf inside addBook instead of accepting it from the caller.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present: types.ts:51 `hasPdf: boolean` duplicates the existence of a `${id}:pdf` row in the blobs store, and useLibrary.tsx:41-52 takes the flag on the draft while taking the bytes in a separate `options.pdf` argument, checking neither against the other. AddBookModal.tsx:76/78 does derive both from the same `pdf` local, so the two agree there by convention (note line 76 also overrides the hasPdf that summarize.ts:31 already put on generated.book — the same fact is stated three times on one path). Discovery's stated failure (`addBook({...draft, hasPdf: false}, {pdf: someBlob})`) has no caller. But there IS a reachable divergence Discovery missed, which is why I am keeping this at medium rather than dropping it: LibraryExport (types.ts:98-103) carries books and summaries but no blobs, and importLibrary at useLibrary.tsx:109-112 re-creates each row with `{...book, profileId}` — including `hasPdf: true`. After any backup restore, every PDF book has hasPdf true with no blob row; BookDetail.tsx:196-198 renders the Open-PDF affordance, `blobs.get` returns undefined, and handleOpenPdf returns silently at line 198. A dead button with no error.
findings.reachability: Export a library containing a PDF-backed book (ProfileView.tsx:96-107) then import it (ProfileView.tsx:109-132 -> useLibrary.tsx:102-122). Also reachable on any second device, since backups are the only transfer mechanism in a local-first app.
findings.blastRadius: Five producers of the flag (AddBookModal.tsx:76, summarize.ts:31, migrate.ts:118, useLibrary.tsx:159, importLibrary at useLibrary.tsx:111); one consumer, BookDetail.tsx:196.
findings.suggestedPatch: Remove hasPdf from BookDraft (useLibrary.tsx:10 already Omits four fields — add 'hasPdf') and derive it inside addBook: `bookRepo.create({ ...draft, profileId: profile.id, summaryId, hasPdf: Boolean(options.pdf) })`. In importLibrary set `hasPdf: false` on restored rows: `bookRepo.create({ ...book, profileId: profile.id, hasPdf: false })`. Risk: none to the stored schema — Book.hasPdf stays; AddBookModal.tsx:76 and summarize.ts:31 simply stop asserting it.

plain.title: Whether a book has an attached PDF is recorded separately from the PDF itself
plain.what: A book carries a flag saying it has a PDF, and the actual bytes live elsewhere. The two are supplied independently and never reconciled.
plain.whyItMatters: A restored backup can set the flag with no file behind it, leaving a dead 'Open Original PDF' button that does nothing when clicked.
plain.whatToDo: Derive the flag from whether the file was actually stored, rather than accepting it as a separate input.

findings.title: LibraryExport.version is a literal tag that no consumer ever narrows on, so older backups import as v2
findings.description: LibraryExport.version (types.ts:99) is a literal-typed discriminant that no consumer reads: ProfileView.tsx:117 asserts an arbitrary parsed file straight into the interface and checks only `Array.isArray(data.books)` (line 119), and importLibrary (useLibrary.tsx:102-122) never inspects payload.version before writing every row into IndexedDB via bookRepo.create (line 111) and summaryRepo.upsert (line 115). The defect is an unvalidated file boundary rather than a missing union — the tag is present and unused.
findings.verifierNote: Verified in full. types.ts:99 `version: 2` is a literal, so within the program every LibraryExport is definitionally v2; useLibrary.tsx:94 is the only producer. On the read side ProfileView.tsx:116-117 does `const content = e.target?.result as string; const data = JSON.parse(content) as LibraryExport;` and the sole check is `if (!Array.isArray(data.books))` at line 119 — nothing reads data.version. importLibrary (useLibrary.tsx:102-122) likewise never mentions payload.version; it iterates payload.books and calls bookRepo.create with `{...book, profileId}` (line 111) and upserts payload.summaries verbatim (line 115). So the one field designed as a schema discriminant is load-bearing for nothing, and arbitrary user-supplied JSON reaches IndexedDB after a single Array.isArray check. Recategorising: the operative defect is the unvalidated file boundary, not a missing tag union — the tag exists and is simply unread. Severity medium holds: the app is local-first with no accounts, the user picks their own file, and the damage is garbage rows rather than compromise.
findings.reachability: Profile -> Import backup -> any JSON file with a `books` array passes ProfileView.tsx:119 and every element is written to IndexedDB. A v1 backup (implied by the `version: 2` literal) imports as v2 with no warning; a hand-edited or truncated file imports its rows verbatim, and useLibrary.tsx:114 `for (const summary of payload.summaries ?? [])` throws TypeError on a non-iterable summaries value.
findings.blastRadius: One writer (useLibrary.tsx:94), one reader (ProfileView.tsx:117 -> useLibrary.tsx:102-122); every book and summary row a restore creates.
findings.suggestedPatch: At ProfileView.tsx:117 parse to a wider type first — `const data = JSON.parse(content) as Partial<LibraryExport> & { version?: number }` — then reject early: `if (data.version !== 2 || !Array.isArray(data.books) || !Array.isArray(data.summaries)) { toast.error('That is not a BookSum backup file.'); setImportStatus('error'); return; }`. Risk: files produced before the version field existed would now be rejected — acceptable, and better than silently merging an unknown shape.

plain.title: The backup format has a version number that nothing ever reads
plain.what: Backup files carry a version tag intended to distinguish formats, but the restore path never looks at it.
plain.whyItMatters: A backup written by the original version of the app is imported as though it were current, which is what allows its embedded file data to land on book records.
plain.whatToDo: Read the version first and route older files to a converter or a clear refusal.

findings.title: noUncheckedIndexedAccess is off — 10 real unchecked-index sites, several on rendered UI paths
findings.description:
`strict: true` is set but `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is not, so every array index and index-signature read is typed as `T` when the runtime can produce `undefined`. Measured empirically: `npx tsc --noEmit --noUncheckedIndexedAccess` produces exactly 10 errors across 4 files (baseline is 0).

The worst cluster is `src/components/QuizModal.tsx` (5 errors), where `questions[currentQuestionIndex]` is dereferenced on the render path at lines 178, 182, 183 and 232 and in the click handler at line 78 — e.g. `questions[currentQuestionIndex].correctAnswerIndex`. `questions` is AI-generated content and `currentQuestionIndex` is React state, so the compiler currently cannot prove the pair is in range; a quiz response with fewer questions than expected, or a state update ordering bug, is a `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` in render. `src/components/BookDetail.tsx` (3) and `src/components/AddBookModal.tsx`/`EReader.tsx` (1 each) are the remainder.

Correct behaviour: enable the flag and resolve each site with a narrowing guard or a destructured local, not with `!`. Adoption cost is genuinely low here — 10 errors in 4 files, all in component code, no library or storage churn.

Important interaction: see L01-F04. `@typescript-eslint/no-non-null-assertion` is currently off, so the cheapest way to silence all 10 of these errors is to append `!`, which converts a compile-time gap into a runtime crash. Enable the lint rule in the same change, or this flag makes things worse.

  9      "noUnusedLocals": true,

$ npx tsc --noEmit --noUncheckedIndexedAccess   (10 errors; baseline 0)

  src/components/QuizModal.tsx(178,18): error TS2532: Object is possibly 'undefined'.
  src/components/QuizModal.tsx(182,18): error TS2532: Object is possibly 'undefined'.
  src/components/QuizModal.tsx(183,45): error TS2532: Object is possibly 'undefined'.
  src/components/QuizModal.tsx(232,22): error TS2532: Object is possibly 'undefined'.
  src/components/BookDetail.tsx(71,25): error TS2532: Object is possibly 'undefined'.
  src/components/BookDetail.tsx(79,31): error TS2345: 'string | undefined' not assignable to 'string'.
  src/components/BookDetail.tsx(85,29): error TS2345: 'string | undefined' not assignable to 'string'.
  src/components/AddBookModal.tsx(43,17): error TS2345: 'string | undefined' not assignable.
  src/components/EReader.tsx(395,15): error TS2322: 'string | undefined' not assignable to 'string'.
findings.verifierNote: Re-measured independently: `npx tsc --noEmit --noUncheckedIndexedAccess` emits exactly 10 errors in 4 files against a clean baseline — QuizModal.tsx 78, 178, 182, 183, 232 (5, as claimed); BookDetail.tsx 71, 79, 85 (3, as claimed — note 79/85 rather than the 72 Discovery names, since `const content = headerMatch[2]` is legal and the error lands where content reaches formatInline); EReader.tsx 395 (1); AddBookModal.tsx 43 (1). Zero in src/lib/**. tsconfig.json:8 sets strict:true with no noUncheckedIndexedAccess anywhere in the file (verified lines 1-20). The QuizModal cluster is the dangerous one and the reasoning holds: questions comes from generateBookQuiz (QuizModal.tsx:44 -> quiz.ts:17, AI-generated and possibly empty) while currentQuestionIndex is React state (line 35), so `questions[currentQuestionIndex].correctAnswerIndex` in the click handler at line 78 is unproven. AddBookModal.tsx:42-43 is a second real one: `(reader.result as string).split(',')[1]` is string|undefined and is passed to resolve(), so a data URL without a comma sends undefined into summarizePdf.
findings.reachability: QuizModal.tsx:78 fires on the first option click; it is safe only while questions.length > 0 and the index stays in range, neither of which the compiler can see. The flag itself changes no runtime behaviour — it surfaces these 10 sites.
findings.blastRadius: 10 compile errors across 4 component files; migration cost is bounded and localized, with no impact on src/lib/**.
findings.suggestedPatch: Add `"noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true` to tsconfig.json after line 8 and fix the 10 sites. QuizModal: hoist once per render — `const question = questions[currentQuestionIndex]; if (!question) return null;` — which resolves 178/182/183/232, and read `question` in the handler at 78. BookDetail 71/79/85: destructure the match (`const [, hashes, content] = headerMatch`) or fall back with `?? ''`. AddBookModal 43: `if (!base64) return reject(new Error('Unreadable file'));` before resolve. Risk: EReader.tsx:395 (`content={pages[currentPage]}`) is a genuine bug rather than a formality and must be fixed properly, not silenced with `!`.

plain.title: Array and lookup reads are described as always succeeding, at ten real sites
plain.what: One compiler option that would flag reads which can come back empty is switched off, so ten places are described as definitely producing a value when they may not.
plain.whyItMatters: Several of these are on rendered screens, including the quiz page indexing AI-produced questions by the current position.
plain.whatToDo: Turn the option on and fix the ten measured sites. None of them are in the core library code, which measures completely clean.

findings.title: exactOptionalPropertyTypes is off — 9 sites write explicit `undefined` into `?:` fields persisted to IndexedDB
findings.description:
`exactOptionalPropertyTypes` is not enabled, so a field declared `priority?: Priority` silently accepts an explicit `priority: undefined`. Measured: `npx tsc --noEmit --exactOptionalPropertyTypes` produces exactly 9 errors across 7 files.

This matters more than usual in this codebase because the offending sites are the paths that build records for IndexedDB, where "key absent" and "key present with value undefined" are not the same thing — they differ on `in` checks, `Object.keys` length, structured-clone round-trips, index population, and JSON export shape. The affected producers are `src/lib/storage/migrate.ts` (3 errors: `Profile`, `Book` and `Summary` construction at lines 90, 105, 122), `src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:45` (`summaryId`/`oneSentenceTakeaway`), `src/lib/goodreads.ts:107` (`isbn13`, `dateRead` from CSV), and `src/components/AddBookModal.tsx:70` (`priority`). Two more are in `src/lib/markdown.test.ts` (lines 60, 84) where fixtures pass `personalNotes: undefined` and `summary: undefined` — per the audit spec these are the higher-value ones, because the fixture shape differs from the production record shape the code claims to handle.

Correct behaviour: decide per field whether it is genuinely optional (`?:`, omit the key) or nullable-but-present (`: T | undefined`), then enable the flag. Adoption cost is moderate rather than trivial — it is only 9 errors, but each is a deliberate modelling decision on a persisted type, and `Book`/`Profile`/`Summary` are shared by many consumers.

plain.what: One compiler option is off, so a field marked optional can be written with an explicit empty value rather than being left out entirely.

findings.title: noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature is off, masking a lying `Record<string, string>` on the Google Books boundary
findings.description:
`noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` is not enabled. Measured: `npx tsc --noEmit --noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` produces exactly 5 errors, and all 5 are in one file — `src/lib/covers/googleBooks.ts` lines 19-23.

The flag itself is a style guard, but here it points at a genuine lying type at an external-API boundary. `src/lib/covers/googleBooks.ts:12-14` casts the Google Books response to `{ items?: { volumeInfo?: { imageLinks?: Record<string, string> } }[] }`. Because `imageLinks` is `Record<string, string>`, the compiler believes every key maps to a present `string`. So in the fallback chain at lines 19-23, `links?.extraLarge` is typed `string | undefined` only because `links` itself may be undefined — the compiler considers the `?? links?.large ?? ... ?? links?.smallThumbnail` tail unreachable whenever `links` exists. In reality the Google Books API commonly returns only `thumbnail` and `smallThumbnail`, so the fallbacks are the hot path. The types describe the opposite of the runtime.

Correct behaviour: replace `Record<string, string>` with an explicit optional-keyed interface (`{ extraLarge?: string; large?: string; medium?: string; thumbnail?: string; smallThumbnail?: string }`), which makes the `??` chain honest and makes these 5 errors disappear without enabling anything. Enabling `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` (L01-F02) would independently make the index reads honest, and notably adds zero errors here because the `??` chain already handles undefined. Adoption cost: trivial, one file, one type.
findings.verifierNote: Re-measured: `npx tsc --noEmit --noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` emits exactly 5 errors, all TS4111 at googleBooks.ts 19, 20, 21, 22, 23 — matching the claim precisely. The substance behind the flag is the real finding and it holds: googleBooks.ts:12-14 casts `await response.json()` to `{ items?: { volumeInfo?: { imageLinks?: Record<string, string> } }[] }`, and `Record<string, string>` asserts total key coverage, so when `links` is defined the compiler believes `links.extraLarge` is a `string` and treats the whole `?? links?.large ?? ... ?? links?.smallThumbnail` tail at lines 19-23 as unreachable. The Google Books API in fact commonly returns only smallThumbnail and thumbnail, so the declared type is false at an external-API boundary — the textbook lying type. No live defect: the `??` chain and the `if (url)` guard at line 24 handle the undefined the type denies, and a miss falls through to OpenLibrary and then the local placeholder. Medium is right for a boundary type that is wrong but currently harmless.
findings.reachability: Every cover lookup hits it, so the wrong type is exercised on essentially every request; only the defensive `??` chain keeps it from mattering.
findings.blastRadius: One file, one boundary; fetchGoogleBooksCover has a single consumer in src/lib/covers/index.ts.
findings.suggestedPatch: Replace the cast at googleBooks.ts:13 with `imageLinks?: Partial<Record<'extraLarge' | 'large' | 'medium' | 'thumbnail' | 'smallThumbnail', string>>`. The `??` chain then type-checks as genuinely fallible and the 5 TS4111 errors disappear without enabling the flag. Risk: none — no runtime change, and it documents the API's real optionality.

plain.title: A loose lookup type on the cover service hides that its fallback chain is the normal path
plain.what: The cover response's image links are described as a lookup that always succeeds for any key, which makes the fallback chain look unreachable to the compiler when it is in fact the common case.
plain.whyItMatters: The compiler cannot help maintain the fallback order, and reordering or removing an entry would raise no complaint.
plain.whatToDo: Describe the image links as a small set of optional named fields; that removes all five reported sites without needing the compiler option at all.

findings.title: Indexed access is typed Book but is Book | undefined at runtime; the author's own guard is dead code per the types
findings.description:
`tsconfig.json` sets `strict: true` but not `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, so `targetPool[Math.floor(...)]` at line 70 is typed `Book` when the runtime value is `Book | undefined`. The type is lying — narrowly, but demonstrably.

NO LIVE DEFECT: `targetPool` is provably non-empty here (line 59 returns early on `books.length === 0`, and line 69 falls back to `books` when the Finished filter is empty), and line 71 guards defensively anyway. Reported because it is the clearest concrete instance in this lot of the flag gap the audit should document: the author wrote a runtime guard that the compiler considers unreachable (`!randomBook` is 'always false' under the current type), which is precisely the signal that the declared type does not match reality. If the guard were ever removed as apparent dead code, line 73-74 would pass `undefined` to `setDailyBook` and `randomBook.id` would throw.

Enabling `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` would make the type honest and the guard mandatory. Be honest about cost: it is a repo-wide flag whose blast radius extends well past this lot — scope it as a project decision, not a local fix. Anchored here as a representative instance; the flag itself belongs to whichever lot owns tsconfig.json.
findings.verifierNote: Verified line for line. AppShell.tsx:70 is `const randomBook = targetPool[Math.floor(Math.random() * targetPool.length)];`, typed `Book` under the current config while the runtime value is `Book | undefined`. The self-declared NO LIVE DEFECT is correct: line 59 returns early on `books.length === 0`, line 69 falls back to `books` when the Finished filter is empty, and line 71 `if (!randomBook) return;` guards anyway. One nuance worth recording: this site does not appear among the 10 errors from `tsc --noUncheckedIndexedAccess` — because the guard at 71 narrows before any use, enabling the flag produces no error here, it merely makes the declared type honest and the existing guard load-bearing. So 'the guard is dead code per the types' is true in the sense that the condition is unreachable under the declared type, but TypeScript never reports it. Low is the right tier and the finding is honest about being an illustration rather than a bug.
findings.reachability: Not reachable as a defect today — targetPool is provably non-empty at line 70 and line 71 guards regardless. It becomes a crash only if someone removes the guard as apparent dead code, after which line 74 `randomBook.id` would throw.
findings.blastRadius: 1 site; it is an instance of the tsconfig gap enumerated in F109, not an independent defect.
findings.suggestedPatch: No code change at this site. Adopting noUncheckedIndexedAccess (F109) types randomBook as `Book | undefined`, at which point the existing guard at AppShell.tsx:71 is the compiler-required narrowing rather than defensive noise. Risk: none — the runtime behaviour is unchanged either way.

plain.title: A random book pick is described as always succeeding, and the author's own guard looks redundant
plain.what: Choosing a random book from a list is described as always producing one, so the check the author wrote for the empty case appears unnecessary to the compiler.
plain.whyItMatters: Nothing preserves that guard: a future cleanup that removes 'dead' checks would introduce a real failure on an empty library.
plain.whatToDo: No change needed here; enabling the compiler option makes the existing guard visibly necessary.

findings.title: Route paths and param names are bare strings with no compile-time link to their navigation consumers
findings.description:
Every route path in `routeTable` is an unbranded `string` literal, and every navigation target elsewhere is an independently-written `string`. Nothing connects producer to consumer, so renaming a route is invisible to the compiler.

CONCRETE FAILURE PAIRS:
- `path: 'review'` (line 21) vs `to: '/review'` in `NAV_ITEMS` (src/app/AppShell.tsx:20). Rename either and the nav link compiles fine, then 404s into the ErrorBoundary — which per L08-F02 shows a generic 'Something went wrong' rather than anything diagnostic.
- `path: 'profile'` (line 23) vs `to: '/profile'` (AppShell.tsx:22). Same.
- `path: 'book/:id'` (line 19) vs the template literals `navigate(`/book/${created.id}`)` (AppShell.tsx:194) and `navigate(`/book/${dailyBook.id}`)` (AppShell.tsx:213).
- The param name `:id` (lines 19-20) vs `useParams<{ id: string }>()` (src/features/book/useBookRoute.ts:8). Renaming `:id` to `:bookId` compiles; `id` then comes back `undefined`, `books.find(c => c.id === undefined)` matches nothing, and useBookRoute.ts:18 redirects the user home. A silent bounce to the library instead of a compile error.

Test coverage does not backstop this: src/app/routing.test.tsx exercises `/`, `/book/:id` and `/stats`, but never `/review` or `/profile`, so a rename of either would ship.

Severity is deliberately LOW — this is the well-known ergonomic gap in react-router's untyped mode, not a defect in the code, and the consumer side (useBookRoute) handles the missing param correctly. Fix shape: react-router 8 ships `href()` plus route typegen for exactly this; short of that, a shared `ROUTES` const object with `as const` paths gives producer/consumer a single source of truth.
findings.evidence:
18:       { index: true, element: <LibraryPage /> },
19:       { path: 'book/:id', element: <BookDetailPage /> },
20:       { path: 'book/:id/read', element: <ReaderPage /> },
21:       { path: 'review', element: <ReviewPage /> },
22:       { path: 'stats', element: <StatsPage /> },
23:       { path: 'profile', element: <ProfilePage /> },
findings.verifierNote: Verified. routes.tsx:12-26 declares six routes as bare string literals ('/' at 14, index at 18, 'book/:id' at 19, 'book/:id/read' at 20, 'review' at 21, 'stats' at 22, 'profile' at 23) and nothing links them to their consumers. The claimed pairs all check out: NAV_ITEMS at AppShell.tsx:19-22 writes '/', '/review', '/stats', '/profile' independently; `navigate(`/book/${created.id}`)` at AppShell.tsx:194 and `navigate(`/book/${dailyBook.id}`)` at AppShell.tsx:213; and useBookRoute.ts:8 `useParams<{ id: string }>()` names the ':id' param a second time with no compile-time tie to routes.tsx:19-20. The blast is wider than Discovery states: a repo-wide sweep finds 13 independently hand-written path strings across 8 files (AppShell 107/120/194/213, LibraryPage 96/191, BookDetailPage 36/48/51, ReaderPage 27, ProfilePage 27, StatsPage 9, ErrorBoundary 19, ReviewPage 66). Low is right — a rename produces an immediately visible 404, not silent corruption.
findings.reachability: Rename any route path in routes.tsx and every navigation to it still compiles; the app 404s into ErrorBoundary at runtime. No test asserts the nav-to-route correspondence.
findings.blastRadius: 6 declared routes vs 13 hand-written path strings in 8 files, plus one duplicated param name (':id' vs useParams<{id:string}>).
findings.suggestedPatch: Add src/app/paths.ts: `export const SEGMENTS = { review: 'review', stats: 'stats', profile: 'profile', book: 'book' } as const; export const PATHS = { home: '/', review: `/${SEGMENTS.review}`, stats: `/${SEGMENTS.stats}`, profile: `/${SEGMENTS.profile}`, book: (id: string) => `/${SEGMENTS.book}/${id}`, reader: (id: string) => `/${SEGMENTS.book}/${id}/read` } as const;` and consume it from routeTable (children take the bare segments), NAV_ITEMS and every navigate/to. Risk: routeTable children are relative, so share the segment constants rather than reusing the absolute PATHS strings there.

plain.title: Route addresses are written out separately in every place they are used
plain.what: Each route path is an independently written piece of text with no connection between where it is defined and where it is navigated to.
plain.whyItMatters: Renaming a route is invisible to the compiler, so the app compiles cleanly and produces a not-found page at runtime.
plain.whatToDo: Define the path segments once and build both the routes and the navigation targets from them.

findings.title: `reader.result as string` asserts away `ArrayBuffer | null` at the PDF file boundary, then indexes the split result without a bounds check
findings.description: `(reader.result as string)` at src/components/AddBookModal.tsx:42 narrows `string | ArrayBuffer | null` to `string` by assertion rather than by proof. The assertion is RUNTIME-CORRECT today: `reader.onload` fires only on successful termination (failure fires `onerror`, abort fires `onabort`), and line 46 uses `readAsDataURL`, so `result` is always a string here. The follow-on claim that `.split(',')[1]` can resolve `undefined` is also not reachable — a `readAsDataURL` output always contains the mandatory comma of `data:[<mediatype>][;base64],<data>`, so a zero-byte file yields `''`, not `undefined`. What remains is refactor fragility, not a live defect: the cast's validity depends on the method choice four lines away with no type link between them, so switching to `readAsArrayBuffer` would compile unchanged and crash at runtime, and there is no test on this file to catch it. Downgraded to `low` per the spec's rule that a cast whose runtime value matches is a lower-severity finding.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present, but the runtime value matches the assertion and both claimed failure modes are unreachable — amending medium -> low. Verified verbatim at src/components/AddBookModal.tsx:38-48; line 42 is `const base64 = (reader.result as string).split(',')[1];` and line 46 is `reader.readAsDataURL(file);`. WHY THE CAST IS CURRENTLY TRUE, not merely lucky: `FileReader` fires `load` only on successful termination — a failed read fires `error` and an aborted read fires `abort`, neither of which routes to `reader.onload`. So inside the handler at line 41, `reader.result` is always the `readAsDataURL` string; `ArrayBuffer` and `null` cannot occur. The spec's verification criterion 2 is explicit about this case: 'A perfect match with the cast still loses (could've been a real type), but lower-severity.' THE SECOND CLAIM DOES NOT HOLD EITHER: `.split(',')[1]` is asserted to be `string | undefined` at runtime, but a `readAsDataURL` result is always of the form `data:[<mediatype>][;base64],<data>` — the comma is mandatory, so index 1 always exists. A zero-byte PDF yields `'data:application/pdf;base64,'` and therefore `''`, not `undefined`; the `Promise<string>` contract at line 38 is not violated, and `summarizePdf('')` fails as an ordinary AI error rather than a type crash. WHAT SURVIVES, and why this is still worth fixing: the assertion's validity is load-bearing on the method choice four lines below it, with no type link between them. Swapping line 46 to `readAsArrayBuffer` compiles unchanged and turns line 42 into a runtime TypeError — that is real refactor fragility, but it is the spec's 'worth fixing for hygiene but won't cause incidents', i.e. `low`. Note the file has no test (src/components/ contains zero *.test.tsx), so nothing would catch such a swap.
findings.reachability: The assertion itself never misfires on any reachable path: Add Book -> Upload PDF -> submit calls `convertFileToBase64` (AddBookModal.tsx:64) whose `onload` only runs on a successful `readAsDataURL`. The read-failure path is handled separately by `reader.onerror = reject` (line 45), which passes a `ProgressEvent` into the catch at lines 81-83 and on to `onAiError` — an object, so no downstream crash there either.
findings.blastRadius: One private arrow function, `convertFileToBase64`, with exactly one caller (AddBookModal.tsx:64). Not exported, not reachable from any other module.

plain.title: A file read result is assumed to be text and then split without a bounds check
plain.what: The PDF upload handler assumes the file reader produced text, when it can also produce raw bytes or nothing, and then indexes into the split result without checking.
plain.whyItMatters: The assumption happens to hold today because of how the read is started, but nothing in the code records that dependency, so changing the read method would break it silently.
plain.whatToDo: Narrow the result by checking it rather than asserting it, so the type follows the method used.

findings.title: A file is accepted as "a PDF" on the strength of the browser-reported `File.type` alone, and the advertised 10MB limit is never enforced
findings.description: src/components/AddBookModal.tsx advertises 'Maximum size: 10MB' at line 250 and enforces it nowhere — `handleFileChange` (lines 89-97) checks only `selected.type === 'application/pdf'`, `handleSubmit` (lines 50-87) has no size guard, and the submit button's disabled condition (lines 264-266) checks only loading state and file presence. A grep for `.size`/`1024`/`MAX_` across the add-book path returns no enforcement anywhere in the repo. A 500MB file is therefore accepted, expanded ~1.37x into a base64 data URL and posted to Gemini. Separately, `File.type` is browser-reported rather than content-sniffed, so a renamed file passes the MIME check. Re-scoped and downgraded to `low` as a type-safety finding: no assertion here claims PDF-ness (`file` is honestly `File | null`, and `StoredBlob.kind` at src/types.ts:71 is a store-slot discriminator used to build the `${bookId}:${kind}` primary key at src/lib/storage/repo.ts:126, not a claim about the bytes), so there is no lying type to fix. The proposed `ValidatedPdf` branded wrapper would have exactly one producer and one consumer and is not justified. The unenforced 10MB limit remains a genuine, cheap-to-fix robustness bug; the MIME-sniffing concern belongs to a security/validation audit.
findings.verifierNote:
One of the two claims is a verified real bug, but neither is a type weakness — amending medium -> low and re-scoping. VERIFIED TRUE, and worth keeping: the advertised size limit is not enforced anywhere. src/components/AddBookModal.tsx:250 renders `

Maximum size: 10MB

`; `handleFileChange` (lines 89-97) checks only `selected.type === 'application/pdf'`; `handleSubmit` (lines 50-87) has no size guard; the submit button's `disabled` expression (lines 264-266) checks only `isLoading`, query text and file presence. I grepped `.size`, `1024` and `MAX_` across AddBookModal.tsx and src/features/library/** — the only hit in the entire repo is src/features/library/useLibrary.test.tsx:67, an unrelated blob-storage test. So a 500MB file is accepted, base64'd into memory at ~1.37x by `convertFileToBase64` (line 64) and posted. That is a genuine UI-copy-versus-code contradiction the audit surfaced. ALSO TRUE: `File.type` is browser-reported, not content-sniffed, so a renamed file passes line 91. WHY THIS IS NOT A TYPE-SAFETY FINDING at the claimed severity: nothing in the code asserts PDF-ness into the type system. `file` is honestly typed `File | null` (line 35); `convertFileToBase64(file: File)` (line 38) claims only File-ness; `summarizePdf(base64: string)` claims only string-ness. The `StoredBlob.kind: 'pdf'` at src/types.ts:71 is not a content claim either — I read src/lib/storage/repo.ts:126-140 and `kind` is a store-slot discriminator that composes the primary key `${bookId}:${kind}` and is passed as a literal by the caller (useLibrary.tsx:51), never derived from or checked against the bytes. There is no assertion here that the runtime contradicts, which is the defining test for `boundary-without-validation` per the spec ('typed as T directly via assertion or any'). And the proposed `ValidatedPdf` wrapper would have exactly one producer (line 92) and one consumer (line 64) — no call site exists where a wrong value could arrive and compile, which is precisely the branded-type recommendation the spec warns is 'easy to recommend, hard to retrofit'. Amending to `low`: keep the finding for the unenforced-limit bug, drop the branded-type recommendation, and note the MIME-sniffing concern belongs to a security/validation audit rather than this one.
findings.reachability: The unenforced limit is trivially reachable: Add Book -> Upload PDF -> pick any large `.pdf`. The MIME-spoofing path requires the user to rename a non-PDF and select it themselves — a self-inflicted local action with no privilege boundary crossed (the app is local-first with no server and no accounts per CLAUDE.md), so the security consequence is limited to a wasted Gemini call and an opaque error.
findings.blastRadius: One handler and one form in src/components/AddBookModal.tsx (lines 89-97, 250, 264-266), plus the single downstream write `blobs.put(book.id, 'pdf', options.pdf)` at src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:51. No exported surface, no other producer of the `pdf` blob kind. The file has no test.

plain.title: A file is accepted as a PDF on the browser's word alone, and the advertised size limit is never applied
plain.what: The upload screen displays a ten-megabyte limit and never enforces it, and it decides a file is a PDF purely from the label the browser attached.
plain.whyItMatters: A renamed file is accepted and stored, and an oversized one is read entirely into memory, freezing the tab during encoding.
plain.whatToDo: Enforce the advertised size limit where the file is selected, and check the file's actual leading bytes.

findings.title: A DOM select's string value is asserted into the Priority union that gets persisted and exported
findings.description: `e.target.value` is `string`; asserting it to `Priority` tells the compiler the option list and the union can never diverge. They can: the `<option>` values are hand-written literals three lines below and nothing links them to `Priority`. Adding or renaming an option compiles clean and writes a value outside the union into `Book.priority`, from where it reaches IndexedDB, the exported backup file, and `LibraryPage`'s sort (`priorityScore[a.priority || 'Low'] ?? 1`, which silently scores the unknown value as 1) and `BookCard.getPriorityColor` (whose `default:` branch silently paints it blue). Nothing throws — the wrong value just becomes permanent data. Same shape appears benignly at BookDetail.tsx:299 and EReader.tsx:319, which assert a literal array rather than a runtime string and so are safe.

...

Export `export const PRIORITIES = ['Low','Medium','High'] as const satisfies readonly Priority[];` from src/types.ts, render `{PRIORITIES.map(p => <option key={p} value={p}>{p}</option>)}`, and narrow on change: `const next = e.target.value; if (PRIORITIES.includes(next as Priority)) setPriority(next as Priority);`. Better still, `<select>` accepts a typed handler if you keep the array as the single source — the assertion then has a runtime check behind it. Risk: none; the rendered markup is identical.

plain.title: A dropdown's raw text value is assumed to be one of three valid priorities
plain.what: The priority dropdown's selected text is assumed to be one of the three valid priority values. The option list is written out separately just below and nothing links the two.
plain.whyItMatters: Adding or renaming an option compiles cleanly and writes a value outside the valid set into permanent storage and into exports.
