It also quietly shadows the ES2022 `Error.cause` that `AiError` inherits, while `super(message)` never forwards it, so `err.cause` reaching a devtools console or a future structured logger is populated by the subclass field rather than by the standard mechanism — an inconsistency nobody can currently notice because there are no readers. Severity is low because there is no runtime hazard; the cost is that the original SDK error is captured and then unreachable, and that the field's type gives a future reader no information about what it might hold.
findings.suggestedPatch: Pick one and commit to it. (a) If the cause is wanted for diagnosis, stop declaring a shadow field and use the standard channel — drop the parameter property and call `super(message, { cause })`, which inherits `Error.cause` and is what devtools, `console.error` and any future logger already understand; then narrow at the single point of use with `error.cause instanceof Error ? error.cause.message : String(error.cause)`. (b) If it is genuinely unused, delete the parameter and the argument at line 63. Do not leave it as `unknown` with no readers — that is the exact state the spec calls out as 'same as any plus extra ceremony'. Option (a) is preferable given `toAiError` collapses eight distinct SDK failure modes into one of eight canned strings; the original message is the only way to tell them apart when a user reports 'Something went wrong talking to Gemini'.

plain.title: Every AI failure captures its underlying cause, and nothing ever reads it
plain.what: The app's error type carries an untyped slot for the original underlying failure and faithfully fills it in every time. No code anywhere reads it.
plain.whyItMatters: Diagnostic information is collected at every failure and thrown away, while the untyped slot suggests it is available for use.
plain.whatToDo: Either use the standard error-cause channel so debuggers can display it, or remove the field.

findings.title: User-controlled book titles are interpolated raw into the prompt that defines the requested output shape
findings.description: recommend.ts:20-22 builds the prompt fragment from unescaped, uncapped user-imported `title`/`author`/`category`, and prompts.ts:39-42 interpolates it directly above the sentence that defines the requested output shape; the same raw interpolation appears at prompts.ts:24, :45, :56 and :79. `Book.title` etc. are plain `string` (types.ts:31-33), with no distinction between 'display text' and 'text that steers a request contract'. In a local-first, single-user, no-server app this crosses no privilege boundary - the only party who can inject is the party who receives the output - so treat it as hygiene (escape newlines, cap length, cap the number of books to bound prompt size) and keep validation at the parse site as the real defence.
findings.verifierNote: The mechanics are exactly as described - prompts.ts:39-42 interpolates `booksList` raw, recommend.ts:20-22 builds it from unescaped, uncapped `b.title` / `b.author` / `b.category`, and the same raw interpolation occurs at prompts.ts:24, :45, :56 and :79, several of which also embed prior model output (`summary.summary`, `summary.keyInsights`). The verified negative is accurate too: prompts.ts has no assertions, no `!`, and :79's `type: 'short' | 'long'` is a proper literal union. But medium under boundary-without-validation overstates it on two counts. (1) Category: nothing external is being TYPED here - data flows OUT of typed code into a string, so no type is claiming correctness the runtime cannot deliver. The argument the finding actually makes ('a string that controls a request's output contract is interchangeable with a display string') is a branded-type argument, and the spec explicitly warns those belong only where the foot-gun cost is real. (2) Cost: BookSum is local-first with no server, no accounts and no other party's data - the 'attacker' supplies their own CSV and their own API key, so a crafted title can only steer the model into returning junk to the user who wrote it, and there is no exfiltration channel. The real defence the finding itself names - validating at the parse site - is already filed separately (the unvalidated Recommendation cast). Amended to low with the category corrected.
findings.reachability: A user imports a Goodreads CSV whose title field contains instructions, then refreshes recommendations. The steered response reaches the consumer as a typed `Recommendation[]`. No privilege boundary is crossed - the only affected party is the author of the input.
findings.blastRadius: 5 prompt builders (prompts.ts:24, :39, :45, :56, :79) fed by 1 unescaped join (recommend.ts:20-22).
findings.suggestedPatch: Cheapest effective step, in recommend.ts:20-22 rather than in every builder: `const clean = (s: string) => s.replace(/[\r\n]+/g, ' ').slice(0, 120); const booksList = userBooks.slice(0, 100).map((b) => `"${clean(b.title)}" by ${clean(b.author)} (${clean(b.category)})`).join(', ');`. The slice(0, 100) also caps prompt size for large imported libraries, which is the more likely real-world problem. Risk: truncation changes recommendation quality for very long titles - acceptable; keep the parse-site validation as the actual defence.

plain.title: Imported book titles are placed into AI prompts exactly as they arrived
plain.what: Titles and authors imported from a spreadsheet are inserted straight into the prompt text, directly above the instructions describing the expected reply.
plain.whyItMatters: In this local, single-user app no privilege boundary is crossed, so the practical impact is limited to derailed or wasted recommendations rather than a security issue.
plain.whatToDo: Strip line breaks and cap the length where the prompt fragment is assembled.

findings.title: pcmToWavBlob stamps a hardcoded 24kHz/mono/16-bit header on unvalidated Gemini bytes while discarding the mimeType the API actually returns
findings.description: Duplicate of F081 filed against the consumer file. src/lib/audio/wav.ts:12 encodes a 24kHz/mono/16-bit format contract in module constants (lines 1-3) that its `Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` parameter type cannot express, and stamps it unconditionally into the RIFF header at lines 23-27. The bytes are unvalidated Gemini output, but the field that would validate them (`inlineData.mimeType`) is discarded upstream at src/lib/ai/tts.ts:27, which is where the fix belongs. wav.ts has one non-test caller, its header arithmetic is verified correct against the RIFF spec, and it contains no type assertions or non-null assertions. Track as the consumer half of F081; do not count as a second medium.
findings.verifierNote: The pattern is present exactly as described: src/lib/audio/wav.ts:1-3 declares SAMPLE_RATE/NUM_CHANNELS/BITS_PER_SAMPLE as module constants and :12 takes `pcm: Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` carrying no format information. I re-checked the header arithmetic against the RIFF/WAVE spec and the finding's verified-negative holds: 'RIFF'@0, 36+len@4, 'WAVE'@8, 'fmt '@12, 16@16, 1@20, 1@22, 24000@24, 48000@28, 2@32, 16@34, 'data'@36, len@40, all little-endian. But this is the CONSUMER HALF of F081, not an independent defect: the discarded `mimeType` lives in tts.ts:27 and the only way to fix wav.ts is for tts.ts to pass the parsed format in. Counting it twice at medium double-weights one defect. wav.ts itself is an honest, correctly documented pure function (JSDoc at :11 states its contract), contains no assertions or non-null assertions, and has exactly one non-test caller. The one genuinely independent claim - that an odd `pcm.length` yields a data chunk that is not a multiple of blockAlign - is arithmetically true but has no producer that can emit it (16-bit PCM is always even-length) and no consequence beyond a truncated final frame.
findings.reachability: Same single path as F081 (tts.ts:30). No independent reachability: `pcmToWavBlob` is exported but has no other production importer.
findings.blastRadius: 1 non-test call site (src/lib/ai/tts.ts:30), plus src/lib/audio/wav.test.ts. Strictly smaller than F081's.
findings.suggestedPatch:
Fix once, at F081's site. If wav.ts is touched at all, widen the signature rather than adding a second validation layer:
  export function pcmToWavBlob(pcm: Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>, sampleRate = SAMPLE_RATE, channels = NUM_CHANNELS): Blob
and write those into the header instead of the constants. Risk: none to existing callers - both parameters default to today's values.

plain.title: A fixed audio format is stamped onto bytes whose real format was discarded
plain.what: The routine that builds a playable audio file encodes a specific sample rate and bit depth as constants, and its input carries no information about what format the bytes actually are.
plain.whyItMatters: This is the same defect as the discarded format label, seen from the other side. Fixing it once at the source covers both.
plain.whatToDo: Fix it where the format label is thrown away; if this routine is touched, widen it to accept the format rather than assuming.

findings.title: Redundant `bytes[i] as number` pre-suppresses exactly the check noUncheckedIndexedAccess would add
findings.description:
Under the current `tsconfig.json` (strict: true, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` NOT set), indexing a `Uint8Array` already yields `number` via its numeric index signature, so `as number` is a no-op assertion that the compiler does not need. It is not currently hiding a bug — the loop bound `i < bytes.length` makes every index provably in range.

It matters for a specific forward-looking reason that is squarely this audit's concern: if `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is enabled (a likely structural recommendation for this repo, since it is otherwise clean under strict), this cast is precisely the construct that would make the new flag a silent no-op at this site instead of surfacing the indexed-access question. A cast that exists only to pre-empt a strictness flag is indistinguishable from one that is masking a real out-of-bounds read, and a reviewer cannot tell them apart without re-deriving the loop bound.

Correct fix shape: delete the assertion (it is unnecessary today), and if `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is later enabled, restructure the loop with `for (const byte of bytes)` so the element type is `number` without any assertion.

Blast radius: one line, internal to this module. `bytesToBase64` itself has no production caller — grep shows it is imported only by `src/lib/base64.test.ts`.
findings.verifierNote: Present verbatim at base64.ts:17 `binary += String.fromCharCode(bytes[i] as number);`. Under the current tsconfig, `Uint8Array`'s numeric index signature already yields `number`, so the assertion is a no-op the compiler does not need, and the loop bound at :16 (`i < bytes.length`) makes every index provably in range - so it is masking nothing today. It is a real instance of the audit's concern all the same: a cast whose only effect is to pre-empt `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is indistinguishable, on review, from one masking a genuine out-of-bounds read. Blast radius re-verified by grep: `bytesToBase64` is imported only by src/lib/base64.test.ts (:2, :7) and has zero production callers, which is why `low` is right.
findings.reachability: Test-only today (the base64.test.ts round-trip). `base64ToBytes`, the sibling that does have a production caller via migrate.ts:136, contains no such cast.
findings.blastRadius: 1 line, 1 module, 0 production call sites.
findings.suggestedPatch: Restructure the loop so no assertion is needed under any flag: `for (const byte of bytes) binary += String.fromCharCode(byte);` replacing :16-18. Risk: none - `target: ES2022` with `lib: ["ES2022", "DOM", ...]` supports iterating a TypedArray directly, and iteration order is identical.

plain.title: An override in the encoding loop pre-suppresses a check that is not yet enabled
plain.what: A value in the byte loop is forced past a warning that the compiler is not currently issuing, so the override does nothing today.
plain.whyItMatters: Enabling the relevant compiler option later would find this site already silenced, defeating the point of turning it on.
plain.whatToDo: Restructure the loop so no override is needed under any configuration.

findings.title: relativeLuminance accepts any string and returns NaN or a plausible wrong number, defeating the project's own WCAG guardrail
findings.description: src/lib/contrast.ts:8 `relativeLuminance(hex: string): number` accepts any string and its `number` return type is a lie for unparseable input: verified at runtime, 'white'/''/'rgb(...)'/'#f00a' all yield NaN, and a 5-digit typo '#12345' yields a confident wrong luminance (0.0260) and wrong ratio (1.519) with no signal. Because `NaN < 4.5` is false, a guard written in the natural direction silently passes. The WCAG maths itself is verified correct. Lowered to low because the module has no production caller whatsoever - src/lib/contrast.test.ts is its only importer - so no incident is reachable today.
findings.verifierNote: Every runtime claim reproduces. I ran the exact implementation from src/lib/contrast.ts:8-23: 'white' -> NaN, '' -> NaN, 'rgb(255,255,255)' -> NaN, '#f00a' -> NaN, and the silent-wrong-value case '#12345' -> luminance 0.02595538497129003 with contrastRatio('#12345','#000000') = 1.5191076994258006. The WCAG maths is correct (#000000 vs #ffffff = exactly 21) and `NaN < 4.5` is `false`, so a guard written in the natural direction silently passes. All true. What does not hold at medium is impact: I grepped the whole tree and src/lib/contrast.ts is imported by exactly one file, src/lib/contrast.test.ts. There is ZERO production call site, so there is no path on which a wrong value can arrive and compile - the bar this batch was told to apply to branded-type findings. Per the spec's scale that is 'worth fixing for hygiene but won't cause incidents', i.e. low. The finding's own text already concedes the module has no production caller, so the severity was set above what its evidence supports.
findings.reachability: Not reachable from the running app. Only src/lib/contrast.test.ts imports it, and Vitest's toBeGreaterThanOrEqual/toBeLessThan both fail on NaN, so a NaN would be caught today. The '#12345' silent-wrong-number case would NOT be caught by a test that only asserts a threshold. Re-rate to medium if a production caller ever lands, which CLAUDE.md invites ('use it when changing colours').
findings.blastRadius: 1 importer, and it is a test file. 0 production call sites (verified by grep over src/).

plain.title: The project's own contrast checker returns a plausible wrong number for unparseable colours
plain.what: The colour helper accepts any text and always returns a number. For values it cannot parse it returns either a nonsense number or one derived from partial input.
plain.whyItMatters: The helper exists specifically to prove colour choices meet accessibility standards, so a silently wrong result defeats the guardrail it was written to provide.
plain.whatToDo: Make the parse explicit and report failure rather than returning a number that looks valid.

findings.title: mockFetch types every API fixture as unknown, so no fixture is checked against the as-asserted response shapes
findings.description: `mockFetch` (src/lib/covers/index.test.ts:5) types its handler's return as `unknown`, so none of the response fixtures (lines 24, 36, 46) is checked against the `as`-asserted shapes at googleBooks.ts:12-14 and openLibrary.ts:6, and drift between fixture and assertion is undetectable in either direction. No fixture exercises `items: [{}]`, `docs: [{}]`, an `imageLinks` object lacking `large`, or a 200 with a non-JSON body. Severity lowered to low: this is the test mirror of F085/F086 (both medium — a test mirror should not outrank its producers), and every untested path is absorbed by the `try/catch {}` in src/lib/covers/index.ts:13-21, whose worst outcome is a locally generated placeholder cover rather than a crash or a bad write. (Minor correction: the code uses `links?.extraLarge`, so the expression already types as `string | undefined`; the `Record<string, string>` index-signature lie is tracked as F111.)
findings.verifierNote: Claims verified: src/lib/covers/index.test.ts:5 is `function mockFetch(handler: (url: string) => unknown)`, so the fixtures at :24 (`{ items: [{ volumeInfo: { imageLinks: { large } } }] }`), :36 (`{ docs: [{ cover_i: 12345 }] }`) and :46 are never checked against the assertions at googleBooks.ts:12-14 and openLibrary.ts:6; no fixture supplies `items: [{}]`, `docs: [{}]`, an `imageLinks` lacking `large`, or a non-JSON 200 body. AMENDED DOWN two steps to low, for three reasons. (1) Inverted ranking: the production-side findings this mirrors — F085 (googleBooks.ts:12) and F086 (openLibrary.ts:6) — are both `medium`, and F111 already carries the `Record<string, string>` lie; a test mirror cannot outrank its producers. (2) Blast radius is cosmetic and fully absorbed: src/lib/covers/index.ts:13-21 wraps both lookups in `try { ... } catch {}` and returns `placeholderCover(title)`, so every untested path — malformed body, missing `imageLinks` key, missing `cover_i` — degrades to a locally generated SVG placeholder. No crash, no persistence, no data corruption; the worst outcome is a book showing initials instead of a cover. (3) Minor imprecision in the write-up: the code reads `links?.extraLarge` (googleBooks.ts:19), so the expression type is already `string | undefined` via the optional chain; the index-signature lie is real but is F111's finding, not this one. I am deliberately not applying a reflexive test-file downgrade — the spec warns against that — but the severity scale explicitly places weak types in test fixtures at low when the blast radius is cosmetic, and here it is.

findings.title: Truthy check on a numeric cover id conflates absent with zero
findings.description: `coverId` is `number | undefined` and openLibrary.ts:8 tests it with a bare truthy check, so a cover id of `0` is treated as absent. The pattern is a genuine numeric-truthiness smell and the one-token fix is worth taking, but the user-visible failure originally claimed is not realizable: OpenLibrary cover ids are positive, and `fetchCover` (covers/index.ts:12-22) already maps a `null` return and a 404 image to the same `placeholderCover` outcome. Hygiene only.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present at openLibrary.ts:7-8: `const coverId = data.docs?.[0]?.cover_i;` then `return coverId ? ... : null;` on a value declared `number | undefined`. That is textbook numeric truthiness and the category is right. The CONCRETE FAILURE claim does not survive, which is why this is amended down to hygiene-only: for `cover_i === 0` to cost the user a real cover, id 0 would have to address a real image in OpenLibrary's cover-id space, which is a positive auto-increment - and even if such a record existed, I traced the consumer: `fetchCover` (covers/index.ts:12-22) treats a falsy return identically to a thrown error and falls through to `placeholderCover(title)`, which is the same tile a 404 on `/b/id/0-L.jpg` would produce after BookCard's `onError` swap. The two paths are indistinguishable to the user, so there is no realizable degradation - just an expression that asks the wrong question. The finding's own note that googleBooks.ts:24's `if (url)` on a `string` is fine is correct (I read :18-28; the empty-string case is desirable there).
findings.reachability: Called from `fetchCover` on every cover lookup that Google Books misses. Reached often; the falsy-zero branch is not reachable with real OpenLibrary data.
findings.blastRadius: 1 expression, 1 module, 1 caller (covers/index.ts:13).
findings.suggestedPatch: openLibrary.ts:8 -> `return typeof coverId === 'number' ? `https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/${coverId}-L.jpg` : null;`. Risk: none, and it additionally rejects a non-number `cover_i` arriving from the unvalidated `as` cast at :6.

findings.title: downloadText takes three adjacent bare-string positional params, so swapping filename and contents compiles cleanly
findings.description:
`downloadText(filename: string, contents: string, mimeType = 'text/markdown')` has three same-typed positional parameters where order is entirely load-bearing and the compiler cannot distinguish them. `downloadText(markdown, filename)` type-checks and silently produces a download whose filename is the entire markdown body (browsers truncate/sanitise it) containing the filename as its content. This is the classic branded-type foot-gun from the audit spec's red-team list.

The risk is live because both call sites build the two arguments inline in the same expression and could easily be transposed during a refactor: `src/components/ProfileView.tsx:92` — `downloadText(\`booksum-library-${new Date().toISOString().split('T')[0]}.md\`, markdown)` — and `src/components/BookDetail.tsx:417` — `downloadText(\`${slugify(book.title)}.md\`, bookToMarkdown(book, summary))`.

`mimeType` is likewise a bare `string` interpolated into a Content-Type at line 3 (`\`${mimeType};charset=utf-8\``); passing an already-parameterised value such as `'text/csv;charset=iso-8859-1'` would emit a double `charset` with no type error. No current call site does.

Correct behaviour: take a single options object (`{ filename, contents, mimeType }`), or brand `Filename` / `MimeType`. An options object is the cheaper fix here and removes the ordering hazard entirely.

VERIFIED NEGATIVES for this file: `document.createElement('a')` is correctly used without a cast (it already returns `HTMLAnchorElement`), there are no element or DOM type assertions anywhere in the file, and `URL.revokeObjectURL(url)` IS called (line 11), so there is no object-URL leak. `slugify`'s `|| 'untitled'` at line 21 is a truthy check on a string where the empty-string branch is the intended behaviour, not a coercion bug.

Blast radius: 2 call sites.
findings.verifierNote: Signature present verbatim at download.ts:2 `export function downloadText(filename: string, contents: string, mimeType = 'text/markdown')`, with `filename` reaching `anchor.download` (:7) and `contents` reaching `new Blob([contents], ...)` (:3). Both call sites verified by grep and both build the two arguments inline in a single expression - ProfileView.tsx:92 and BookDetail.tsx:417 - so a transposition during a refactor is exactly the ordering hazard the spec's red-team list names ('function signatures with multiple same-typed parameters where order matters'). `downloadText(markdown, filename)` type-checks. The `mimeType` sub-point is weaker and should be treated as secondary: no call site passes it, so the double-`charset` scenario is hypothetical. The file's verified negatives also hold: `document.createElement('a')` is used without a cast and `URL.revokeObjectURL` is called at :11.
findings.reachability: Both call sites are user-triggered exports (library backup, single-book markdown). Live code; no current call site is transposed.
findings.blastRadius: 1 exported function, 2 production call sites, 0 tests.
findings.suggestedPatch: Collapse to one options object: `export function downloadText({ filename, contents, mimeType = 'text/markdown' }: { filename: string; contents: string; mimeType?: string })`, and update ProfileView.tsx:92 / BookDetail.tsx:417 to named form. Risk: only 2 call sites, but it is an API-shape change - do it in one commit so no caller is left on the positional form.

findings.title: coverForIsbn is tested with one perfect ISBN and undefined, so unvalidated ISBN text becomes Book.coverImageUrl
findings.description: src/lib/goodreads.test.ts:95-105 tests `coverForIsbn` with only a canonical 13-digit ISBN and `undefined`, leaving every real-world Goodreads ISBN shape (hyphenated, 10-digit, placeholder '0') uncovered. Those inputs do produce a truthy but dead cover URL that bypasses the `?? placeholderCover(...)` fallback at src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:158 and is persisted to `Book.coverImageUrl`. Lowered to low: the return type `string | undefined` is honest and no wrong value can compile where the compiler could have helped, and src/components/BookCard.tsx's `handleError` swaps in the same placeholder on load failure, so the end state is identical to the intended fallback. Worth fixing for correctness hygiene, not for incident risk.
findings.verifierNote: The described state of the tests is exactly right: src/lib/goodreads.test.ts:95-105 has precisely two `coverForIsbn` cases, a clean 13-digit ISBN and `undefined`. The underlying behaviour is real too - src/lib/goodreads.ts:69-72 `cleanIsbn` only strips the `="..."` wrapper via `replace(/^="?|"?$/g, '')` and returns whatever remains if non-empty, then :121-122 interpolates it unconditionally, so src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:158 `coverForIsbn(row.isbn13) ?? placeholderCover(row.title)` never reaches the `??` for a truthy-but-garbage ISBN. What does not hold up is medium. (a) It is filed as `branded-type-opportunity` on a TEST file, but there is no call site where a wrong value arrives and compiles into something the compiler could have caught - `string | undefined` is an honest description of what `coverForIsbn` returns, so the branded-type framing does not apply. (b) I verified the user-visible impact is nil: src/components/BookCard.tsx defines `handleError` which sets `placeholderCover(book.title)` on image load failure, plus a `useEffect` that pre-empts empty/'null' URLs, so a dead OpenLibrary URL renders as exactly the placeholder the `??` would have produced, one failed request later.
findings.reachability: Reachable on any Goodreads import containing hyphenated, 10-digit or placeholder ISBNs, which real exports do contain. Outcome: one wasted image request per affected book, then the placeholder renders. No crash, no wrong data displayed.
findings.blastRadius: 1 non-test call site of `coverForIsbn` (src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:158). The value lands in `Book.coverImageUrl` and is read only by BookCard's guarded ``.

findings.title: `columnOf` returns a bare `number` hiding a `-1` not-found sentinel that no type can narrow
findings.description: `columnOf` (goodreads.ts:83) has no return annotation and infers `number` from `Array.prototype.indexOf`, so the `-1` not-found sentinel is invisible in the type and all six derived column constants (:85-90) make 'column 3' and 'column absent' indistinguishable to the compiler. Index `0` is both a valid column and falsy, and the repo's own test at goodreads.test.ts:66-70 exercises Title at index 0, so a refactor to the idiomatic-looking `if (titleAt)` would silently drop it - only the `index >= 0` check inside `cell` (:96) makes the current code correct, and the type does not require it. The originally-claimed user-facing failure is softer than stated: when the title header is missing entirely, GoodreadsImport already surfaces 'No books found in that file. Is it a Goodreads CSV export?', so the user is pointed at the right cause even though the parser cannot distinguish the case internally.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern confirmed at goodreads.ts:83 `const columnOf = (name: string) => header.indexOf(name.toLowerCase());` - no return annotation, infers `number`, and the `-1` not-found sentinel is invisible in the type across all six derived constants (:85-90). The falsy-zero footgun is real and the repo's own test proves index 0 is meaningful: goodreads.test.ts:66-70 ('tolerates a missing optional column') parses `'Title,Author,Exclusive Shelf\nDune,Herbert,read'`, where Title is column 0; a future refactor to `if (titleAt)` would silently break it, and only `cell`'s `index >= 0` check at :96 keeps it correct today. CONCRETE FAILURE 2 is overstated and is the reason for the amendment: I read the consumer, and when the title header is missing the user does NOT get an unexplained result - GoodreadsImport.tsx shows `toast.error('No books found in that file. Is it a Goodreads CSV export?')`, which names the likely cause. So the user-facing consequence is a correct-but-imprecise message, not a silent dead end. Severity stays `low`.
findings.reachability: Every CSV import. The `-1` path is reachable with any non-Goodreads or localised-header CSV, and is handled correctly at runtime by :96 - the weakness is that nothing in the type enforces that handling.
findings.blastRadius: 6 uses inside this file (:85-90 feeding :98-113). `columnOf` is a function-local arrow, not exported - no external consumers.
findings.suggestedPatch: `const columnOf = (name: string): number | null => { const index = header.indexOf(name.toLowerCase()); return index >= 0 ? index : null; };` and `const cell = (index: number | null) => (index === null ? '' : (cells[index] ?? '').trim());`. Risk: none - all six consumers go through `cell`, and the compiler will flag any that does not.

findings.title: `dateRead` is parsed and typed as `string` with no format contract, then silently discarded
findings.description: `GoodreadsRow.dateRead` (goodreads.ts:9) is parsed at :113 and never consumed by anything - `importGoodreadsRows` (useLibrary.tsx:150-160) drops it - and its natural destination, `Book.finishedAt` (types.ts:40), is declared with zero writers and zero readers repo-wide. The defect is therefore a type-honesty one of the dead-declaration kind: the exported parse result advertises data the pipeline discards, so a consumer reasonably concludes read-dates survive an import. There is no present validation gap, because nothing consumes the value and `string` is the honest type for a raw CSV cell. The `YYYY/MM/DD` parsing hazard (Goodreads' format is not ISO-8601 and `new Date` handling of it is engine-dependent, with `Invalid Date` still typed `Date`) is a note to attach to any future wiring-up, not a present-tense finding.
findings.verifierNote: The facts are all verified, but the framing overstates the type weakness. Confirmed: `dateRead?: string` is declared at goodreads.ts:9 and populated at :113 `dateRead: dateRead || undefined` from a raw CSV cell. Repo-wide grep confirms `dateRead` appears only in goodreads.ts (:9, :90, :105, :113) and goodreads.test.ts:22 - `importGoodreadsRows` (useLibrary.tsx:150-160) maps title/author/category/status/rating/coverImageUrl/hasPdf and never reads it - and `finishedAt` appears ONLY at its declaration, types.ts:40, with zero readers and zero writers in src/. So the real, provable defect is a dead field on both ends of the pipeline, not a validation gap: `string` is the honest type for 'whatever was in that CSV cell', and there is no consumer whose assumption it violates. PROBLEM 2 (the `new Date('2023/05/14')` hazard) is explicitly contingent on future code the finding itself confirms does not exist - it should be recorded as a note attached to any future wiring-up, not as a present-tense boundary finding. Severity `low` is right.
findings.reachability: Not reachable as a defect: no code reads `GoodreadsRow.dateRead` or writes `Book.finishedAt`. The only cost today is a misleading exported type.
findings.blastRadius: 2 declared-but-unused fields (goodreads.ts:9, types.ts:40); 1 write site (:113); 0 readers.
findings.suggestedPatch: Cheapest and YAGNI-consistent: delete `dateRead?: string` (goodreads.ts:9), the `dateReadAt` lookup (:90), the local at :105 and the field at :113, and drop the `dateRead` expectation in goodreads.test.ts:22. Risk: if the intent is to keep the data, the alternative is to validate it into an ISO string at :113 and map it to `Book.finishedAt` in useLibrary.tsx:150-160 - do one or the other, not neither.

findings.title: `isbn13` is an unvalidated bare `string` interpolated unencoded into a persisted cover URL
findings.description: `cleanIsbn` (L69-72) strips Goodreads' `="..."` spreadsheet armour and returns whatever is left, typed as `isbn13?: string` (L8). Nothing checks it is 13 characters, or digits, or an ISBN at all — the name is the only thing asserting the domain. `coverForIsbn` (L121) then takes a bare `string | undefined` and interpolates it into a URL WITHOUT `encodeURIComponent`. CORRECT BEHAVIOR: a branded `Isbn13` type produced by a validating parser (`/^\d{13}$/`), plus `encodeURIComponent` at the interpolation site. CONCRETE FAILURE 1 (type mix-up — the classic branded-type footgun): `coverForIsbn(isbn13: string | undefined)` accepts ANY string, so `coverForIsbn(row.title)` type-checks perfectly and produces a garbage URL. Same-typed primitives with distinct domains are exactly what branding prevents. CONCRETE FAILURE 2 (live data quality): a 10-digit ISBN, an ASIN, or an ISSN passes through untouched and yields a 404 cover; an ISBN cell containing a space, `#`, `?`, or `/` (hand-edited CSV, or a mis-detected column) produces a malformed URL. That URL is PERSISTED to `Book.coverImageUrl` in IndexedDB at src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:158 and later rendered as an ``, so the bad value outlives the import session and is only masked by BookCard's `onError` placeholder swap (src/components/BookCard.tsx:18/27). SECURITY BOUNDING (checked, deliberately not overclaimed): the value is interpolated after a fixed `https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/` path prefix, so it cannot change origin, and it lands in an `img src` rather than a script context — this is a data-quality and URL-correctness issue, not an SSRF or XSS one. VERIFIED CORRECT: the `/^="?|"?$/g` regex does handle Goodreads' real formats — `="9780735211292"` -> `9780735211292`, `=""` -> `''` -> `undefined` (matching the test at src/lib/goodreads.test.ts:27), and a bare ISBN passes through unchanged.
findings.verifierNote: Both halves verified in the current source. `cleanIsbn` (goodreads.ts:69-72) strips the `="..."` armour and returns whatever remains with no digit, length, or checksum test; `coverForIsbn` (:121-123) takes a bare `string | undefined` and interpolates it into a URL with no `encodeURIComponent`. The mixup is concretely available at the one production call site: useLibrary.tsx:158 `coverForIsbn(row.isbn13)` sits six lines below `title: row.title` (:152) in the same object literal, and `coverForIsbn(row.title)` would type-check exactly the same - this is the 'wrong value could actually arrive and compile' bar the spec sets for a branded-type finding, and it is met. The persistence claim also holds: the produced URL is written to `Book.coverImageUrl` at :158 and outlives the session, masked only by BookCard's `onError`. The finding's security bounding is correct and appropriately not overclaimed (fixed origin and path prefix, `img src` context). The verified-correct note on the regex matches the tests at goodreads.test.ts:12-23 and :47-49.
findings.reachability: Every Goodreads import with an ISBN column. A 10-digit ISBN, ASIN, or hand-edited cell reaches the URL builder unchecked and is persisted.
findings.blastRadius: 1 exported function, 1 production call site (useLibrary.tsx:158), 2 tests; the bad value is persisted to IndexedDB so its lifetime exceeds the call.
findings.suggestedPatch: Validate where the value is produced rather than branding every consumer: goodreads.ts:70-71 -> `const digits = (raw ?? '').replace(/^="?|"?$/g, '').trim(); return /^\d{13}$/.test(digits) ? digits : undefined;`. Risk: this now drops 10-digit ISBNs, so those rows fall back to `placeholderCover` at useLibrary.tsx:158 - acceptable, and the existing tests are unaffected (the only non-empty fixture ISBN is the 13-digit 9780735211292).

findings.title: Summary fixture always supplies real arrays, so the one consumer that would crash on an AI-shaped Summary is never exercised
findings.description: The `Summary` fixture at src/lib/markdown.test.ts:20-29 always supplies real arrays and the suite's only variation is the empty array at line 70, so `bookToMarkdown` is never exercised against a `Summary` whose array fields came off the wire — and markdown.ts:24-25 / :27-28 would throw `TypeError: ... .map is not a function` on a non-empty string. The observation is correct but low severity: the fixture is explicitly `Summary`-annotated and complete, the missing test could only be written with an `as unknown as Summary` cast that this audit flags as its own defect class, and the correct remedy is to validate once at the producer (F033, summarize.ts:36-37) rather than to add defensive array checks to every consumer of a type that is supposed to be validated. Third mirror of a defect already carried by F033 and F096.
findings.verifierNote: Claims are accurate: src/lib/markdown.test.ts:20-29 declares `const summary: Summary` with real arrays at :25-26, and the only variation the suite tries is the empty array at :70; src/lib/markdown.ts:24-25 and :27-28 do `if (x.length > 0) { ... x.map(...) }`, which a non-empty string would pass and then throw on. But the finding argues against itself. AMENDED DOWN to low for three reasons. (1) The fixture is annotated `: Summary` and complete — the finding says so itself ('otherwise exemplary'). Writing the missing test would require `as unknown as Summary` to smuggle a wire-shaped value past the compiler, which this same audit flags as `double-cast-as-unknown-as-T`; you cannot ask a suite to test a state its types forbid without introducing the exact defect class under audit. (2) The architecturally correct fix is at the producer, not the consumer: validate once in summarize.ts (F033's patch) and markdown.ts can legitimately trust `string[]`. Adding runtime array checks to every consumer of a validated type is the anti-pattern. (3) It is the third mirror of one defect — the producer is F033 (now medium) and the localStorage variant is F096 (medium); a test-file mirror should sit below both.
findings.reachability: No path of its own. markdown.ts only throws if a non-array `Summary` was already persisted, which requires F033's or F096's producer defect to fire first.
findings.blastRadius: One fixture in one 99-line test file; the consumer it under-tests (`bookToMarkdown`) has 2 call sites (itself via libraryToMarkdown, and the library export UI).

findings.reachability: No runtime path. The file is a test; the behaviour it describes lives in srs.ts and repo.ts and is assessed under F092, where I found no producer of a non-canonical `dueAt`.
findings.blastRadius: 0 production call sites. The claim's real surface is `ReviewCard.dueAt` at src/types.ts:93 with 2 consumers (srs.ts:58, repo.ts:88-89), one of which has no production caller.
findings.suggestedPatch: Merge into F092 rather than fixing separately. If a test is wanted now, add the cheap cross-check to src/lib/srs.test.ts:97: assert that `isDue(card, now)` and `card.dueAt <= now.toISOString()` agree for the same fixture, which pins the two comparison semantics together. Risk: none - it is a new assertion over existing canonical fixtures.

plain.title: The scheduling tests only use timestamps they generated themselves
plain.what: The due-date tests feed the checker only values it produced, so nothing pins its comparison method to the one the queue actually uses.

findings.title: dueAt is a bare string whose fixed-width-UTC-ISO invariant is unenforced, and two consumers compare it in incompatible ways
findings.description: `ReviewCard.dueAt` is a bare `string` (src/types.ts:93) whose canonical-UTC-ISO invariant lives only in comments, and two consumers read it incompatibly: src/lib/srs.ts:58 semantically via `Date.parse`, src/lib/storage/repo.ts:88-89 lexicographically. Lowered to low because there is no reachable way for a non-canonical value to enter the store - `newCard` and `scheduleCard` are the only writers and both emit `toISOString()`, migrate.ts never writes `reviewCards`, and `LibraryExport` carries only books and summaries. The related real finding is that `isDue` has zero production callers (verified by grep), so the codebase tests a due-date predicate it never runs while the predicate it does run is untested; deleting `isDue` or routing repo.ts:88 through it is the concrete fix. Note also that the finding's worked example about a '+02:00' offset sorting first 'forever' is incorrect - the '+' only decides the byte compare when the preceding 19 characters match.
findings.verifierNote: The pattern is present and the two-comparisons observation is factually right: `ReviewCard.dueAt` is `string` at src/types.ts:93; producers are src/lib/srs.ts:33 and :52, both `toISOString()`; src/lib/srs.ts:58 compares with `Date.parse(card.dueAt) <= now.getTime()` while src/lib/storage/repo.ts:88-89 compares with `card.dueAt <= cutoff` then `localeCompare`. I confirmed the finding's strongest sub-claim by grep: `isDue` has ZERO production callers - src/lib/srs.test.ts is its only importer. But that cuts against the severity rather than for it. There is no path by which a non-canonical `dueAt` can enter the store: the only writer of `reviewCards` is `newCard` (srs.ts:22-36, called from src/components/QuizModal.tsx:52) and `scheduleCard` (srs.ts:42-55, called from src/features/review/useReviewQueue.ts:38), both of which emit `toISOString()`; src/lib/storage/migrate.ts never touches `reviewCards`; and `LibraryExport` carries only books and summaries (src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:94-98, :109-116), so the backup import cannot inject one either. No concrete call site exists where a wrong value arrives and compiles - the bar this batch was told to apply to branded-type findings. I also found the finding's headline mechanism inaccurate: it claims an offset form like '2026-08-12T10:00:00+02:00' 'sorts before every digit under a byte compare... so listDue would report it due immediately and sort it first, forever'. The '+' at index 19 only decides the comparison when the first 19 characters are identical; against a cutoff of '2026-08-12T09:00:00.000Z' the offset string compares GREATER at index 12 and is correctly not due. The unsoundness of mixing formats is real; that specific worked example is wrong.
findings.reachability: Not reachable today. Every `dueAt` in the store is `Date.prototype.toISOString()` output by construction, and no import, migration or external writer can produce another form. The `Date.parse` -> NaN -> permanently-not-due path exists only in `isDue`, which no production code calls.
findings.blastRadius: 1 field (src/types.ts:93) with 2 consumers, of which only src/lib/storage/repo.ts:88-89 runs in production. Adopting a branded `IsoUtcTimestamp` properly would also touch `Book.addedAt`, `Book.finishedAt`, `Summary.generatedAt` and `Profile.createdAt` - a wide, mechanical retrofit with no live defect driving it.
findings.suggestedPatch: Cheapest real win first: delete the dead `isDue` (src/lib/srs.ts:57-59) and its tests, or make repo.ts:88 call it, so there is exactly one definition of 'due'. If branding is wanted later: `export type IsoUtc = string & { readonly __iso: unique symbol }` with a single `toIsoUtc(d: Date): IsoUtc` factory, applied to `ReviewCard.dueAt` first. Risk: deleting `isDue` removes tested-but-unused API surface, so confirm no planned consumer before removing.

plain.title: Two parts of the app compare review due dates in incompatible ways
plain.what: The due date is plain text, and one place compares it as a date while another compares it as text. The rule that makes those agree is written only in comments.
plain.whyItMatters: A differently-formatted timestamp would put cards in the wrong order or make them due at the wrong time, silently.
plain.whatToDo: Delete the unused comparison or route both through one function, so there is exactly one definition of 'due'.

findings.title: scheduleCard declares a total return of ReviewCard but throws RangeError once ease/interval go non-finite; ease has a floor and no ceiling
findings.description: src/lib/srs.ts:42 `scheduleCard(card, grade, now): ReviewCard` declares a total return but line 52 throws `RangeError: Invalid time value` once `intervalDays * DAY_MS` leaves the Date range - reproduced at exactly 14 consecutive grade-4 reviews (ease 3.9, interval 480,395,074 days), because line 43 applies a MIN_EASE floor with no ceiling. `Math.max(1.3, NaN)` is NaN, so a non-finite `card.ease` would propagate straight through as well. The unguarded caller at src/features/review/useReviewQueue.ts:38 would turn the throw into an unhandled rejection that dead-ends the review session. Lowered to low because neither trigger is reachable: `listDue` gates each review on the previous interval elapsing, so 14 consecutive Easy grades needs ~325,000 years of wall clock, and no writer of `reviewCards` can produce a non-finite ease (only `newCard` and `scheduleCard` write the store; migrate.ts and the backup import do not). Real type-honesty defect, latent trigger - fix it because the two-line cap is free, not because it is on fire.
findings.verifierNote: The code defect is real and I reproduced it precisely. src/lib/srs.ts:43 applies only a floor (`Math.max(MIN_EASE, card.ease + EASE_DELTA[grade])`) with `EASE_DELTA[4] = 0.1` at :10 and no MAX_EASE anywhere in the file; :46 multiplies by `ease * INTERVAL_MODIFIER[grade]`; :52 calls `new Date(now.getTime() + intervalDays * DAY_MS).toISOString()`. Simulating consecutive grade-4 reviews reproduces the finding's numbers exactly: review 13 gives ease 3.80 / interval 94,752,480 days, review 14 gives ease 3.90 / interval 480,395,074 days and `.toISOString()` throws RangeError. `Math.max(1.3, NaN)` and `Math.max(1, NaN)` both return NaN, and `new Date(NaN).toISOString()` throws - all verified. The caller is unguarded as claimed: src/features/review/useReviewQueue.ts:38 `await cardRepo.upsert(scheduleCard(current, gradeValue))` sits in an async `useCallback` with no try/catch, and `setQueue(...)` on the next line would never run. What is wrong is the finding's assertion of 'two reachable triggers' - NEITHER is reachable. (1) Reaching review 14 requires 14 consecutive Easy grades on ONE card, and the queue is gated by `listDue` (repo.ts:84-90), which only returns cards whose `dueAt <= now`; the cumulative wall-clock wait across intervals 3, 11, 40, 151, 589, 2374, 9876, 42368, 187267, 852065, 3987664, 19180664, 94752480 days is roughly 325,000 years. `grade` also drops the card from the queue (`setQueue((rest) => rest.slice(1))`), so it cannot be re-graded within a session. (2) A non-finite `card.ease` has no producer: `reviewCards` is written only by `newCard` (ease 2.5) and `scheduleCard`, migrate.ts never touches the store, and the backup import carries only books and summaries. A latent, genuinely unreachable overflow is low, not medium.
findings.reachability: Not reachable by any user. The exponential interval growth that causes the overflow is the same mechanism that gates it: each successive review is only offered after the previous (growing) interval elapses, so trigger (1) needs ~325,000 years of wall clock. Trigger (2) needs a non-finite ease in IndexedDB, for which no writer exists. Would become live if a cram/relearn mode ever re-grades a card within a session, or if any code path writes `reviewCards` from external data.
findings.blastRadius: 1 non-test call site (src/features/review/useReviewQueue.ts:38), which is the only write path for review scheduling. `reviewCards` has 4 non-test call sites in total (QuizModal.tsx:49, :52; useReviewQueue.ts:20, :38).

plain.title: The review scheduler claims it always produces a card but can fail on extreme intervals
plain.what: The scheduler's declared result says it always returns a card. Once the computed interval grows past what a date can represent, it throws instead.
plain.whyItMatters: Reaching that point needs fourteen consecutive top grades and, because each review waits for the previous interval, roughly three hundred thousand years of real time. It is a contract inaccuracy, not a live failure.
plain.whatToDo: Add an upper limit on the interval and the ease factor so the declared result is true for every input.

findings.title: DBSchema value types promise every read row is a valid domain object, but IndexedDB validates nothing on the way out
findings.description: src/lib/storage/db.ts:7-17 declares `DBSchema` value types (`value: Book`, `value: Summary`, ...) that make `idb` type every read as a valid domain object, a guarantee IndexedDB structurally cannot provide - and the store genuinely can hold non-conforming rows, because src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:111 writes elements of a user-supplied backup file behind only an `Array.isArray` check (ProfileView.tsx:119). Compounding it, `DB_VERSION` is 1 and the `upgrade` handler (db.ts:24-39) ignores `oldVersion` and contains no reshaping step, so a malformed row is never repaired. Lowered to low as the schema-side framing of a defect already counted on its producer and consumer files by F004 (critical), F022, F046, F047, F048 and F049 (all high). There is no line in db.ts to change; the fix is repo.ts's write-side validation.
findings.verifierNote: Everything factual in this finding checks out: src/lib/storage/db.ts:7-17 declares `books: { key: string; value: Book; ... }` etc., which makes `idb` type every read as `Book | undefined` with no runtime basis; `DB_VERSION` is 1 (db.ts:5) and the `upgrade(db)` handler at :24-39 ignores the `oldVersion` argument and only creates stores, so no row-reshaping path exists; and the real writer of unvalidated rows is present - src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:111 `await bookRepo.create({ ...book, profileId: profile.id })` over `payload.books` from a user-supplied backup, where the only guard upstream is `Array.isArray(data.books)` at src/components/ProfileView.tsx:119, which checks the array but never the shape of its elements. The problem is double-counting. This is the SCHEMA-SIDE statement of a defect already carried, at higher severity, by six other aggregate findings on the actual producer and consumer files: F004 (critical, ProfileView.tsx:117), F022 (high, useLibrary.tsx:102), F046 (high, repo.ts:8), F047 (high, repo.ts:44), F048 (high, repo.ts:52) and F049 (high, repo.ts:143). db.ts has no code to fix - the `DBSchema` value types are the correct declaration of intent, and the finding's own recommendation says so ('keep the DBSchema value types as the intended shape, but treat repo.ts as the trust boundary'), which is F046-F049's fix, not this one's. Keep it as the structural framing at low; the weight belongs on the producer findings.
findings.reachability: Reachable, but through the paths already counted: import a hand-edited or foreign backup JSON via ProfileView.tsx:109-135, and every subsequent `books.get`/`books.listByProfile` (repo.ts:44, :47) hands the malformed row out stamped as a `Book`. Nothing in db.ts can prevent or detect it.
findings.blastRadius: 5 store declarations in one file, 0 fixable lines. The consuming read paths are repo.ts:8, :13, :44, :47, :79, :95, :113, :143 - all already enumerated by F046-F049.
findings.suggestedPatch: No change in src/lib/storage/db.ts. Land the fix at the trust boundary instead, per F046-F049: add a `parseBook`/`parseSummary` normaliser in repo.ts applied on the write paths that accept external data (`books.create`, `summaries.upsert`) so the DBSchema type is earned. Risk: validating on the read path instead would cost a pass over every row on every list call - validate on write only.

plain.title: The database schema promises every stored row is a valid record, which no database can guarantee
plain.what: The storage layer declares the exact shape of every row, and the database library then describes every read accordingly. The database itself validates nothing on the way out.
plain.whyItMatters: This one declaration is what makes the whole storage layer look trustworthy in review, which is why the unchecked write paths went unnoticed.
plain.whatToDo: Leave the declaration alone and add the checks at the read and write boundaries instead.

findings.title: blobs store key is a composite `${bookId}:${kind}` but is declared plain string, identical to the by-book index key
findings.description: src/lib/storage/db.ts:11 declares the `blobs` primary key as bare `string`, but the real key space is the composite `${bookId}:${kind}` built at src/lib/storage/repo.ts:126, and the same store's `by-book` index key - a raw bookId - is also `string`. Two structurally different key spaces share one type in one declaration, so `db.get('blobs', someBookId)` type-checks and silently returns `undefined`, indistinguishable from 'no blob stored'. Lowered to low because no current call site is wrong (verified: every access routes through `blobKey`, and `removeByBook` feeds `getAllKeysFromIndex` results back to `delete`), so no wrong value can arrive and compile today. Keep it in the report as a cheap structural fix: a template-literal type on db.ts:11 and src/types.ts:69 closes it with no runtime change. Related observation retained: `StoredBlob` lets `key`, `bookId` and `kind` disagree even though repo.ts:133-139 always derives one from the others, and the `by-profile-due` index is declared correctly but never queried.
findings.verifierNote: Factually correct on every point I checked. src/lib/storage/db.ts:11 declares `blobs: { key: string; value: StoredBlob; indexes: { 'by-book': string } }`, while the real primary key is composite - src/lib/storage/repo.ts:126 `const blobKey = (bookId: string, kind: BlobKind) => `${bookId}:${kind}``. Two different key spaces share one type inside one store declaration, so `db.get('blobs', someBookId)` compiles and silently returns `undefined`. src/types.ts:68-69 does document the format in a comment (`/** `${bookId}:${kind}` */ key: string;`) that the type does not encode. I verified the index declarations against their keyPaths in db.ts:28/31/34/38 and they are all correct, and that `by-profile-due` is indeed never queried (repo.ts:79 and :95 both do a full-store `getAll` and filter in memory). With no call site where a wrong value can arrive and compile, this is a structural recommendation, not a medium defect - which is exactly the bar this batch was told to apply to branded-type findings. The fix is genuinely cheap, so it belongs in the report as a low with a one-line patch rather than being dropped.
findings.reachability: No reachable failure today. It becomes reachable the moment anyone adds a blob call site that does not go through `blobKey`; the failure would then be a silent `undefined` indistinguishable from 'no PDF stored', which BookDetail.tsx:197 treats as 'nothing to open'.
findings.blastRadius: 1 declaration line; 4 non-test blob call sites (BookDetail.tsx:197, useLibrary.tsx:51, migrate.ts:137, migrate.ts:143), all of which use the `blobs.get/put(bookId, kind)` wrapper rather than raw keys.

plain.title: The attachment key is a composite value but is declared as plain text
plain.what: Attachments are keyed by a combination of book and kind, but the key is declared as ordinary text, identical to a different key used by the same store's index.

findings.title: The cascade test omits reviewCards, and the whole reviewCards store surface is untested

findings.title: profiles.update and books.update write whatever the caller hands them, persisting NaN as a typed number
findings.description: src/lib/storage/repo.ts:30-33 (`profiles.update`) and :63-66 (`books.update`) are unvalidated pass-throughs to `put()`, so record correctness rests entirely on the caller's static type. REFUTED sub-claim: the finding's only concrete failure - that src/components/ProfileView.tsx:239 persists `monthlyGoal: NaN` when the user clears the field - cannot happen. That control is `<input type="range" min="1" max="20">`, which has no empty state and always yields a valid numeric string, so `parseInt` never returns NaN. No other persisted path produces a non-finite number either (AddBookModal.tsx:162 uses `Number()` on a number input, and `Number('')` is 0). Blast radius was also overstated: 9 `profiles.*` and 14 `books.*` non-test call sites, not 26 and 22. Lowered to low - the residual observation is real but duplicates F048 (high, repo.ts:52) on the write side and F046/F047 on the read side.
findings.verifierNote: The finding's sole named failure mode is FALSE. I opened src/components/ProfileView.tsx around line 239 and the control is `<input type="range" min="1" max="20" value={editedProfile.monthlyGoal} onChange={(e) => setEditedProfile({ ...editedProfile, monthlyGoal: parseInt(e.target.value) })} />`. A range input has no empty state - the browser guarantees `.value` is always a valid numeric string and clamps it into [min,max] - so 'clearing the monthly-goal field and saving' is not an action the UI offers and `parseInt` can never return NaN there. I swept every other numeric coercion in src/components, src/features and src/app: only AddBookModal.tsx:162 `setRating(Number(e.target.value))` (an `<input type="number">`, where an emptied field yields `''` and `Number('') === 0`, not NaN) and AudioPlayer.tsx:69/:87 (transient playback state, never persisted). There is no producer of a non-finite number on any persisted path. What remains true is only that src/lib/storage/repo.ts:30-33 and :63-66 are unvalidated pass-throughs to `put()` - which is a design property of a thin repo, and is already counted at high by F048 (repo.ts:52, 'books.create and summaries.upsert persist caller objects with no validation') and F046/F047 on the read side. The blast radius was also inflated: I measured 9 non-test `profiles.*` call sites and 14 non-test `books.*` call sites, not the claimed 26 and 22.
findings.reachability: The claimed path is not reachable: a range slider cannot be cleared. The residual - a caller handing `update()` a structurally valid but semantically wrong record - is reachable only through the backup-import path already covered by F004 (critical) and F022 (high), and that path goes through `books.create`, not `update`.
findings.blastRadius: Recounted excluding tests: 9 `profiles.*` and 14 `books.*` non-test call sites (the finding claimed 26 and 22 - inflated roughly 2x, consistent with this audit's known test-file overcount). Two update methods, both thin.

plain.title: Record updates write whatever the caller supplies with no checking

findings.title: Every identifier in the persistence API is a bare string, including two adjacent methods that take different id kinds
findings.description: Every identifier in the persistence API is a bare `string`, so the compiler cannot distinguish profileId, bookId, summaryId or a composite blob key. The sharpest example is inside `summaries`: `getByBook(bookId)` at src/lib/storage/repo.ts:112 and `remove(id)` at :121 are nine lines apart, take different id kinds with identical types, and `summaries.remove(bookId)` compiles and silently deletes nothing. Same exposure for `blobKey(bookId, kind)` at :126, `reviewCards.removeByBook` vs the card ids deleted at :107, and `books.create`'s `profileId`/`id` pair. Lowered to low: I verified that no current call site passes the wrong id kind (repo.ts:70, :106-107, :149-150 are all correct, and the external callers in useLibrary.tsx and migrate.ts pass the right kinds), so nothing wrong can arrive and compile today; and the blast radius is ~37 non-test call sites, not the claimed 75+. But I checked every call site and none is wrong: repo.ts:70 correctly does `summaries.getByBook(id)` then `summaries.remove(summary.id)`; :106-107 deletes by `card.id` after `listByBook(bookId)`; :149-150 feeds `getAllKeysFromIndex` results straight to `delete`; and outside repo.ts, `summaryRepo.getByBook` is only ever passed a book id (useLibrary.tsx:76, :92) and `summaryRepo.upsert` a full `Summary` (useLibrary.tsx:48, :80, :115, migrate.ts:122). With no call site where a wrong id can arrive and compile into a defect, this is a structural recommendation, not a medium - which is exactly the bar this batch was told to apply to branded-type findings. findings.blastRadius: Recounted excluding tests: ~37 non-test repo call sites across src (profiles 9, books 14, summaries 6, blobs 4, reviewCards 4), not the claimed 75+. Every exported repo method except `blobs.put` takes at least one bare-string id.
