plain.title: Every identifier in the storage layer is plain text, including two neighbouring methods that take different kinds
plain.what: Book, profile, summary and attachment identifiers are all plain text, so nothing prevents one being passed where another is expected. Two adjacent methods in the same module take different kinds.
plain.whyItMatters: A swap compiles cleanly and returns nothing rather than failing, so the symptom is missing data rather than an error.
plain.whatToDo: If adopted, introduce distinct identifier types at the single place they are created so the change stays mechanical.

findings.title: reviewCards read path loads every row unvalidated and sorts on dueAt with a string method
findings.description: reviewCards.listByProfile/listByBook (repo.ts:78-81, 94-97) load every row unvalidated and listDue (repo.ts:88-89) then relies on dueAt being an ISO string for both the `<=` comparison and localeCompare. The declared type is unchecked, but the store has no external ingress: its only writers are QuizModal.tsx:52 and useReviewQueue.ts:38, both routed through srs.ts, which always writes `new Date(...).toISOString()`. No migration or import path writes review cards, and listDue filters by profileId before comparing, so a corrupt row cannot cross profiles. Hygiene-grade.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present: repo.ts:78-81 listByProfile does `getAll('reviewCards')` then reads `card.profileId`, repo.ts:94-97 listByBook does the same for bookId, and listDue at repo.ts:84-90 filters on `card.dueAt <= cutoff` (line 88) and sorts with `a.dueAt.localeCompare(b.dueAt)` (line 89) on rows typed only by the declaration at db.ts:12-16. Two of Discovery's claims do not survive. First, there is no ingress: the only writers to the reviewCards store are QuizModal.tsx:52 and useReviewQueue.ts:38, both routed through srs.ts, and both newCard (srs.ts:33) and scheduleCard (srs.ts:52) set dueAt from `new Date(...).toISOString()`. Neither the legacy migration nor the backup import touches reviewCards — so unlike summaries (F113) or profiles (F103) no non-string dueAt can arrive without direct database tampering. Second, the cross-profile claim is wrong: listDue calls listByProfile (line 86), which filters by profileId at line 80 before the comparison at 88-89, so another profile's row never reaches localeCompare. The full-table-scan vs by-profile-due-index point is a performance observation, which the spec places out of scope. Downgrading to low.
findings.reachability: No producer path can write a malformed card. Reaching the throw requires hand-editing IndexedDB or a future writer that bypasses srs.ts.
findings.blastRadius: Recounted excluding tests: 4 call sites — QuizModal.tsx:49, QuizModal.tsx:52, useReviewQueue.ts:20, useReviewQueue.ts:38 (plus repo-internal removeByBook at repo.ts:106). Discovery's '10' counted tests and repo-internal uses.
findings.suggestedPatch: Cheap defensive guard at repo.ts:88: `.filter((card) => typeof card.dueAt === 'string' && card.dueAt <= cutoff)`, so a tampered row drops out of the queue instead of throwing in the sort. Risk: it silently hides a corrupt record — pair it with a console.warn so the row stays attributable.

plain.title: Review cards are read back and sorted without any checking
plain.what: Every review card is loaded and then filtered and sorted on a timestamp that nothing has verified is text of the expected form.
plain.whyItMatters: Nothing outside the app writes to this store, so the risk is confined to a tampered database rather than a normal path.
plain.whatToDo: Add a cheap check in the due-date filter so a tampered row is skipped rather than breaking the queue.

findings.title: setup.ts provides no typed fetch stub, so four hand-rolled stubs diverge from typeof fetch and one leaks across tests
findings.description: src/test/setup.ts provides no shared, typed fetch stub, so four hand-rolled stubs (smoke.test.tsx:43; covers/index.test.ts:8, :56, :64) are each written against an ad-hoc signature that nothing checks against `typeof globalThis.fetch`. The practical consequence is not the omitted `init` parameter (legal in TS) but that `mock.calls` entries are typed to whatever the stub declared, so an assertion over the request options is untypeable, and that cleanup is per-file convention: smoke.test.tsx:61 unstubs inside the test body, so a failing assertion at lines 49-60 leaks a blanket 200 stub into the rest of the file. Test-hygiene severity; no production path is affected.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present. src/test/setup.ts is 14 lines (jest-dom, fake-indexeddb, configure({asyncUtilTimeout:5000}) at line 9, afterEach cleanup at 11-14) with no fetch helper. All four stubs verified: smoke.test.tsx:43, covers/index.test.ts:8, :56 (zero-param throwing stub), :64. vite.config.ts:24 sets restoreMocks:true with no unstubGlobals, and smoke.test.tsx:61 does call vi.unstubAllGlobals() as the last statement of the test BODY while covers/index.test.ts:16-18 uses afterEach — the asymmetry is real. Two claims overstate: (a) a one-parameter function IS legally assignable to typeof fetch in TS, so 'drops init' is not a type error and no production init is 'silently discarded' any differently than by a stub that ignores it; (b) the category unknown-misuse points at vitest's own vi.stubGlobal(name, value: unknown) signature, which is third-party, not source — the spec excludes library-side types from per-file findings. What survives is genuine but test-only: nothing checks the stubs against typeof globalThis.fetch, and the leak risk at smoke.test.tsx:61 is real test hygiene rather than a type weakness. Spec reserves low for exactly this ('any in test fixtures ... worth fixing for hygiene but won't cause incidents').
findings.reachability: Test-only. If any assertion between smoke.test.tsx:49-60 throws, line 61 never runs and the 200-'{}' stub leaks into the two later tests in the file (lines 64 and 85), which would then exercise a stubbed network. No production path is affected.
findings.blastRadius: 4 stub sites in 2 test files; 0 production files.
findings.suggestedPatch: In src/test/setup.ts add `export function stubFetch(impl: typeof globalThis.fetch) { vi.stubGlobal('fetch', vi.fn(impl)); }` and extend the existing afterEach (line 11) with `vi.unstubAllGlobals();`. Replace the four hand-rolled stubs with stubFetch(...) and delete smoke.test.tsx:61 plus covers/index.test.ts:16-18. Risk: the global unstub in afterEach would also clear a stub a test intended to outlive it — no test does that today.

plain.title: Four hand-written network stubs each invent their own shape
plain.what: There is no shared, checked network stub, so four separate test files each write their own against an informal signature, and one is left installed after its test finishes.
plain.whyItMatters: The stubs can drift from the real browser interface without any failure, and the leaked one can influence a later test.
plain.whatToDo: Add one shared, typed stub helper and route all four through it.

findings.title: The 'no Gemini call on boot' invariant is asserted by a for-loop that runs zero times when nothing is captured
findings.description: smoke.test.tsx:58-60 asserts the 'no Gemini call on boot' invariant with a for-loop over fetchSpy.mock.calls that runs zero times on the intended-pass path, so the test passes having asserted nothing. Real test-strength defect (the invariant is unguarded against a refactor that moves the call outside the spy), but it is not a type-safety finding: no external data is typed by assertion here. Reclassified low.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present exactly as described: smoke.test.tsx:58-60 is `for (const call of fetchSpy.mock.calls) { expect(String(call[0])).not.toContain('generativelanguage'); }` with no expect.assertions and no toHaveBeenCalled, so on the intended-pass path (zero captured calls) the assertion body never executes. That is a genuinely vacuous test guarding a stated CLAUDE.md invariant. However this is a test-assertion-strength defect, not a type weakness: nothing here is typed via assertion and no external data enters typed code, so the assigned category boundary-without-validation does not hold. The only type-adjacent residue is that the stub at line 43 declares one parameter, so `call` is a 1-tuple and `String(call[0])` is the only expressible assertion (see F101). Discovery's alternative (b) — a fetch reference captured at module-import time before the stub at line 47 — is not supported: the Gemini client is resolved lazily via getClient() at call time, not at import.
findings.reachability: The vacuous branch is the normal green path — the test passes today having asserted nothing. A future refactor that moves the Gemini call outside the spy's reach would also pass silently.
findings.blastRadius: 1 test; the same vacuous-loop shape is repeated at covers/index.test.ts:72-74.
findings.suggestedPatch: Replace smoke.test.tsx:58-60 with `const geminiCalls = fetchSpy.mock.calls.filter(([input]) => String(input).includes('generativelanguage')); expect(geminiCalls).toEqual([]);` and move vi.unstubAllGlobals() out of the body into an afterEach. Risk: none — the new form fails on exactly the same condition but is non-vacuous and prints the offending URL.

plain.title: The 'no AI call on boot' check is written as a loop that runs zero times when it passes
plain.what: The smoke test asserts the invariant by looping over captured network calls. On the intended path there are none, so the loop body never runs and nothing is asserted.
plain.whyItMatters: One of the project's stated invariants is protected by a test that would pass even if the capture mechanism stopped working entirely.
plain.whatToDo: Filter the captured calls and assert the filtered count is zero, which is meaningful whether or not calls were captured.

findings.title: Book/Summary/Profile/ReviewCard ids are all bare string, and one adjacent-line call site would silently swallow a swap
findings.description: All entity ids are bare `string`, so repo signatures (repo.ts:12/47/68/112/121) cannot distinguish a book id from a summary id and a swap would compile. The nearest juggling site, useLibrary.tsx:81-83, is dead code on the live path, and no producer currently passes the wrong kind — this is a latent refactor hazard rather than a present defect.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present: types.ts:29-30 (Book.id, profileId), :50 (summaryId), :55-56 (Summary.id, bookId), :18 (Profile.id), :84-86 (ReviewCard ids) are all bare `string`, and repo.ts:12/47/68/112/121 accept an undifferentiated `id: string`, so any id kind satisfies any signature. The cited call site is real and reads exactly as quoted at useLibrary.tsx:81-83. But it is a hypothetical-typo hazard, not a wrong value arriving: no producer in the codebase passes the wrong id kind, and per the established baseline the backfill at useLibrary.tsx:82-83 is dead code (addBook at lines 44-45 always sets summaryId when a summary exists, so `book.summaryId !== summary.id` is never true on the live path). The spec's own note applies — branded types are 'easy to recommend, hard to retrofit' — and the bar of a concrete call site where a wrong value could actually arrive and compile is not met. Downgrading to low, which is where the spec puts hygiene-grade type weakness.
findings.reachability: No live path. The failure requires a future edit to substitute one id for another; the immediate `if (book && ...)` guard at useLibrary.tsx:82 would then swallow the resulting undefined silently.
findings.blastRadius: Recounted non-test id-accepting call sites: books 12 (useLibrary 32/45/62/70/81/83/91/106/111/136/150, migrate 105), summaries 6 (useLibrary 48/76/80/92/115, migrate 122), reviewCards 4 (QuizModal 49/52, useReviewQueue 20/38), blobs 4 (BookDetail 197, useLibrary 51, migrate 137/143). Only one site — useLibrary.tsx:81 — juggles two id kinds in one expression.
findings.suggestedPatch: If taken: `type Brand<K, T> = K & { readonly __brand: T }; export type BookId = Brand<string, 'BookId'>; export type SummaryId = Brand<string, 'SummaryId'>;` in types.ts, with casts confined to the three producers (repo.ts:4 newId, the route param at useBookRoute.ts:8, and the import path at useLibrary.tsx:109-115). Risk: every test fixture and every string-literal id in the suite needs a cast, so the change is wide even though it is mechanical — treat as a structural recommendation, not a fix.

plain.title: All record identifiers share one plain-text type across the whole app
plain.what: Books, summaries, profiles and review cards all identify themselves with plain text, so the compiler cannot tell one kind from another anywhere.
plain.whyItMatters: The nearest place two kinds are handled together is currently unreachable code, so this is a latent footgun rather than a live defect.
plain.whatToDo: If adopted, introduce distinct identifier types, accepting that retrofitting them touches every producer and consumer.

findings.title: Book.category is an unconstrained string fed by the LLM, while the Category enum declared right above it is dead code
findings.description: types.ts:6-15 exports a `Category` enum that no code references, while types.ts:33 leaves Book.category an unconstrained string filled by Gemini (schemas.ts:8 has no enum constraint; summarize.ts:26 takes the value straight off the JSON.parse cast). Consumers compare exactly (LibraryPage.tsx:47) but the chip list at LibraryPage.tsx:65 is derived from the stored books, so no book becomes unreachable — the consequence is category fragmentation in the filter chips and the StatsView breakdown, plus a dead enum that misleads readers.
findings.verifierNote: Both halves of the pattern verified. types.ts:6-15 declares the eight-member `Category` enum and types.ts:33 declares `category: string`; a repo-wide grep for the identifier returns only its own declaration at types.ts:6 — every other hit is JSX label text (BookDetail.tsx:321, StatsView.tsx:133/138) or an `activeCategory` local (LibraryPage.tsx:22/47/110/174-177). The enum is dead. Producers confirmed: summarize.ts:26 `category: data.category || 'Other'` where data is the raw JSON.parse cast at summarize.ts:52/73, schemas.ts:8 `category: { type: Type.STRING }` with no enum constraint, useLibrary.tsx:154 and migrate.ts:109. What breaks Discovery's severity is the consumer: LibraryPage.tsx:65 builds the chip list as `['All', ...Array.from(new Set(books.map((b) => b.category)))]` — derived from the books themselves — so the exact-match filter at LibraryPage.tsx:47 always has a matching chip and no book is ever unreachable. The real consequence is fragmentation ('Self-Help' vs 'Self Help' become two chips and two rows in the StatsView breakdown at StatsView.tsx:23-28), which is cosmetic. Spec low: 'worth fixing for hygiene but won't cause incidents'.
findings.reachability: Every AI-generated book takes an arbitrary Gemini string into Book.category and into IndexedDB. It renders and filters correctly; it merely fragments the filter chips and the category breakdown.
findings.blastRadius: One dead enum; four producers (summarize.ts:26, useLibrary.tsx:154, migrate.ts:109, plus the raw model value); three consumers (LibraryPage.tsx:47/65, StatsView.tsx:23-28, markdown.ts:13).
findings.suggestedPatch: Cheapest honest fix: delete the dead enum at types.ts:6-15. If the constraint is wanted instead, add `enum: Object.values(Category)` to schemas.ts:8 and coerce at summarize.ts:26 (`category: (Object.values(Category) as string[]).includes(data.category ?? '') ? data.category! : 'Other'`), leaving Book.category as `string` so already-stored free-form values still load. Risk: narrowing Book.category to the enum type would make existing IndexedDB rows violate their declared type — do not do that without a migration.

plain.title: A list of valid book categories exists in the code and is never used
plain.what: A defined set of categories sits in the shared types and nothing references it, while the actual category field accepts any text the AI supplies.
plain.whyItMatters: Dead code that looks authoritative is worse than none: a reader assumes categories are constrained when they are not.
plain.whatToDo: Either delete the unused list or wire it into both the AI template and the field type.

findings.title: The quiz-question shape is declared three separate times across types.ts and srs.ts
findings.description: `QuizQuestion` (types.ts:105-110) declares `question`, `options`, `correctAnswerIndex`, `explanation`. `ReviewCard` (types.ts:86-89) re-declares the identical four fields inline alongside its id and SRS fields. `NewCardInput` (src/lib/srs.ts:13-20) declares them a third time alongside `profileId`/`bookId`, and `src/lib/srs.ts:26-30` then copies them across field-by-field. One shape, three declarations, one hand-written copy loop. Adding or renaming a quiz field means editing three types and the copy loop, and the compiler only flags a subset of those — a field added to `QuizQuestion` alone silently fails to reach `ReviewCard`, which is how quiz data would quietly stop being persisted. Correct shape: define the four fields once and compose — `interface ReviewCard extends QuizQuestion { id; profileId; bookId; ease; intervalDays; dueAt; reviewCount }` and `type NewCardInput = QuizQuestion & { profileId: string; bookId: string }` — which also collapses the copy loop in `newCard` to a spread.
findings.verifierNote: Three declarations verified line by line: `QuizQuestion` at types.ts:105-110 (`question`, `options`, `correctAnswerIndex`, `explanation`); the same four inline on `ReviewCard` at types.ts:87-90; and again on `NewCardInput` at srs.ts:13-20 - plus the hand-written field-by-field copy at srs.ts:27-30 inside `newCard`. The failure mode claimed is real and mechanical: a field added to `QuizQuestion` alone reaches neither `ReviewCard` nor the copy loop, and nothing errors, so newly-generated quiz data would silently fail to persist. This is exactly the spec's `generic-opportunity` definition ('duplicated type definitions across modules that could collapse'), and unlike the other two generic-opportunity findings in this batch there really are duplicated declarations here. Not generated code.
findings.reachability: The copy loop at srs.ts:22-36 runs for every quiz question turned into a review card - the whole spaced-repetition feature.
findings.blastRadius: 3 type declarations across 2 files plus 1 copy loop; `ReviewCard` is the IndexedDB record shape (db.ts, repo.reviewCards) so the composition must be behaviour-preserving.
findings.suggestedPatch: `export interface ReviewCard extends QuizQuestion { id: string; profileId: string; bookId: string; ease: number; intervalDays: number; dueAt: string; reviewCount: number; }` (move `QuizQuestion` above it in types.ts), `export type NewCardInput = QuizQuestion & { profileId: string; bookId: string };`, and collapse srs.ts:23-35 to `{ ...input, id: crypto.randomUUID(), ease: STARTING_EASE, intervalDays: 1, dueAt: now.toISOString(), reviewCount: 0 }`. Risk: the spread version copies any extra property present on `input` at runtime, so keep `NewCardInput` exact-shaped; the persisted record shape is unchanged.

plain.title: The quiz-question shape is written out three separate times
plain.what: The same four fields describing a quiz question are declared independently in three places across two files.
plain.whyItMatters: Changing the shape in one place and not the others compiles cleanly and produces cards that are missing a field.
plain.whatToDo: Declare the shape once and have the other two extend it.

findings.title: noImplicitOverride is off — one unmarked override in the AI error class hierarchy
findings.description:
`noImplicitOverride` is not enabled. Measured: `npx tsc --noEmit --noImplicitOverride` produces exactly 1 error, at `src/lib/ai/errors.ts:15`, where a constructor parameter property redeclares a member inherited from `Error` without an `override` modifier.

Without the flag, a subclass member that shadows a base-class member is indistinguishable from one that was meant to be new. On an `Error` subclass this is the classic footgun: silently redeclaring `message`, `name` or `cause` as a parameter property can shadow the base field that `Error.prototype.toString`, the `stack` header and most logging paths read from, so the error renders with an empty or stale message while the subclass field holds the real one. It also means a future rename in the base type would silently orphan the subclass member rather than erroring.

Correct behaviour: enable `noImplicitOverride` and add the explicit `override` keyword at that one site — or, if the redeclaration is not actually intended to override, drop the parameter property and pass the value through to `super()`. Adoption cost: trivial, one line, and it is the only blocker for turning the flag on permanently.
findings.evidence:
tsconfig.json
  8      "strict": true,          // noImplicitOverride is NOT part of the strict family

$ npx tsc --noEmit --noImplicitOverride   (1 error; baseline 0)
  src/lib/ai/errors.ts(15,5): error TS4115: This parameter property must have an
    'override' modifier because it overrides a member in base class 'Error'.
findings.verifierNote: Re-measured myself: `npx tsc --noEmit --noImplicitOverride` produces exactly one error - `src/lib/ai/errors.ts(15,5): error TS4115: This parameter property must have an 'override' modifier because it overrides a member in base class 'Error'.` - against a baseline of 0. Confirmed at the source: errors.ts:15 declares `readonly cause?: unknown` as a constructor parameter property while `Error.cause` already exists in the ES2022 lib the project targets (tsconfig.json:3-4), so the subclass field genuinely shadows a base member. tsconfig.json:8 has `strict: true` and `noImplicitOverride` is correctly identified as outside the strict family. The general risk described (silently redeclaring `message`/`name`/`cause` and desynchronising from what `Error.prototype.toString` and the `stack` header read) is the right rationale; here it is benign because the parameter property assigns the same value `super()` would have. Adoption cost is one line.
findings.reachability: `AiError` is constructed on every AI failure (errors.ts:63) and `cause` is written every time. No current misbehaviour - the shadowing is value-identical.
findings.blastRadius: 1 site; enabling the flag is a whole-project ratchet with exactly this one blocker.
findings.suggestedPatch: Preferred: stop shadowing - drop the parameter property and pass the value through, `constructor(readonly kind: AiErrorKind, message: string, cause?: unknown) { super(message, { cause }); this.name = 'AiError'; }`, then add `"noImplicitOverride": true` to tsconfig.json. Risk: `super(message, { cause })` sets `cause` only when the ES2022 Error options overload is present (it is, given `target`/`lib` ES2022), and it makes `cause` non-enumerable where the parameter property made it enumerable - if any code enumerates AiError's own keys, use `override readonly cause?: unknown` instead.

plain.title: One compiler check that would catch accidental method shadowing is off, with a single site to fix
plain.what: A checking option that requires deliberate marking when a class member replaces an inherited one is not enabled. Exactly one place would need changing.
plain.whyItMatters: Small on its own, but it is a one-line fix that permanently locks in the check for future code.
plain.whatToDo: Fix the single site and enable the option.

findings.title: Four zero-cost strictness flags are unset — they add 0 errors today but nothing locks the property in
findings.description:
Four checking flags outside the `strict` family are not enabled, and each measures **0 errors** against the current source, so enabling them is a pure ratchet with no remediation work at all:

- `noImplicitReturns` (0 errors) — would catch a function with a conditional return path that falls through to `undefined`.
- `noUncheckedSideEffectImports` (0 errors) — would catch `import './missing.css'`-style imports that resolve to nothing.
- `allowUnreachableCode: false` (0 errors) — currently unreachable code is a suggestion-level hint, not an error.
- `allowUnusedLabels: false` (0 errors).

Because `strict: true` already covers the whole strict family (verified below), these four plus the flags in L01-F02/F03/F05/F09 are the entire remaining strictness surface. The codebase is clean enough today that all four can be turned on in a single commit with no code changes; leaving them off means the first violation lands silently rather than failing CI.

For completeness, I verified that `strict: true` really does enable every sub-flag in TypeScript 6.0.3 — passing each explicitly adds 0 errors: `noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitThis`, `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictBindCallApply`, `strictPropertyInitialization`, `strictBuiltinIteratorReturn`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables`. So there is no hidden strict-family gap; the codebase is genuinely null-aware, and the multi-week `strictNullChecks` migration the audit spec warns about does not apply here.
findings.evidence:
tsconfig.json — current checking flags
  8      "strict": true,
  9      "noUnusedLocals": true,
 10      "noUnusedParameters": true,
 11      "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true,
 12      "isolatedModules": true,

$ npx tsc --noEmit --<flag>        (error counts, baseline 0)
  noImplicitReturns              0      strictNullChecks             0
  noUncheckedSideEffectImports   0      strictFunctionTypes          0
  allowUnreachableCode false     0      strictBindCallApply          0
  allowUnusedLabels false        0      strictPropertyInitialization 0
  noImplicitAny                  0      strictBuiltinIteratorReturn  0
  noImplicitThis                 0      useUnknownInCatchVariables   0
findings.verifierNote: Re-measured all four flags against the current tree, each on top of the existing config: `--noImplicitReturns`, `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports`, `--allowUnreachableCode false` and `--allowUnusedLabels false` each produce 0 errors, matching the finding exactly. tsconfig.json:8-12 confirms the current checking flags (`strict`, `noUnusedLocals`, `noUnusedParameters`, `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`, `isolatedModules`) and none of the four is present. This is a genuine `tsconfig-strictness-gap` with zero remediation cost - the honest 'be honest about the cost of strictness flags' caveat in the spec cuts in this finding's favour rather than against it. `low` is the right tier: nothing is broken, the value is a ratchet that makes the first violation fail CI instead of landing silently.
findings.reachability: n/a - a configuration gap, not a code path. No current source violates any of the four.
findings.blastRadius: Whole program (tsconfig.json applies to all 86 files in `include`), but zero files need changing.
findings.suggestedPatch: Add to tsconfig.json compilerOptions alongside :9-11: `"noImplicitReturns": true, "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true, "allowUnreachableCode": false, "allowUnusedLabels": false`. Risk: none measured today; `noUncheckedSideEffectImports` is the only one that can start failing on a dependency bump (a package whose side-effect-only import stops resolving), so land it in its own commit if CI stability matters.

plain.title: Four checking options are off even though enabling them costs nothing today
plain.what: Four additional compiler checks are not switched on, and each of them reports zero problems against the current code.
plain.whyItMatters: They are free protection that is simply not being taken, and nothing prevents future code from introducing the problems they catch.
plain.whatToDo: Enable all four now; there is no remediation work at all.

findings.title: skipLibCheck: true masks an unresolved module in the @google/genai type surface (legitimate, but undocumented)
findings.description:
`skipLibCheck: true` is set. Measured what it hides: `npx tsc --noEmit --skipLibCheck false` produces exactly 2 errors, both in `node_modules`, none in source:

1. `node_modules/@google/genai/dist/genai.d.ts(1,29)` — cannot resolve `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`. This is an **optional** peer dependency of `@google/genai` (`peerDependenciesMeta: { "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk": { optional: true } }`) and is deliberately not installed.
2. `node_modules/@testing-library/jest-dom/types/jest.d.ts(1,23)` — cannot find type definitions for `jest`, which this project correctly does not have (it uses Vitest).

So `skipLibCheck` is load-bearing, not laziness — this is the "compatibility lock-in" pattern the audit spec says to isolate rather than rip out, and the recommendation is NOT to turn it off. Blast radius today is nil: the unresolved `Client` type is only referenced by `@google/genai`'s MCP tool helper, and the app imports only `GoogleGenAI`, `Chat`, `Type` and `Modality` (`src/lib/ai/client.ts:1`, `chat.ts:1`, `schemas.ts:1`, `tts.ts:1`), none of which touch it.

The real gap is that this is undocumented. Every other non-obvious setting in this repo carries a comment explaining why (see `vite.config.ts:5-8` and `:13-15`, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml:15-16`), but `skipLibCheck` does not — so a future contributor cannot tell whether it is deliberate insulation or an unexamined default, and will not know that flipping it breaks the build for a reason unrelated to their change. Correct behaviour: add a comment naming both causes, and re-run `--skipLibCheck false` on dependency bumps so newly-introduced third-party type drift is noticed rather than permanently silenced.
findings.evidence:
tsconfig.json
 14      "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
 15      "skipLibCheck": true,          // <-- no comment explaining what it is insulating
 16      "noEmit": true,

$ npx tsc --noEmit --skipLibCheck false   (2 errors, both third-party)
  node_modules/@google/genai/dist/genai.d.ts(1,29): error TS2307:
    Cannot find module '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js'
  node_modules/@testing-library/jest-dom/types/jest.d.ts(1,23): error TS2688:
    Cannot find type definition file for 'jest'

@google/genai package.json: peerDependenciesMeta.@modelcontextprotocol/sdk.optional === true
findings.verifierNote: Re-measured: `npx tsc --noEmit --skipLibCheck false` produces exactly the 2 errors claimed, both under node_modules and none in source - `@google/genai/dist/genai.d.ts(1,29) TS2307` for the unresolved `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`, and `@testing-library/jest-dom/types/jest.d.ts(1,23) TS2688` for the absent `jest` types (this project uses Vitest). tsconfig.json:15 confirms `"skipLibCheck": true` with no adjacent comment, while other non-obvious settings in the repo are commented. This is precisely the spec's 'compatibility lock-in' pattern and the finding correctly does NOT recommend turning it off; the audit-author note that a suppression-with-a-reason is still a finding whose recommendation is documentation-and-isolation is what keeps it in scope. `low` is correct.
findings.reachability: n/a - both suppressed errors are in third-party declaration files. The unresolved MCP `Client` type is only referenced by @google/genai's tool helper, which this app never imports.
findings.blastRadius: Whole program, but zero source files are affected; the only cost is a future contributor's inability to tell deliberate insulation from an unexamined default.

plain.title: A skipped library-checking option is load-bearing but undocumented
plain.what: The build skips type-checking of third-party declaration files. Disabling that skip produces exactly two failures, both in third-party packages and neither in this project's code.
plain.whyItMatters: The setting is correct and should stay, but nobody reading it can tell whether it is masking a real problem.
plain.whatToDo: Keep the setting and add a short comment recording exactly what it hides.

findings.title: Vitest and jest-dom globals are in the type scope of production source, not just tests
findings.description:
`"types": ["vite/client", "vitest/globals", "@testing-library/jest-dom"]` applies to the whole program, and `node_modules/vitest/globals.d.ts` uses `declare global` to publish `describe`, `it`, `test`, `expect`, `vi`, `beforeEach`, `afterEach` and friends. Combined with `include: ["src", "vite.config.ts"]` — a single program covering all 86 source files, of which 21 are tests — this means a production module such as `src/lib/storage/repo.ts` or a React component can reference `vi.fn()` or `expect(...)` and `tsc --noEmit` will accept it. The failure only appears in the browser at runtime as `vi is not defined`, and it ships in the bundle.

ESLint does not backstop this either: `no-undef` is explicitly disabled for TypeScript files by the `tseslint` recommended preset (confirmed via `--print-config`: `no-undef: [0, {"typeof": false}]`), on the assumption that the compiler catches undefined identifiers — which here it does not, because the globals are genuinely declared.

Correct behaviour: split the program so test globals are scoped to test files — either a `tsconfig.test.json` covering `**/*.test.ts(x)` and `src/test/**` that adds `vitest/globals` and `@testing-library/jest-dom`, with the root config dropping them; or drop `globals: true` from `vite.config.ts:11` and import `describe`/`it`/`expect`/`vi` explicitly in tests. Adoption cost is moderate: the second option touches all 21 test files (mechanical, one import line each) and would require dropping `"vitest/globals"` from `types` in the same commit. Severity is Low because no production file currently does this — the finding is that nothing prevents it.
findings.evidence:
tsconfig.json

 18    },
 19    "include": ["src", "vite.config.ts"]      // one program: 86 files, 21 of them tests

node_modules/vitest/globals.d.ts
  1  declare global {
  2    let suite: typeof import('vitest')['suite']
  4    let describe: typeof import('vitest')['describe']
  5    let it: typeof import('vitest')['it']
  8    let expect: typeof import('vitest')['expect']
 11    let vi: typeof import('vitest')['vitest']

$ npx eslint --print-config src/lib/storage/repo.ts  ->  no-undef  [0,{"typeof":false}]
findings.verifierNote: Every load-bearing claim re-verified independently. tsconfig.json:17 is `"types": ["vite/client", "vitest/globals", "@testing-library/jest-dom"]` and :19 is `"include": ["src", "vite.config.ts"]` - one program spanning production and test files. node_modules/vitest/globals.d.ts opens with `declare global {` and publishes `suite`, `test`, `describe`, `it`, `expect`, `assert`, `vitest`, `vi`, `beforeAll`, `afterAll`, `beforeEach` as ambient `let` bindings, so those identifiers are in scope for every file in the program, production included. I also re-ran the ESLint backstop check: `npx eslint --print-config src/lib/storage/repo.ts` reports `no-undef: [0, {"typeof": false}]`, so nothing catches a stray `vi.fn()` in a production module - it would typecheck, lint clean, and fail only in the browser as `vi is not defined`, inside the shipped bundle. `low` is right because no production file currently does this; the finding is that nothing prevents it.
findings.reachability: Latent by construction: the hole is open on all 65 non-test source files. No current production file references a test global (verified by the clean typecheck plus the fact that the app runs).
findings.blastRadius: Whole program. The remediation touches 21 test files (one import line each) or adds one tsconfig.test.json.
findings.suggestedPatch: Lowest-churn option: keep `globals: true` for the test runner but scope the ambient types - drop `"vitest/globals"` and `"@testing-library/jest-dom"` from tsconfig.json:17, add a `tsconfig.test.json` that extends the root, re-adds those two entries and sets `"include": ["src/**/*.test.ts", "src/**/*.test.tsx", "src/test/**"]`, and point the `typecheck` script at both. Risk: the two programs overlap on the files each test imports, so keep `skipLibCheck` and expect slightly slower typecheck; the alternative (drop `globals: true` from vite.config.ts:11 and import explicitly) is mechanical but touches all 21 test files and must land in the same commit.

plain.title: Test-runner globals are visible to production code as well as tests
plain.what: The ambient type definitions for the test runner and its matchers are applied to the whole project rather than just the test files.
plain.whyItMatters: Production code can reference test-only globals and compile cleanly; it would only fail once running in a browser.
plain.whatToDo: Scope the test type definitions to the test files.

refuted.title: The 200-book scale test hand-builds rows and bypasses parseGoodreadsCsv, the only validation in the feature
refuted.correctedUnderstanding: No type weakness exists here. The 200-row fixture at goodreadsImport.test.tsx:101-106 contains no cast: `status: 'Want to Read' as const` is literal-type narrowing (the opposite of a bypass), and `isbn13` / `dateRead` are declared optional at goodreads.ts:7-8, so omitting them makes the fixture a genuinely valid `GoodreadsRow` - not a lying fixture missing required fields. `importGoodreadsRows(rows: GoodreadsRow[])` (useLibrary.tsx:128-129) receives in-test literals, not external data, so the category boundary-without-validation ('external data typed as T via assertion or any') does not apply: nothing crosses a boundary in this test. Bypassing parseGoodreadsCsv in a test whose stated subject is 'imports a large library without any AI cost' is correct unit-test scoping, not a defect - and the parser IS exercised by the file's other three tests at :44, :65 and :88. The residual claims (the title|author dedupe key at useLibrary.tsx:132-133 untested for case/whitespace variants; the openlibrary ISBN branch at goodreads.ts:121-122 covered by one row) are accurate but are pure test-coverage observations with no type-system component, and belong to a coverage audit rather than this one.

refuted.title: Cover lookups declare `Promise<string | null>` but can also reject — the signature lies to new callers
refuted.correctedUnderstanding: The claimed type weakness does not exist. src/lib/covers/googleBooks.ts:1 and src/lib/covers/openLibrary.ts:1 both declare `Promise<string | null>`, and that type is ACCURATE for every value either function ever resolves with: googleBooks returns `url.replace(...)` at :24 or `null` at :28; openLibrary returns a template string or `null` at :8. TypeScript's `Promise<T>` parameter describes the fulfilment value only - the language has no checked exceptions and no way to express rejection in a return type - so 'the signature lies' is a claim about a guarantee the type never made and that no TypeScript signature can make. Under this rule every fetch-calling function in every TS codebase is a finding. Verification criterion 4 also fails outright: there is no achievable replacement. The finding's own suggested fix ('catch internally and genuinely return string | null') would break the design the suite pins - src/lib/covers/index.test.ts:53-61 stubs fetch to throw and asserts `fetchCover` falls through to `placeholderCover`, which works only because the provider functions propagate. The alternative fix ('make it explicit in JSDoc') is prose, not type safety. Two further defects in the finding: the category `js-ambiguous-return` is defined by the spec as JavaScript-only and these are .ts files under `strict: true`; and the one concrete throw it names (`url.replace` on a non-string) is already counted as F085. Nothing survives that is not either inexpressible or double-counted.

refuted.title: DialogProps.size is a raw string interpolated into className, and no test ever passes a non-default value
refuted.correctedUnderstanding: The cited line contains no type weakness. Dialog.test.tsx:11 is `<Dialog open title="Add a book" onClose={onClose}>` inside the Harness — an omitted optional prop, not an assertion, an any, or a lying fixture (the spec's 'lying types in test fixtures are high-value' note applies to fixtures that assert an incomplete shape as complete; nothing is asserted here). The actual defect the finding describes — `size?: string` at Dialog.tsx:11-12 interpolated into className at Dialog.tsx:35 — is on the producer file and is already counted as F123 in this same batch, with the same two call sites (ConfirmDialog.tsx:43, ApiKeyDialog.tsx:38) and the same fix. What is left over is 'no test exercises a non-default size', which is a test-coverage observation, outside this audit's scope and not a duplicate-worthy finding on its own. Refuted as a test-side mirror of F123.

refuted.title: The subscribe/emit store shape is hand-rolled twice, byte-identically, in `toastStore.ts` and `lib/ai/apiKey.ts`
refuted.correctedUnderstanding: Read both files in full. The duplication is real (toastStore.ts:10 `const listeners = new Set<() => void>()`, :12-14 `emit()`, :39-44 `subscribeToToasts`; apiKey.ts:3 `listeners`, :5-7 `notify()`, :30-35 `subscribeToApiKey`) but it is not a type-safety defect and does not meet the spec's definition of `generic-opportunity` ('duplicated TYPE DEFINITIONS across modules that could collapse to a single generic'). Zero type definitions are duplicated: the only shared type is the builtin `() => void`, and toastStore's sole declared type (`ToastMessage`, :3-7) has no counterpart in apiKey.ts. The proposed `createStore<T>` has no `T` to bind on the apiKey side, because apiKey.ts holds no snapshot state at all - `getApiKey()` (:9-12) reads `localStorage` on every call, so there is nothing for `useSyncExternalStore` to snapshot except a derived value. What actually overlaps is a listener Set plus a 1-line for-loop, ~6 lines total across 2 modules; extracting a generic store for that is the speculative abstraction the project's own rules forbid. The finding's own text concedes 'the types are correct in both... this is a duplication finding, not a soundness one'.

refuted.title: Two non-null assertions on array indexing that are no-ops today and would become the only unguarded spots if `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` were enabled
refuted.correctedUnderstanding: Both assertions are present (useFocusTrap.ts:47 `const first = items[0]!;`, :48 `const last = items[items.length - 1]!;`) but they are correct as written and the proposed fix does not improve them. Line 45 (`if (items.length === 0) return;`) proves both accesses in-range, which the established baseline already records. Under the current tsconfig (`strict: true`, no `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`) they are no-ops; under `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` they would become load-bearing and STILL correct - and TypeScript has no control-flow analysis that can narrow `items[items.length - 1]`, so the suggested alternatives do not remove the assertion: `items.at(-1)` returns `HTMLElement | undefined` and `const [first] = items` is likewise `HTMLElement | undefined`. The 'inconsistent with line 26' argument does not hold either: `focusable()[0]?.focus()` at :26 sits in a scope with no length guard and makes a single optional call, so `?.` is the right idiom there and `!` is the right idiom here. A guarded, provably-true non-null assertion is not what the `non-null-assertion` category targets ('crashes at runtime if the assumption is wrong' - this assumption cannot be wrong).

refuted.title: AiError.kind carries the full union on every instance, so MissingKeyError does not narrow its own tag and per-kind payloads have nowhere to live
refuted.correctedUnderstanding: The pattern is present as described (errors.ts:13 `readonly kind: AiErrorKind` as a base-class parameter property; MissingKeyError at :22-26 always passes 'missing-key') but it is the correct type at every existing consumer, and the spec's bar for a discriminated-union finding - a concrete call site where a wrong value could arrive and compile - is not met. I grepped every consumer: the only tag branch in the repo is AppShell.tsx:49 `if (aiError.kind === 'missing-key' || aiError.kind === 'invalid-key')`, and the value it inspects comes from `toAiError(error)` (errors.ts:45), whose declared return is the BASE `AiError` - so the full union is genuinely the right type there and refining a subclass would change nothing. The only subclass is `MissingKeyError`, constructed once at client.ts:11 and immediately `throw`n, so its static type is erased at the catch; there is no site where narrowing is wanted and unavailable. TypeScript already rejects a renamed member at :49 as a no-overlap comparison, which the finding concedes. The remaining argument - that per-kind payloads have nowhere to live except `cause: unknown` - is explicitly conditional ('if per-kind data is ever needed') and no consumer in src/ reads `cause`; recommending a class-to-union restructure for a payload nobody consumes is speculative design, not a defect.

refuted.title: Summary.model is a bare string, so nothing type-checks that a persisted model id is a real one
refuted.correctedUnderstanding: The pattern is present (types.ts:64 `model: string`, with the doc comment at :63 naming 'legacy' as the migration sentinel) but the recommended narrowing would introduce the very defect this audit exists to find, so this should not be actioned. `Summary.model` is a PERSISTED HISTORICAL PROVENANCE field: it records which model produced a stored summary, and models.ts's own comment says 'A Google rename is a one-line change here'. The moment that rename happens, every already-persisted summary in IndexedDB still carries the OLD id - which would no longer be a member of `(typeof MODELS)[keyof typeof MODELS] | 'legacy'`. Narrowing the field therefore makes the declared type false about the data on the read path, i.e. a lying type, which is strictly worse than the current honest `string`. The branded-type bar is also not met: I grepped every write (chat.ts:14, quiz.ts:11, recommend.ts:25, summarize.ts:39/47/63/89, tts.ts:19 all pass `MODELS.*` to the SDK, not to this field; the only writes to `Summary.model` are summarize.ts's own value, migrate.ts:131 `'legacy'`, and three test fixtures) and there is no read anywhere in src/ - so there is no call site where a wrong value could arrive and be consumed, and no adjacent same-typed parameter to swap it with. The project invariant 'model IDs live only in src/lib/ai/models.ts' is about where IDs are AUTHORED, which migrate.ts:131 does not violate ('legacy' is not a model id).
